story.title: Juno and Clover the Bee
story.subtitle: A buzzy bedtime trip to a honeybee hive

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Amber Bead Wakes Up
chapters.text:
Juno sat on her bedroom floor. Her dinosaurs stood in a line. Rex the triceratops stood tall. Spike the stegosaurus stood taller. All ready for bed.

Something glowed under her pillow. It was a tiny golden bead. **Amber** is old, hard, see-through stuff. It comes from sticky tree juice that turned hard like glass.

The bead began to hum. **BZZZZZ!**

Juno picked it up. Crack! A tiny door popped open. Out buzzed a friendly bee.

"Hello, Juno! I'm Clover," said the bee. "Did you know bees buzzed around even when dinosaurs stomped the earth?"

Juno's eyes went wide. "Dinosaurs AND bees?"

"Yes! Want to see where bees live?" Clover asked.

"Yes, yes, YES!" said Juno.

Whoooosh! The amber glowed bright. Juno shrank down, down, down — until she was bee-sized herself.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Busy Buzzing Home
chapters.text:
They landed at a huge, buzzing hive. Bees zoomed in and out, busy as can be.

"This hive can hold up to eighty thousand bees," said Clover. "That's like one giant, buzzing family."

"There's one queen," Clover said. "She's the mom of them all."

Juno peeked inside. A big bee walked slowly, with other bees patting her gently.

"The queen can lay about two thousand eggs every single day," said Clover.

Juno counted on her fingers. "One, two, three... that's SO much counting!"

Most bees are girls, called workers. A few are boys, called **drones** — they help make new bees, but they don't make honey.

"Can I help find the queen?" Juno asked.

She looked for the biggest bee, the one everybody bowed to. "There she is!" Juno shouted.

"You found her!" said Clover. "Great job, Juno!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Jobs for Everyone
chapters.text:
Worker bees never sit still.

Some clean tiny rooms. Some guard the front door, buzzing at strangers. Some fly far away to find flowers.

"Every worker bee does every job, when it's her turn," said Clover.

Juno wanted a job too. "Can I be a flower-finder?"

"Perfect job for you," said Clover. "Climb on my back!"

Juno hopped on. Up, up, up they flew, over the grass, toward a field of yellow flowers.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Flying to the Flowers
chapters.text:
The flowers smelled sweet. Bees landed on each one, sipping something called **nectar** — sweet juice flowers make just for bees.

"Bees use it to make honey," said Clover.

Juno looked closer at a bee's face. "Whoa, your eyes are funny!"

"I have five eyes," said Clover. "Two big ones see shapes and colors. Three tiny ones on top just feel sunshine."

Juno counted them. "One, two, three, four, five! Five eyes!"

To make just one jar of honey, bees visit about two million flowers. Juno's mouth fell open. "TWO MILLION?!"

"Bees work together," said Clover. "That's called teamwork."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Waggle Wiggle Dance
chapters.text:
Back at the hive, a bee wiggled in a funny circle.

"That's the waggle dance," said Clover. "A scientist named Karl von Frisch figured out bees dance to show each other where the best flowers are."

Juno giggled. "Like a treasure map, but wiggly!"

"Exactly," said Clover.

Juno tried her own wiggle dance, right there in the hive. She wiggled left. She wiggled right. She flapped her arms like wings.

The bees buzzed louder, like they were laughing.

"I found a great flower too!" Juno said. "It's called MY BED, and it's very comfy!"

Clover laughed so hard she almost fell off a honeycomb.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Six-Sided Rooms
chapters.text:
Inside the hive were tiny rooms, all shaped the same.

"Those are **hexagons**," said Clover. "Six-sided shapes. Bees build with them because they hold the most honey and use the least wax."

Juno thought of her dinosaur blocks at home. She loved building shapes!

"Can hexagons fit together with no gaps?" she asked.

"Try it and see," said Clover.

Juno pretended to lay six little sticks in a circle. They fit together perfectly, snug as puzzle pieces.

"IT FITS!" Juno cheered.

"Bees are very good builders," said Clover, smiling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Keeping Cozy in Winter
chapters.text:
Pretend snow began falling outside, just for Clover's story.

"On cold days, bees squeeze together in a ball," said Clover. "They shiver their wings to make heat, keeping the hive warm as a cozy bath."

Juno hugged herself. "Like a bee blanket!"

"Exactly like that," said Clover. "Nobody gets cold, because everybody helps."

One tiny bee landed near Juno. "She'll only make a tiny speck of honey her whole life," said Clover. "But with all her sisters together, that makes a whole jar."

Juno waved gently at the bee, careful not to touch. "Thank you for the honey," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Oldest Honey Jar
chapters.text:
"Did you know honey never goes bad?" said Clover. "Grown-ups found honey jars painted by people long, long ago, and the honey inside was still good to eat!"

Juno's jaw dropped. "Still yummy? After THAT many years?"

"Still yummy," said Clover, nodding.

Bees also help make lots of food people eat, like apples, blueberries, and almonds. "One out of every three yummy bites comes because of bees," said Clover.

Juno thought of her own breakfast. "Thank you, bees!" she said.

The amber bead began to glow again. "Time for home," said Clover.

Whooosh! Juno grew back to her own size, right on her bedroom floor. Her dinosaurs still stood in their line.

Clover landed on the amber bead, tucked safely in Juno's hand.

"Buzz well, Juno," Clover whispered. "Goodnight."

story.ending_line: Buzz well, Juno. Goodnight.

true_facts.text: Bees were buzzing around even when dinosaurs stomped the earth, and we know because tiny bees got stuck in **amber** long, long ago.
A beehive has one queen bee, lots of girl worker bees, and some boy bees called **drones**.
A queen bee can lay about **two thousand eggs** every single day.
One beehive can hold up to **eighty thousand bees**.
Worker bees take turns doing every job, like cleaning, guarding, and flying out to find flowers.
A bee has **five eyes** — two big ones for seeing colors, and three tiny ones for feeling sunshine.
Bees visit about **two million flowers** just to make one jar of honey.
A scientist named **Karl von Frisch** figured out that bees do a wiggly **waggle dance** to show each other where the best flowers are.
Honeycomb rooms are six-sided shapes called **hexagons**, which hold the most honey using the least wax.
On cold days, bees squeeze together and shiver to keep the hive warm.
One bee only makes a tiny speck of honey in her whole life.
Honey found in jars from long, long ago was still good to eat.
Bees help make about **one out of every three** yummy bites of food people eat.

new_recurring.name: Clover the Bee
new_recurring.rule: A tiny bee who lives inside a glowing amber bead. When Juno holds the bead, it hums and Clover appears to take her on a true, real-science adventure, always returning her home safely the same size she started.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Juno shrinks back to her normal size on her bedroom floor, tucking the glowing amber bead with Clover inside into her hand while her lined-up dinosaur toys stand watch.

fact_pack.summary: Bees are flying insects living almost everywhere flowers grow, and a honeybee hive works together like one giant family. Beyond making honey, bees pollinate much of the food people eat, and scientists still study how these tiny insects talk and find their way home.

facts.text: A honeybee colony usually has one queen, tens of thousands of female worker bees, and a smaller number of male drones.
A healthy queen bee can lay up to about 2,000 eggs a day during the busy spring season.
Worker bees are all female and take turns doing every job in the hive, from cleaning cells to guarding the entrance to flying out to find flowers.
A drone's only job is to mate with a queen, and hives push drones out before winter because they cannot forage or sting to help defend the colony.
Scientists have described roughly 20,000 species of bees around the world, and only a few of them, like the honeybee, make the honey people eat.
Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch discovered that honeybees perform a 'waggle dance' to tell each other a flower's direction and distance.
Karl von Frisch won the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973 for figuring out how bees communicate through dance and scent.
One worker honeybee makes only about a twelfth of a teaspoon of honey in her entire lifetime.
Bees in a colony together may visit roughly two million flowers to gather enough nectar to make just one pound of honey.
Because honey has very little water and is naturally acidic, sealed pots of honey found in ancient Egyptian tombs are still edible thousands of years later.
A bee has five eyes in total: two large compound eyes for seeing shapes and colors, plus three tiny simple eyes on top of its head for sensing light.
A honeybee's wings beat about 200 times every second, and that fast flapping is what makes the buzzing sound people hear.
Only female bees have a stinger, and a honeybee worker's stinger is barbed so it stays in mammal skin, which means she dies soon after she stings.
Bees and other pollinators help produce roughly one out of every three bites of food humans eat, including apples, blueberries, and almonds.
Each spring, truckloads of honeybee hives are shipped into California to pollinate its almond orchards.
Beekeepers began widely reporting Colony Collapse Disorder in 2006, when many adult worker bees mysteriously left their hives and did not return.
Researchers link colony losses to several causes together: mites, disease, pesticides, and lost flowering habitat.
Honeycomb cells are built in a six-sided hexagon shape because it lets bees store the most honey while using the least amount of wax.
On cold days bees cluster and shiver their flight muscles to keep the hive near 95°F (35°C).
Bees preserved in amber roughly 100 million years old show bees lived alongside dinosaurs.
Egyptian wall art from around 2400 BC shows beekeepers collecting honeycomb, among the oldest farming records.
A single honeybee hive can hold 20,000 to 80,000 bees at the height of summer.

timeline.event: Bees appear in the fossil record, preserved in amber
Egyptian art shows people keeping bees and collecting honey
Karl von Frisch wins the Nobel Prize for decoding the bee waggle dance
Colony Collapse Disorder is first widely reported in the United States

story.title: Omar and the Bicycle That Traveled Through Time
story.subtitle: A bedtime ride through two hundred years of wheels

chapters.heading: Stop 1: The Running Machine (1817)
chapters.text:
Omar was doing his best BMX tricks at the skate park, way past bedtime. The streetlights buzzed. His tires went **WHIRRR** on the ramp.

Then his front wheel bumped something small and metal. A rusty old bell, half-buried in the dirt.

He picked it up. It gave one soft **DING** — and glowed bright green.

"Whoa," Omar whispered, and the bell wobbled in his hand like it was waking up.

"Hello!" said a tiny voice. "I'm Ting. Want to see where bikes came from?"

Before Omar could answer, the world spun — **WHOOOOSH** — and he landed in muddy German countryside, in the year **1817**.

A man was pushing a wooden two-wheeler with his feet, no pedals at all. "I'm Karl von Drais," he said proudly. "I call it my running machine!"

It even had handlebars, just like Omar's BMX. "That's basically a balance bike," Omar laughed. "I could do that in my sleep!"

chapters.heading: Stop 2: The Boneshaker (1860s)
chapters.text:
Ting the bell jingled, and the ground turned to cobblestones. France, this time.

A man named Pierre Michaux was bolting something onto a front wheel. "Pedals!" he announced. "Now your feet push, and the wheel turns itself!"

Another man, Pierre Lallement, rode past, bouncing hard over every bump. "They call it the boneshaker," he groaned, "because it shakes your bones on these rough streets!"

Omar winced. "That sounds worse than rolling over a curb without bending your knees."

He hopped on for one wobbly loop, rattling the whole way. "BUMPY!" he yelled, laughing.

Ting chimed in. "Lallement even got a paper from the government in **1866**, saying the pedal idea was officially his."

"Nice," said Omar. "First guy to patent a bike. That's like landing the first trick ever."

chapters.heading: Stop 3: The Giant Wheel (1870s)
chapters.text:
The next **DING** dropped them somewhere strange. A bicycle rolled by with a front wheel taller than Omar himself, and a tiny back wheel trailing behind.

"It's called a penny-farthing," said Ting, "named after two old coins — one big, one small, just like the wheels."

"One turn of the pedal and you fly super fast," Ting added. "But sit up that high, and if you stop too quick, you can tip right over the front. Riders called it 'taking a header.'"

Omar pictured faceplanting off a skate ramp and grinned. "I've taken a header off my BMX. Everyone's fine, you just dust off and try again."

A rider wobbled, caught his balance, and gave a thumbs up. No one was hurt — just a laugh and a muddy knee.

"See?" said Ting. "Totally fine. Just wobbly."

chapters.heading: Stop 4: The Safety Bicycle (1885)
chapters.text:
**DING!** Omar landed in England, in **1885**, in front of a bike with two wheels the same size. No giant front wheel at all.

"I'm John Kemp Starley," said a man, patting the frame. "I built the Rover Safety Bicycle. A chain connects the pedals to the back wheel, so you sit low and steady."

Omar rode it in one smooth circle. No tipping, no wobbling. "This feels like a real bike," he said. "This is basically my BMX's great-great-grandpa!"

"Exactly," said Ting. "Low and even wheels meant almost anyone could ride safely. It became the new standard, everywhere."

Omar tried a tiny bunny hop off the curb. The bike landed clean.

"Nailed it," he grinned.

chapters.heading: Stop 5: The Bouncy Tire (1888)
chapters.text:
Next stop: a workshop in Scotland, **1888**. A man knelt by a little tricycle, wrapping a rubber tube around the wheel and pumping it full of air.

"I'm John Boyd Dunlop," he said. "My son's ride was so bumpy, I built him an air-filled tire instead of solid rubber. Much smoother."

Omar pressed the tire with his thumb. It squished, then bounced right back. "That's basically the suspension on my bike," he said. "It soaks up the bumps."

"Exactly," said Ting. "His tire company grew into a tire brand you still see today, on bikes and cars."

Omar rolled the trike down the path. **SPLOOSH** went a puddle — and he barely felt the bump.

"Smooth," he said happily.

chapters.heading: Stop 6: The Golden Age (1890s)
chapters.text:
Ting rang twice, and suddenly the street was packed with bicycles — hundreds of them, bells jingling everywhere.

"This is the **Golden Age of Bicycles**," said Ting. "In the 1890s, millions of people bought bikes, all across Europe and America."

A woman rode past in loose, comfy pants instead of a long skirt. "Long skirts used to get caught in the gears," Ting explained. "So riders started wearing roomier outfits called bloomers instead."

"A famous woman named Susan B. Anthony said bicycles gave women more freedom to go places on their own than almost anything else," said Ting.

Omar thought about riding wherever he wanted, whenever he wanted. "That's huge," he said. "Bikes basically gave people wheels for freedom."

chapters.heading: Stop 7: The Bike Shop Brothers (1890s, Dayton)
chapters.text:
**DING!** Now they stood in a small shop in Dayton, Ohio. Two brothers were fixing a bicycle wheel, spokes gleaming.

"I'm Wilbur," said one. "And I'm Orville," said the other. "We fix bikes here — light metal tubes, strong spoked wheels."

"These guys built bikes," said Ting, "but soon they'd use those same tricks — light frames, spinning wheels — to build something way bigger."

"Like what?" asked Omar.

"In **1903**," said Ting, "they built the first airplane that really flew."

Omar's jaw dropped. "Wait — bike guys invented FLYING?"

"Pretty much," said Ting. "Turns out wheels teach you a lot about balance."

Omar spun a bike wheel just to watch it blur. "No way," he whispered, grinning.

chapters.heading: Stop 8: Gears and the Big Race (1903–1930s)
chapters.text:
The bell rang again, and Omar found himself beside a long, winding road, racers zooming by on bikes.

"This race started in **1903**," said Ting. "It's called the **Tour de France**. Today it's about **3,500 kilometers** — that's longer than riding across a whole bunch of states — and it takes almost three weeks."

"Three weeks of pedaling?" Omar gasped. "My legs would fall off."

"By the **1930s**," Ting added, "bikes got gears called derailleurs, little gadgets that shift the chain so climbing hills is easier."

Omar imagined shifting gears up the big skate park ramp. "That would help so much," he laughed, pedaling in place just to feel it.

chapters.heading: Stop 9: Back to the Skate Park
chapters.text:
One last **DING**, and Omar landed right back on the ramp, bell warm in his hand.

"In the **1970s**," said Ting, "riders in California built bikes with thick, bumpy tires for rough dirt trails. Mountain bikes."

"And around the same time," Ting went on, "other riders built small, tough bikes for tricks and dirt jumps, like yours. They're called BMX bikes."

Omar looked down at his own bike. "So my bike is basically history on wheels."

"There are over a **billion** bikes in the world now," said Ting. "More than any other kind of ride. In places like the Netherlands and Denmark, some cities even have more bikes than cars."

Omar clipped the glowing bell onto his handlebars. It gave one last happy **DING**, then quietly went still and shiny, like it belonged there all along.

He wheeled his bike home under the stars, bell gleaming.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Omar. Ring and ride, and dream of wheels.

true_facts.text: In **1817**, a man named **Karl von Drais** built a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals, steered by handlebars.
In the 1860s, **Pierre Michaux** added pedals straight onto the front wheel, making the bumpy **boneshaker**.
**Pierre Lallement** got official credit for a pedal bike design in the United States in **1866**.
The **penny-farthing** had a giant front wheel and a tiny back wheel, named after two different-sized coins.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky — a sudden stop could tip the rider over the front, called 'taking a header.'
In **1885**, **John Kemp Starley** built the **Safety Bicycle**, with two even wheels and a chain, much safer to ride.
In **1888**, **John Boyd Dunlop** invented the air-filled tire, making rides much smoother.
In the 1890s, the **Golden Age of Bicycles** saw millions of bikes sold, and riders started wearing comfier clothes called bloomers.
**Wilbur and Orville Wright** ran a bicycle shop before using bike-building tricks to build the first airplane in **1903**.
The **Tour de France** race started in **1903** and covers about **3,500 kilometers** across France.
**BMX bikes**, small and tough for tricks, became popular in the United States in the **1970s**.
Today there are more than a **billion** bicycles in the world, more than any other kind of ride.

fact_pack.summary: Bicycles evolved over 200 years from a wooden walking machine with no pedals to today's lightweight, geared bikes ridden by billions of people. Along the way inventors added pedals, chains, air-filled tires, and gears, making bikes faster, safer, and more comfortable.

facts.text: In 1817, German inventor Karl von Drais built the 'Laufmaschine' or 'running machine,' a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals that riders pushed along with their feet.
Von Drais's invention was nicknamed the 'draisine' or 'hobby horse' and was steered with handlebars, much like a modern bike.

In the 1860s, French makers Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement added pedals directly to the front wheel, creating the 'velocipede,' nicknamed the 'boneshaker' for its rough ride on cobblestone streets.
Pierre Lallement patented a pedal-driven bicycle design in the United States in 1866.
In the 1870s, the 'penny-farthing' bicycle appeared, with a giant front wheel (sometimes taller than a person) and a tiny back wheel, letting riders go faster with one pedal turn.
Penny-farthings were named after two British coins of very different sizes, the large penny and the small farthing.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky because the rider sat high above the front wheel and could be thrown headfirst in a sudden stop, a fall nicknamed 'taking a header.'
In 1885, Englishman John Kemp Starley invented the 'Rover Safety Bicycle,' with two similarly sized wheels and a chain driving the back wheel, much closer to modern bikes.
The safety bicycle's lower, even wheels made it much easier and safer to ride than the penny-farthing, and it quickly became the standard design worldwide.
In 1888, Scottish inventor John Boyd Dunlop developed the practical pneumatic (air-filled) rubber tire, making bike rides much smoother than solid rubber tires.
Dunlop's tire company grew into the Dunlop Tyre brand, still famous today for tires on bikes and cars.
The 1890s bicycle craze, called the 'Golden Age of Bicycles,' saw millions of bikes sold across Europe and the United States.
Bicycles gave women new freedom to travel independently in the 1890s, and American reformer Susan B. Anthony said cycling 'has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world.'
Because long skirts were dangerous around bike gears and wheels, the bicycle craze helped popularize more practical clothing for women, including bloomers.
Wilbur and Orville Wright, who later invented the first successful airplane in 1903, ran a bicycle repair and manufacturing shop in Dayton, Ohio in the 1890s.
The Wright brothers used bicycle-building skills, like lightweight metal tubing and spoked wheels, to help design their early flying machines.
Multi-speed gear systems, called derailleurs, became common on bikes in the 1930s, letting riders shift gears to handle hills more easily.
The Tour de France, the world's most famous long-distance cycling race, began in 1903 and today covers about 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) across France over about three weeks.
BMX bikes, small and sturdy for tricks and dirt racing, became popular in the United States in the 1970s, inspired by motocross motorcycles.
Mountain bikes with wide, knobby tires were developed in the 1970s in Marin County, California, by riders who wanted to bike down rough dirt trails.
Today, an estimated one billion or more bicycles exist worldwide, more than any other kind of vehicle.
The Netherlands and Denmark are famous today for having more bicycles than cars in some cities, with wide bike lanes built for everyday cyclists.
Modern bicycles are made from lightweight materials like aluminum and carbon fiber, letting racing bikes weigh less than 8 kilograms (about 17 pounds).

story.title: Tom and the Bell Called Torque
story.subtitle: Two hundred years of wheels, in one long night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Running Machine (1817)
chapters.text:
Tom was elbow-deep in bike grease at 11:40 p.m., garage light buzzing overhead.

He'd found the frame at a yard sale — dented, rusted, perfect. His engineering teacher wanted a restoration project with a story attached. Tom wanted a project with actual gears.

The last part to clean was the bell. Its metal looked bent and hammered straight again, over and over. Under the rust, five scratched letters: TORQUE.

He flicked it. CLACK, not ding.

The garage light sank to a sick green, and the bell spoke in a voice like a chain pulling tight. "Finally. Someone with grease under their nails."

Tom dropped his rag. "You talk."

"I remember," Torque said. "Every bike I've ever hung on. Want to meet the first one?"

Before Tom could answer, the garage floor tilted like a launch ramp, and — WHOOOSH — he was standing on cobblestones in 1817, next to a man straddling two wooden wheels with no pedals at all.

"Karl von Drais," said Torque, swinging from the man's handlebar. "German inventor. Calls this his **Laufmaschine** — his 'running machine.'"

The man pushed off with his boots, scooting the wooden thing along like a kid on a scooter with no deck.

"No pedals? He's just running, sitting down," Tom said.

"In **1817**," Torque said, "that counted as flying."

People were calling it a hobby horse, steered with handlebars — same as Tom's own bike. The first part that still felt familiar.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Boneshaker (1860s, Paris)
chapters.text:
The next stop rattled Tom's teeth before he'd even landed.

He was standing on a Paris street in the 1860s, watching a man named Pierre Michaux pedal something that looked like von Drais's machine — except now the pedals bolted straight onto the front wheel.

"Pierre Lallement worked on it too," Torque said. "Together they built the **velocipede**. Riders call it the 'boneshaker.'"

Tom understood why the second the rider hit a cobblestone. The whole frame jolted, no springs, no cushion — straight up through the handlebars.

"Every bump goes right into your hands," Tom said, wincing in sympathy. "Nobody's fixed the ride yet."

"Give it time," said Torque.

A boy offered Tom the seat. Tom climbed on, pedaled the front wheel directly — no chain yet, your feet *were* the gears — and bounced down the block, laughing the whole rattling way.

"Lallement **patented** this pedal design in America, in 1866," Torque added. "Patented means he filed the paperwork that said: this idea is officially mine."

Tom hopped off, rubbing his wrists. "Somebody needs to put air in these wheels."

"Patience, Chief Mechanic," said Torque. "That's two chapters away."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Penny-Farthing (1870s)
chapters.text:
The next bike Tom saw made him laugh out loud.

It had a front wheel almost as tall as Tom, and a back wheel the size of a dinner plate.

"The **penny-farthing**," Torque said. "Named after two old British coins — a big one and a tiny one."

"Why so huge?" Tom asked.

"One turn of the pedals, way more distance covered," said Torque. "Bigger wheel, bigger stride."

A rider wobbled past, perched high above the front wheel like he was riding a unicycle with a seat bolted on top.

"Looks risky," Tom said.

"It was. Sudden stop, and the rider could pitch straight over the handlebars, headfirst. They called that 'taking a header.'"

As if summoned, the rider's wheel caught a stone. He tipped forward — and Tom lunged, grabbing the man's arm, steadying him before he hit the ground.

The rider laughed it off, dusting his coat. "Happens weekly, lad. Part of the thrill."

Tom exhaled. "Maybe make the wheels... closer to the same size?"

"Funny you should say that," said Torque.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Safety Bicycle (1885, England)
chapters.text:
They landed in an English workshop smelling of oil and metal shavings.

A man named John Kemp Starley was wheeling out something that made Tom's chest tighten with recognition — two wheels, the same size, and a chain looping from the pedals back to the rear wheel.

"The **Rover Safety Bicycle**," Torque said. "Built in **1885**."

Tom crouched by the chain. "This is it. This is basically my frame."

"Closest thing to modern yet," Torque agreed. "No more towering over the front wheel. No more headers."

Starley offered Tom a test ride. Tom pedaled a slow loop around the yard, feet low, balance easy, nothing underneath him trying to throw him over the bars.

"It's just... sensible," Tom said, grinning.

"Sensible sold millions," said Torque. "Everyone wanted one. The penny-farthing's big-wheel days were numbered."

Tom parked the bike by the workshop door, patted the chain once like he was shaking its hand, and gave Torque a look. "Okay. Now give these tires some air."

"Next stop," Torque said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Smooth Ride (1888, Belfast)
chapters.text:
The garage — or whatever this was now — smelled like rubber.

A Scottish veterinarian named John Boyd Dunlop was crouched over a child's tricycle, wrapping a rubber tube around the wheel and pumping it full of air.

"He's a vet," Torque explained. "Built this for his son's tricycle, so it wouldn't rattle him silly on the cobblestones."

"A **pneumatic tire**," Tom said slowly. "Air-filled. Like a cushion instead of solid rubber."

"Exactly, in **1888**," said Torque.

Dunlop let Tom push the tricycle down the path. It rolled almost silent, bouncing lightly over every crack instead of slamming through it.

"No more boneshaking," Tom said, delighted.

"His tire company grew into a name you'll recognize," Torque said. "Dunlop. Still on tires today — bikes, cars, the lot."

Tom crouched and pressed a thumb into the tire's side, feeling it give and spring back. An engineer's handshake with an invention.

"Finally," he said. "A bike that doesn't try to shake your fillings loose."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Golden Age (1890s)
chapters.text:
The street outside was suddenly packed with bicycles — hundreds of them, wheels flashing in the sun.

"The 1890s," Torque said. "Historians call it the **Golden Age of Bicycles**. Millions sold, all over Europe and America."

A woman rode past in a split skirt, steering confidently through the crowd, and waved at Tom like they were old friends.

"Bikes gave women somewhere to go, on their own," Torque said. "An American named Susan B. Anthony said cycling had **freed women** more than almost anything else."

"Why'd it matter so much?" Tom asked.

"Long skirts could catch in the gears and wheels," Torque said. "Dangerous. So people started wearing looser, practical clothes called **bloomers** — more like wide trousers than a skirt."

Tom watched the woman pedal off, laughing with a friend, both of them faster than anyone on foot could follow.

"That's not just a bike thing," Tom said. "That's a whole different kind of freedom."

"Most good inventions are," said Torque. "They just don't always look like it at first."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Two Brothers and a Gear (1890s–1930s)
chapters.text:
The next shop had bicycle frames hanging from every wall — and a sign reading WRIGHT CYCLE CO.

"Dayton, Ohio," Torque said. "Wilbur and Orville Wright ran a bike repair shop here in the **1890s**."

Tom ran a hand along a spoked wheel. "Wait — the Wright brothers? Airplane guys?"

"Same ones," said Torque. "They used lightweight metal tubing and spoked-wheel tricks from bike building to help design their first flying machine, in **1903**."

Tom grinned. "So planes owe bikes a favor."

The scene shifted again, years sliding past like gears clicking up a cassette. A pack of racers streamed by on a dusty road.

"The **Tour de France** — the world's biggest bike race — started in **1903** too," Torque said. "Today it's about **3,500 kilometers** across France, over three weeks."

"That's insane," Tom said. "How do you climb mountains on one gear?"

"You don't, not after the **1930s**," Torque said. "That's when **derailleurs** showed up — gear-changers that slide the chain between different-sized cogs, so riders can shift down for hills."

Tom flexed an imaginary shifter with his thumb. "Finally. The good stuff."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Dirt, Chrome, and Home
chapters.text:
The last stop smelled like dust and pine trees.

Tom knew this one before Torque said a word — fat, knobby tires, riders bombing down a dirt hill on bikes that looked bolted together from spare parts.

"**Marin County, California**," Torque said. "**1970s**. Riders wanted to bomb down rough trails, so they built bikes tough enough to take it. Mountain bikes."

"This is literally my bike," Tom said, grinning at the knobby tread.

"Around the same time, kids in the U.S. were building small, sturdy **BMX** bikes for tricks and dirt racing," Torque added. "Copied off motocross motorcycles."

Tom crouched to touch a tire, feeling the same deep tread as his own bike at home.

"There are over a **billion bicycles** on Earth now," Torque said. "More than any other vehicle. In places like the Netherlands and Denmark, some cities have more bikes than cars."

"And modern ones?" Tom asked.

"Carbon fiber, aluminum — a racing bike today can weigh under **eight kilograms**. Lighter than your backpack."

The dirt trail tilted, folded, and — CLICK — Tom was back in the garage, frame half-restored, bell warm in his palm.

He looked at TORQUE, scratched and ordinary again. "Same time tomorrow?"

"Depends," said Torque, "on whether you finish that chain."

Tom grinned and picked up his wrench.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, after school, he had a chain to finish.

fact_pack.summary: Bicycles evolved over 200 years from a wooden walking machine with no pedals to today's lightweight, geared bikes ridden by billions of people. Along the way inventors added pedals, chains, air-filled tires, and gears, making bikes faster, safer, and more comfortable.

facts.text: In 1817, German inventor Karl von Drais built the 'Laufmaschine' or 'running machine,' a wooden two-wheeler with no pedals that riders pushed along with their feet.
Von Drais's invention was nicknamed the 'draisine' or 'hobby horse' and was steered with handlebars, much like a modern bike.

In the 1860s, French makers Pierre Michaux and Pierre Lallement added pedals directly to the front wheel, creating the 'velocipede,' nicknamed the 'boneshaker' for its rough ride on cobblestone streets.
Pierre Lallement patented a pedal-driven bicycle design in the United States in 1866.
In the 1870s, the 'penny-farthing' bicycle appeared, with a giant front wheel (sometimes taller than a person) and a tiny back wheel, letting riders go faster with one pedal turn.
Penny-farthings were named after two British coins of very different sizes, the large penny and the small farthing.
Riding a penny-farthing was risky because the rider sat high above the front wheel and could be thrown headfirst in a sudden stop, a fall nicknamed 'taking a header.'
In 1885, Englishman John Kemp Starley invented the 'Rover Safety Bicycle,' with two similarly sized wheels and a chain driving the back wheel, much closer to modern bikes.
The safety bicycle's lower, even wheels made it much easier and safer to ride than the penny-farthing, and it quickly became the standard design worldwide.
In 1888, Scottish inventor John Boyd Dunlop developed the practical pneumatic (air-filled) rubber tire, making bike rides much smoother than solid rubber tires.
Dunlop's tire company grew into the Dunlop Tyre brand, still famous today for tires on bikes and cars.
The 1890s bicycle craze, called the 'Golden Age of Bicycles,' saw millions of bikes sold across Europe and the United States.
Bicycles gave women new freedom to travel independently in the 1890s, and American reformer Susan B. Anthony said cycling 'has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world.'
Because long skirts were dangerous around bike gears and wheels, the bicycle craze helped popularize more practical clothing for women, including bloomers.
Wilbur and Orville Wright, who later invented the first successful airplane in 1903, ran a bicycle repair and manufacturing shop in Dayton, Ohio in the 1890s.
The Wright brothers used bicycle-building skills, like lightweight metal tubing and spoked wheels, to help design their early flying machines.
Multi-speed gear systems, called derailleurs, became common on bikes in the 1930s, letting riders shift gears to handle hills more easily.
The Tour de France, the world's most famous long-distance cycling race, began in 1903 and today covers about 3,500 kilometers (2,175 miles) across France over about three weeks.
BMX bikes, small and sturdy for tricks and dirt racing, became popular in the United States in the 1970s, inspired by motocross motorcycles.
Mountain bikes with wide, knobby tires were developed in the 1970s in Marin County, California, by riders who wanted to bike down rough dirt trails.
Today, an estimated one billion or more bicycles exist worldwide, more than any other kind of vehicle.
The Netherlands and Denmark are famous today for having more bicycles than cars in some cities, with wide bike lanes built for everyday cyclists.
Modern bicycles are made from lightweight materials like aluminum and carbon fiber, letting racing bikes weigh less than 8 kilograms (about 17 pounds).

story.title: Sam and the Gecko Who Could Climb Anything
story.subtitle: A sticky-toed night tour of every wall-climber in the garden

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Gecko in the Night-Light
chapters.text:
Sam lay on his bedroom floor. He held his magnifying glass up high. Inside his bug jar sat a little roly-poly he found today.

"Hello, friend," Sam whispered. "You rolled into a ball. That was so cool."

The night-light on his dresser flickered. It flickered green, then gold, then green again. Sam sat up fast. "Lights don't DO that," he said.

CLICK! The little lizard shape on the night-light peeled right off the wall. It stretched out its toes. It blinked two big orange eyes.

"Finally!" said the lizard. "My name is Tiko. I'm a Tokay gecko. Want to see something sticky?"

Sam's mouth fell wide open. "You're REAL?"

"Real and ready," said Tiko. He walked straight up the window glass. Then he strolled across the ceiling, upside down, cool as anything.

"WHOOO!" Sam yelled, flopping onto his back to watch. "How do you DO that?"

"My toes have millions of tiny hairs," said Tiko. "So tiny, you'd need a special looking tool called a microscope just to see them. It makes small things look huge."

"Like my magnifying glass, but stronger?" Sam asked.

"Exactly like that," said Tiko. "Each tiny hair grabs onto bumps on the glass. Bumps so small your eyes can't even see them. It's not glue. My toes never get goopy."

Sam pressed his whole hand flat on his window. He pulled. Nothing happened. He fell right over backward, giggling. "Why can't I do it?"

"You don't have gecko toes," laughed Tiko. "But I can show you who does. Hold my tail. Tonight, we climb EVERYTHING."

Sam grabbed on tight. The glass began to glow. "STICKY FEET, HERE WE GO!" Sam shouted.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Peel Like Tape
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! The glow set them down on the backyard fence.

Tiko walked up the fence post like it was flat ground. "Watch my toes," he said. He lifted one toe. Then another. Then another, like peeling tape off a present.

"You're peeling your FEET?" Sam asked.

"That's how I let go," said Tiko. "My toes stick tight. But I peel them up, one by one, fast as a blink. No mess. No goo left behind, ever."

Sam tried peeling a sticker off his own hand, toe by toe. It did not work one bit. He laughed so hard he snorted.

A fat black fly landed on the fence beside them. It walked upside down along the bottom of a leaf.

"That fly is NOT a gecko," said Sam. "How is it sticking up there?"

"Flies use a different trick," said Tiko. "Their feet have tiny pads. The pads ooze out a little drop of sticky goo. That's how flies stick to smooth things."

"Ew! Sticky goo feet!" Sam laughed, scrunching his nose.

"Everybody climbs their own way," said Tiko. "Glue feet. Hair feet. There's more than one trick in this garden, Sam."

Sam looked closer at the fly through his magnifying glass. "Its feet are so tiny. I never saw that before tonight."

"Most people never look," said Tiko. "You do. That's why we're friends already."

Sam grinned so big his cheeks hurt. "Where next?"

Tiko's toes began to glow gold. "Somewhere SILKY," he said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Eight Sticky Feet
chapters.text:
They landed by the garden shed, right next to a big spiderweb.

A fat garden spider sat in the middle, bouncing gently on her silk.

Sam's eyes went wide. "SPIDERS! I love spiders!"

"I thought you might," said Tiko. "Watch her climb her own web."

The spider scooted straight up a silky thread. Then she walked sideways across the shed wall, easy as pie.

"How does SHE stick?" Sam asked.

"Spiders have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet too," said Tiko. "Just like mine, only even smaller. That's why so many spiders can climb right up glass windows."

Sam gently cupped his hands near the web, careful not to touch it. "Hi there," he whispered. "You're not scary. You're just AMAZING."

The spider waved one leg, almost like she was waving back.

"She likes you," said Tiko. "Spiders get a bad reputation. But look what their feet can do."

Sam watched the spider climb all the way to the top of the shed, quick as a blink.

"I always pick up bugs in my yard," Sam said proudly. "Now I know why their feet feel so grippy."

"Some feet are grippy. Some are hairy. Some are glued," said Tiko. "Let's go see a few more."

The glow swirled around them like fireflies. "Next stop," said Tiko, "a wall with LOTS of climbers at once."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Two Tricks at Once
chapters.text:
They landed on a brick wall by the back porch.

An ant marched straight up the bricks. A cockroach scuttled right behind it.

"Those two use TWO tricks," said Tiko. "On a rough wall, like bumpy brick, they use sharp little claws to grab the bumps."

"Like tiny grappling hooks!" Sam said.

"Just like that," said Tiko. "But watch what happens on smooth glass instead."

He pointed to the back door. The ant marched right onto the glass and kept climbing just fine.

"On smooth glass, they switch tools," said Tiko. "They use sticky pads on their feet instead of claws."

"So bugs carry TWO tools?" Sam asked, bouncing on his toes.

"Claws for bumpy. Pads for smooth," said Tiko. "They pick whichever one works."

Sam tried climbing the porch railing like the ant, scrambling with both hands. He slipped off onto the soft grass with a THUMP and giggled the whole way down.

"I don't have switchy feet," Sam said, lying in the grass, laughing.

"Nobody does, except bugs," said Tiko, grinning with all his gecko teeth. "That's what makes them so good at walls."

Sam watched the ant disappear over the top of the brick wall. "Good job, little guy," he whispered.

Tiko's toes glowed gold again. "Ready for something HUGE?" he asked.

"HUGE?" Sam sat straight up. "Yes, yes, YES!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Goat on the Cliff
chapters.text:
The glow swirled Sam up, up, up, until they stood on a windy mountain ledge.

Far below, rocks dropped straight down. Sam grabbed Tiko's tail, just a little bit nervous.

"Don't worry," said Tiko. "We are perfectly safe up here. Look over there."

A mountain goat stood on a cliff that looked almost straight up and down. It hopped from rock to rock like it was nothing at all.

"That goat is going to FALL!" Sam gasped.

"She won't," said Tiko gently. "Watch her hooves."

The goat's hooves had hard edges around the outside. But the middle part was soft and squishy.

"The hard edge grips the rock," said Tiko. "The soft middle squishes to fit every little bump. Like a sneaker that changes shape with every single step."

The goat hopped higher, calm as could be, and stopped to munch some grass.

"She's not scared at all," Sam said, feeling braver already. "She's just... walking."

"Climbing a cliff is just walking, if your feet are built for it," said Tiko.

Sam waved at the goat from far away. "Good climbing, goat!" he called out across the wind.

The goat flicked an ear, like it heard him.

"One more wall trick before bed," said Tiko. "This one is in the TREES."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Claws and Sticky Toe-Pads
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! They landed in a backyard, right beside a tall tree.

A squirrel zipped straight up the trunk in two seconds flat.

"Whoa, SPEEDY!" Sam laughed.

"Squirrels have sharp, curvy claws," said Tiko. "Tiny claws dig into cracks on the bark. Cracks so small, you and I can't even see them."

The squirrel stopped on a branch and looked down, tail flicking.

"Hi, squirrel!" Sam waved. The squirrel flicked its tail again and scampered even higher.

On a leaf near the bottom of the tree sat a small green tree frog.

"Now watch her," said Tiko.

The tree frog hopped onto a wet leaf and stuck there, upside down, without sliding one single bit.

"Her toes are flat and a little bit slimy," said Tiko. "They have a tiny pattern on them, kind of like a soccer ball. That pattern helps her stick to wet, slippery leaves."

"She's like a gecko, but squishier," said Sam.

"And slimier," Tiko added, wrinkling his nose.

Sam leaned close to say hello, keeping his hands to himself. "You're so cool," he told the frog. "I won't touch you. I just want to look."

"That's exactly right," said Tiko, nodding. "Looking is the best way to say hello to a wild friend."

The night air shimmered gold once more.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Slow and Upside Down
chapters.text:
They landed by a garden wall, damp with cool dew.

A snail glided slowly up the bricks, leaving a shiny trail behind it.

"Snails climb on SLIME," said Tiko. "Her whole body is like one big squishy foot. It ripples along, and the slime helps her grip the wall while she slides."

"That's the slowest climber yet," Sam giggled.

"Slow and steady," said Tiko. "She'll get to the top eventually, no rush at all."

Above them, under the roof of the garden shed, something small and dark hung upside down.

"Is that a BAT?" Sam whispered, eyes wide.

"It sure is," said Tiko. "Don't worry, she's just sleeping. Bats can't run up walls fast like me. But their curvy claws are perfect for hanging upside down from a ceiling, safe and snug."

Sam tiptoed closer, just to look, not to touch. "She looks comfy," he whispered.

"Bats sleep hanging all day long," said Tiko. "Upside down is just... cozy, to a bat."

Sam yawned a huge yawn. "Upside down sounds cozy to ME too, right about now."

"One more stop," said Tiko softly, "then home to your own cozy bed."

The glow wrapped around them both like a warm blanket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Sticky Gloves for People
chapters.text:
The glow set Sam down soft as a pillow, right back on his own bedroom floor.

"One last secret," said Tiko, "before you sleep."

He hopped onto Sam's dresser. "People wanted sticky feet too. So some clever scientists, people whose whole job is studying how things work, made special paddles copying gecko toes."

"Did it work?" Sam asked, sitting up on his knees.

"In the year 2014, a person wearing those paddles climbed straight up a glass wall," said Tiko. "Just like me."

"A whole PERSON climbed like a gecko?" Sam gasped, grinning ear to ear.

"A whole person," said Tiko proudly. "All because somebody looked closely at sticky little toes, just like you did tonight."

Sam looked down at his own bug jar, still sitting by his pillow. The roly-poly inside was curled up, fast asleep.

"I looked at everything tonight," Sam said softly. "Spiders, geckos, goats, frogs, even a slow little snail."

"You sure did," said Tiko, climbing back onto the night-light. His colors faded from gold back to quiet green. "There's a whole garden full of sticky feet, waiting for you to look even closer."

Sam snuggled under his blanket, bug jar tucked close beside him.

"Climb high," Tiko whispered, glowing softer and softer.

"Sleep tight," Sam whispered back, his eyes already closing.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Sam. Climb high, sleep tight.

A gecko can peel its toes up one at a time, like peeling tape, so its feet never get messy.
**Flies** stick to walls using tiny foot pads that ooze out a drop of sticky goo.
**Spiders** have thousands of tiny hairs on their feet, which is why many spiders can climb glass.
**Ants** and cockroaches use sharp claws on bumpy walls and sticky pads on smooth ones like glass.
**Mountain goats** climb steep cliffs with hooves that have a hard edge and a soft, squishy middle.
**Squirrels** climb trees using sharp, curvy claws that dig into tiny cracks in the bark.
**Tree frogs** have flat, slightly slimy toe pads with a tiny pattern that helps them stick to wet leaves.
**Snails** climb walls by gliding along on a layer of slime.

In **2014**, a person climbed a glass wall using special sticky paddles copied from gecko toes.

fact_pack.summary: Lots of animals can climb smooth walls and even walk upside down on ceilings, using clever tricks like sticky pads, tiny hooked claws, or millions of microscopic hairs. Scientists who study these tricks have even copied them to invent new kinds of sticky tape and climbing gloves for people.

facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk across ceilings because their toes have millions of microscopic hairs called setae.
Each gecko seta splits into hundreds of even tinier tips called spatulae, which get so close to a surface that weak molecular attractions called van der Waals forces hold the foot in place.
A gecko's sticky grip is not glue, so its feet never get messy or leave residue, and it can lift its toes off instantly by peeling them, toe by toe, like pulling up tape.
Flies and some beetles climb using tiny pads on their feet that ooze a sticky liquid, acting like natural glue drops.
Spiders have thousands of microscopic hairs called setules on their feet, similar in idea to gecko hairs, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches use a combination of sharp claws for rough surfaces and sticky footpads for smooth ones, switching tools depending on the wall.
Mountain goats and some wild sheep climb near-vertical cliffs using hooves with a hard outer rim and a soft, grippy inner pad that molds to rock.
Squirrels climb trees and walls using sharp curved claws that dig into tiny cracks and bumps invisible to human eyes.
Tree frogs have special flattened, mucus-covered toe pads with tiny hexagon-shaped patterns that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Snails and slugs climb smooth walls by gliding on a layer of slime, which lets their muscular foot grip and move in rippling waves.
Some crabs and lobsters use small hooked bristles on their legs to cling to rocky, underwater walls against strong currents.
Bats cannot climb walls quickly like geckos, but they use curved claws on their feet to hang upside down from cave ceilings and cliff walls.
Woodpeckers climb straight up tree trunks using stiff tail feathers as a prop and two toes forward, two toes back for extra grip.
In 2014, scientists built a gecko-inspired handheld paddle that let a person climb a glass wall by pressing sticky synthetic pads against it.
Engineers have copied gecko foot structure to create reusable sticky tape and gripping robot feet that work in space, where regular glue fails in a vacuum.
A gecko's sticking ability is so strong that scientists calculated a gecko the size of a human could theoretically support its whole body weight from one finger, though real geckos are small.
Geckos keep their sticky feet clean and dust-free through a self-cleaning effect, where dirt particles roll off the tiny hairs as the gecko walks.
Praying mantises and stick insects use both small claws and sticky pads called arolia, choosing which one to use depending on the surface.
Some climbing animals, like certain ants, are so light compared to their sticky footpad area that they could theoretically hold many times their own body weight while hanging upside down.
Rock climbers sometimes study gecko and insect feet for ideas on new types of climbing shoes and gloves with better grip.
Many wall-climbing animals rely on physics tricks rather than suction, since true suction cups need airless pockets that are hard to maintain on rough or dusty surfaces.
Remoras, a type of fish, use a modified dorsal fin shaped like a suction pad to stick to sharks, whales, and boat hulls rather than walls.

story.title: Rosa, Isla, and the Sticky-Toed Gecko
story.subtitle: A climb up walls, ceilings, and one very shiny window

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Ladybird
chapters.text:
Rosa sat on her bedroom floor, holding her favorite toy. It was a round, red ladybird. She loved to count its black spots, every single night.

Isla sat cross-legged on the bed, stretching her fingers. Tomorrow was her rock climbing class, and she wanted strong hands.

Rosa tapped the ladybird's shiny shell. One spot began to glow, soft and green.

"Isla, look!" Rosa said, pointing with both hands.

The green spot grew bigger and bigger. It became a tiny door, right in the middle of the shell. Out popped a small, colorful lizard, waving one tiny claw.

"Hello!" he said. "My name is Tokay. I am a gecko."

Isla's mouth fell open. "A talking gecko, in our room?"

Tokay grinned a toothy grin. "I can climb glass," he said. "Want to see how?"

Rosa nodded so hard her hair bounced. Isla grabbed her shoes, just in case of adventure.

Tokay tapped the window twice. It turned into a big, shiny wall of glass, right there in the bedroom.

"Follow me," said Tokay. He scampered straight up, upside down and sideways, quick as a blink.

"My toes have **millions of tiny hairs**," he said. "That is how I stick, without any glue."

Isla squinted at his feet. "Like Velcro?" she asked.

"Sort of," said Tokay. "But I can **peel my toes off, one by one**, like pulling up tape. No mess at all."

Rosa giggled and pressed her own hand on the glass. It did not stick one bit.

"That's because you don't have gecko toes," said Tokay, laughing too.

"STICKY FEET!" Rosa shouted, bouncing on her toes.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Buzzy Window
chapters.text:
Tokay led them to a sunny patch on the window. A little fly buzzed close by.

It landed on the glass, upside down, and just hung there.

"How does it do that?" asked Isla, leaning in.

"Flies have **tiny sticky pads** on their feet," said Tokay. "The pads make a sticky little drop, like a tiny bit of honey."

Rosa leaned close too. "Like glue?" she asked.

"A little bit like glue," said Tokay. "Beetles use that same clever trick."

Isla watched the fly zoom away in a loop. "That's so weird. And so cool."

Tokay winked one shiny eye. "Weird and cool go together a lot around here."

Rosa pretended to be a tiny fly herself, buzzing around the room. Isla pretended to swat at her, laughing the whole time.

Rosa clapped her hands, and the fly buzzed right past her nose. She giggled and ducked, flapping her arms like tiny wings.

"BUZZZZ!" she said, spinning in a circle.

Isla laughed so hard she nearly tumbled off her chair.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Eight Sticky Feet
chapters.text:
Next, they spotted a spider up on the ceiling. Its web sparkled in the corner like tiny beads.

"Spiders climb glass too," said Tokay. "They have **thousands of tiny hairs** on their feet, just like me."

Isla tilted her head, thinking hard. "So that's why spiders don't fall off the bathtub wall?"

"Exactly," said Tokay, nodding.

Rosa was not so sure about spiders. She hid behind Isla's arm, just a little.

"It's okay, Rosa," said Isla gently. "This spider only wants to climb. It's not here to bother you."

The spider waved one leg, almost like a tiny hello.

Rosa peeked out and waved back, very quickly, then hid again.

"See?" said Tokay. "Spiders are climbers, not scary monsters."

Rosa took a deep breath, then slowly gave the spider a tiny thumbs up.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Claws and Pads
chapters.text:
Down on the floor, two ants marched along in a perfectly straight line.

"Ants are clever little climbers," said Tokay. "On rough, bumpy walls, they use **sharp little claws**."

"And on smooth walls?" asked Isla, already guessing the answer.

"They switch to **sticky pads**," said Tokay. "Cockroaches use that same handy trick."

Isla grinned wide. "So they have two tools, like a little climbing kit."

"Exactly like that," said Tokay, impressed.

Rosa found a tiny toy ant in her toy bin. She marched it slowly up the wall, pretending hard.

"Go, ant, go!" she cheered, wiggling the toy higher.

The toy ant marched right off the edge and bonked softly onto the carpet.

Rosa giggled loudly and picked it back up. "Try again, ant!" she said, starting over.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Climbing Goat
chapters.text:
Tokay tapped the glass again. Now it showed a tall, rocky cliff, far away.

A mountain goat stood calmly near the very top. It looked down without any worry at all.

Isla gasped. "That cliff is almost straight up and down!"

"Mountain goats climb cliffs like that all the time," said Tokay. "Their **hooves**—that means their feet—have a hard edge, and a soft, squishy middle."

"The hard edge grips the rock," said Isla slowly, thinking it through. "And the soft part grips too, kind of like a car tire?"

"Just like that," said Tokay, clearly impressed.

Rosa pointed at the goat. "Silly goat, come down from there!"

"He's not silly at all," laughed Isla. "He's basically wearing climbing shoes already, built right onto his feet."

Isla thought about her own climbing shoes waiting by the door. Maybe they worked a little bit the same way.

The goat hopped from rock to rock, never slipping once, calm as can be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Claws and Squishy Toes
chapters.text:
Next, a bushy-tailed squirrel zipped straight up a tree trunk outside the window.

"Squirrels have **sharp, curved claws**," said Tokay. "The claws grab onto tiny bumps you can't even see with your eyes."

Rosa squinted hard at the tree bark. "I don't see any bumps."

"They're super, super tiny," said Tokay. "Smaller than a crumb on your plate."

Then a little green tree frog hopped onto a wet leaf nearby.

"Tree frogs have **squishy, honeycomb-shaped toe pads**," said Tokay. "The pads are covered in slippery goo, and they help the frog stick."

Isla leaned in close. "That's how they stick to wet, slippery leaves?"

"Yes," said Tokay. "Wet and smooth is easy for tree frog toes."

Rosa tried to copy the frog, hopping on her bed with her toes spread wide.

"HOP HOP STICK!" she shouted, flopping happily onto her pillow.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Slow Slimy Climber
chapters.text:
On the windowpane, a little snail inched along, slowly, upside down.

"Snails climb glass with **slime**," said Tokay. "Their whole body is really just one big, squishy foot."

Rosa wrinkled her nose. "Slime is yucky!"

"Slime is awesome," said Tokay. "The slime lets the snail's foot grip and ripple, like tiny little waves."

Isla watched closely, fascinated. "It's so slow, but it never once falls off."

"Slow and steady," said Tokay, "and very, very sticky."

Rosa touched the window gently, careful not to touch the snail itself.

"Hello, slimy friend," she whispered softly.

The snail kept gliding along, slow as ever, leaving a shiny trail behind it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Climbing Like a Gecko
chapters.text:
Tokay led them back toward Rosa's bedroom window, which was turning ordinary again.

"People can climb like this too," he said. "Scientists studied my sticky toes very carefully. They made **special gloves** for climbing glass walls."

Isla's eyes went wide. "Gloves like Spiderman wears?"

"A little bit like that," said Tokay, chuckling softly. "Real climbers borrow ideas from real animals."

Isla thought about her climbing class tomorrow morning. Maybe she would think about gecko toes on every single wall.

The glass window turned back into plain, quiet glass. The glowing spot on Rosa's ladybird toy faded to a soft, sleepy red.

Tokay waved one tiny claw. "Climb high, sleep tight," he said, and popped back inside the ladybird's shell.

Rosa hugged her ladybird close to her chest. Isla tucked the blanket snugly around her little sister.

Outside, the real world was quiet and dark. Inside, two girls felt like the very best climbers in the whole wide world.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Rosa. Goodnight, Isla. Climb high, sleep tight.

true_facts.text: Geckos can climb glass because their toes have **millions of tiny hairs**.
A gecko can **peel its sticky toes off, one by one**, like pulling up tape, with no mess left behind.
Flies and beetles climb using **tiny sticky foot pads** that ooze a drop like a bit of honey.
Spiders climb smooth glass because their feet have **thousands of tiny hairs** too.
Ants and cockroaches use **sharp claws** on bumpy walls and **sticky pads** on smooth ones.
Mountain goats climb steep cliffs with **hooves** that have a hard edge and a soft, grippy middle.
Squirrels climb trees using **sharp, curved claws** that grab onto tiny bumps.
Tree frogs have **squishy, honeycomb-shaped toe pads** that help them stick to wet leaves.
Snails climb smooth walls by gliding along on a trail of **slime**.
Scientists studied gecko feet and used the idea to make **special gloves** for climbing glass.

new_recurring.name: Tokay the Gecko
new_recurring.rule: A small, colorful, chatty gecko who pops out of Rosa's glowing ladybird toy to guide the girls through a real science or history adventure. He always ends the night by saying 'Climb high, sleep tight' before popping back inside.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Rosa hugs her ladybird toy as its glow fades to sleepy red, and Isla tucks the blanket around her, both girls drifting off feeling like champion climbers.

fact_pack.summary: Lots of animals can climb smooth walls and even walk upside down on ceilings, using clever tricks like sticky pads, tiny hooked claws, or millions of microscopic hairs. Scientists who study these tricks have even copied them to invent new kinds of sticky tape and climbing gloves for people.

facts.text: Geckos can run up glass and walk across ceilings because their toes have millions of microscopic hairs called setae.
Each gecko seta splits into hundreds of even tinier tips called spatulae, which get so close to a surface that weak molecular attractions called van der Waals forces hold the foot in place.
A gecko's sticky grip is not glue, so its feet never get messy or leave residue, and it can lift its toes off instantly by peeling them, toe by toe, like pulling up tape.
Flies and some beetles climb using tiny pads on their feet that ooze a sticky liquid, acting like natural glue drops.
Spiders have thousands of microscopic hairs called setules on their feet, similar in idea to gecko hairs, which is why many spiders can climb smooth glass.
Ants and cockroaches use a combination of sharp claws for rough surfaces and sticky footpads for smooth ones, switching tools depending on the wall.
Mountain goats and some wild sheep climb near-vertical cliffs using hooves with a hard outer rim and a soft, grippy inner pad that molds to rock.
Squirrels climb trees and walls using sharp curved claws that dig into tiny cracks and bumps invisible to human eyes.
Tree frogs have special flattened, mucus-covered toe pads with tiny hexagon-shaped patterns that help them stick to wet leaves and glass.
Snails and slugs climb smooth walls by gliding on a layer of slime, which lets their muscular foot grip and move in rippling waves.
Some crabs and lobsters use small hooked bristles on their legs to cling to rocky, underwater walls against strong currents.
Bats cannot climb walls quickly like geckos, but they use curved claws on their feet to hang upside down from cave ceilings and cliff walls.
Woodpeckers climb straight up tree trunks using stiff tail feathers as a prop and two toes forward, two toes back for extra grip.
In 2014, scientists built a gecko-inspired handheld paddle that let a person climb a glass wall by pressing sticky synthetic pads against it.
Engineers have copied gecko foot structure to create reusable sticky tape and gripping robot feet that work in space, where regular glue fails in a vacuum.
A gecko's sticking ability is so strong that scientists calculated a gecko the size of a human could theoretically support its whole body weight from one finger, though real geckos are small.
Geckos keep their sticky feet clean and dust-free through a self-cleaning effect, where dirt particles roll off the tiny hairs as the gecko walks.
Praying mantises and stick insects use both small claws and sticky pads called arolia, choosing which one to use depending on the surface.
Some climbing animals, like certain ants, are so light compared to their sticky footpad area that they could theoretically hold many times their own body weight while hanging upside down.
Rock climbers sometimes study gecko and insect feet for ideas on new types of climbing shoes and gloves with better grip.
Many wall-climbing animals rely on physics tricks rather than suction, since true suction cups need airless pockets that are hard to maintain on rough or dusty surfaces.
Remoras, a type of fish, use a modified dorsal fin shaped like a suction pad to stick to sharks, whales, and boat hulls rather than walls.

timeline.event: Scientists begin seriously studying gecko feet with early microscopes
Researchers identify van der Waals forces as the true secret of gecko stickiness
DARPA-funded scientists demonstrate a human climbing a glass wall using gecko-inspired paddles

story.title: Milo, Juno and the Brick Full of Dinosaurs
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip back 230 million years

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick Glows Again
chapters.text:
Milo sat on his bedroom floor, in his pajamas.

Juno sat right beside him, hugging his dinosaur blanket.

Their LEGO tower stood tall in the middle of the rug. It had clicked and held all week, ever since their big brick adventure.

On the shelf sat Milo's favorite toy, a grinning plastic shark. It was already way past bedtime. But the little red brick never seemed to mind that at all.

Juno poked the top brick of the tower. "It still works!" he said.

Then the very bottom brick began to glow. Red light filled the whole room.

CLICK. CLICK. CLICK.

The brick hummed like a happy bee.

"It's doing the thing again!" Milo said, scrambling closer.

Juno grabbed Milo's hand tight. WHOOOOSH!

The room spun around and around, like a top. Then it stopped, all at once.

Milo and Juno stood somewhere brand new. The ground was soft and green. Giant ferns brushed against their knees.

A friendly voice called out. "Welcome, explorers!"

A woman in a dusty hat waved at them. She held a little brush in one hand. "I'm Pip," she said. "I dig up old bones for a living."

"Like a dinosaur doctor?" Juno asked.

"Sort of," said Pip, smiling. "I'm called a **paleontologist**. That's just a fancy word for a bone detective."

Milo grinned wide. "We like fancy words."

Pip laughed. "Good, because today we go way, way back. Back before your grandma's grandma's grandma. Back **230 million years**!"

Juno's eyes went huge and round. "That's SO many years!"

"The very first dinosaurs lived then," Pip said. "Little ones, scampering all around, just getting started."

Milo looked out at the tall green ferns. "Where are they now?"

Pip smiled and pointed ahead. "Follow me and see."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Bone Detectives
chapters.text:
Pip led them down a dusty hill.

She knelt in the dirt and brushed gently. SCRITCH. SCRITCH. SCRITCH.

"What are you doing?" asked Milo, crouching next to her.

"Looking for **fossils**," said Pip. "A fossil is old bone that turned hard, like a rock. It happens when bones get buried for a long, long time."

Juno patted the dirt with his palm. "Bones just turn into rocks?"

"Exactly," said Pip. "Tiny bits sneak in, slow as a nap, until the bone turns hard as stone."

Pip handed Milo a small brush of his own. "Want to try?" Milo brushed softly, grinning the whole time.

Then he leaned in close and spotted something pale in the dirt. "Pip! Look over here!"

Pip gasped and scooted over. "A real bone! Good eyes, Milo!"

She brushed it clean with soft little strokes. It was long, curved, and smooth.

"People tell a story," Pip said. "A farmer's dog once dug up a big dinosaur bone, long ago. That part might just be a fun made-up tale. Nobody really knows for sure if it's true. But it's still a fun story to tell."

Juno giggled so hard he snorted. "A doggy detective!"

"Now," said Pip, standing and brushing off her knees, "let's find out whose bone this belonged to."

She pointed across the ferns. Milo squinted and saw something huge moving, far off in the distance.

"Is that a dinosaur?" he whispered.

"Let's go see," said Pip, already walking.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Giant Footprints
chapters.text:
They walked across ground that was cracked and dry.

Milo spotted strange, deep dents in the dirt. "Pip, look! Giant footprints!"

Pip knelt down to check. "These are footprints that turned to stone. We call them **trace fossils**. They tell us exactly how dinosaurs walked."

Juno hopped from print to print, counting out loud. "One foot, two foot, three big jumps!"

"This spot," said Pip, looking around, "sort of looks like a faraway place called the **Gobi Desert**. It has more old dinosaur bones and footprints than almost anywhere else in the whole world."

Milo pressed his whole foot inside one giant toe-mark. His foot looked tiny next to it. "This dinosaur was HUGE."

The footprints zigzagged left, then right, like a dance.

Juno hopped straight into the biggest footprint of all. He fit inside with lots of room to spare.

"Giant steps!" Juno shouted, hopping happily along the row of prints.

Pip laughed and clapped. "Want to follow where they lead?"

"YES!" they both shouted together.

Off they went, hopping and giggling, footprint after footprint, all the way across the dusty ground.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Three Horns
chapters.text:
They tiptoed through the tall ferns. RUSTLE. RUSTLE. RUSTLE.

A huge head popped out of the leaves. It had three sharp horns and a big bony shield around its neck.

Juno jumped behind Milo's back. Then slowly, he peeked back out.

"That's a **Triceratops**," said Pip. "Three horns on its face. A big **frill**, kind of like a shield, to keep its neck safe."

Milo counted the horns carefully. "One, two, three! Just like you said!"

The Triceratops chewed some ferns, slow and calm. It looked gentle, not scary at all.

"Can we pet it?" Juno asked, reaching his hand out.

Pip gently caught his hand. "We watch wild animals. We never touch them, even the friendly ones."

Milo nodded. "We just look. That's still pretty awesome."

"I could build one," Milo said, thinking hard, "out of LEGO bricks. Three horns, one big frill. Easy!"

Pip smiled. "Add it to your tower tonight."

Juno copied the horns with his fingers on his head. "Look, I'm a Triceratops too!" he said, giggling.

The Triceratops swished its tail and wandered off into the ferns.

"Bye, horn friend!" Juno waved both arms.

"Ready for the next stop?" asked Pip.

"YES!" both boys shouted at once.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Spiky Tail
chapters.text:
CLONK. CLONK. CLONK.

Something with tall, spiky plates clomped by.

"Whoa!" said Milo, pointing. "Look at those plates on its back!"

"That's a **Stegosaurus**," said Pip. "Bony plates all down its back. Sharp spikes on its tail, to swing at danger."

Juno backed up one small step. "Spikes?"

"Only if something bothers it," said Pip. "Mostly, it just munches on plants, all day long."

The Stegosaurus swung its spiky tail. WHUMP! It smacked a bush, not a person.

Juno burst out laughing. "It's just playing!"

Milo studied the bony plates closely. "I could build those with flat LEGO pieces. Easy peasy."

"Great idea," said Pip. "Dinosaurs make excellent LEGO models, if you ask me."

The Stegosaurus ambled slowly away, swishing its spiky tail behind it.

"Next up," said Pip, grinning, "some cousins who aren't quite dinosaurs at all."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Not Quite Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
A shadow swept over them. WHOOSH!

Juno looked straight up. "A flying dinosaur!"

Pip shook her head. "Close, but no. That's a **Pterosaur**. It can fly, but it's not really a dinosaur. It's more like a cousin — a flying reptile, a cousin of lizards."

Milo frowned, thinking hard. "A cousin, like my cousin Max?"

Pip laughed. "Sort of! Same family, different job."

Something small zipped between the trees, four tiny wings fluttering fast.

"And that," said Pip, "is a **Microraptor**. It has four little wings. It glides from tree to tree, like a tiny kite."

Juno spread his arms wide, like wings. "Like this?"

"Just like that!" said Pip.

They walked on, right to the edge of a big blue lake. Something long and sleek swam past, with flippers instead of legs.

Milo's eyes lit up. "Is that a shark?!"

Pip smiled. "Not quite. That's a **Plesiosaur**. It swims in the water, like a dinosaur's ocean cousin. But it's not actually a dinosaur either."

Another shape glided by, even bigger.

"And that one," said Pip, "is a **Mosasaur**. Also an ocean reptile. Also not a real dinosaur. Dinosaurs mostly stayed on land."

Juno splashed his toes at the water's edge. "No dinosaurs swimming?"

"Nope," said Pip. "But plenty of other giant creatures did, at the very same time."

Milo watched the Mosasaur glide away, smooth and quick. "Still pretty awesome. Almost like a shark."

"WHOOOOSH!" Juno shouted, flapping his arms again, pretending to fly and swim at once.

Pip grinned. "You two are naturals, on land, air, or sea."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Biggest Teeth
chapters.text:
THUD. THUD. THUD.

The ground shook under their feet. Juno grabbed Milo's hand, tight.

A giant shadow stretched across the ferns.

"Is it going to get us?" Juno whispered.

Pip smiled, calm as ever. "Nope. This **T. rex** is busy hunting lizards, not kids. We'll just watch, safe and sound, right here."

A huge dinosaur stomped past, close but far enough. Its teeth were as long as a banana.

"Those teeth can grow **12 inches** long," said Pip. "Longer than this whole book!"

Milo thought about his shark book at home. "Even bigger than shark teeth!" he said, amazed.

A much smaller dinosaur scurried by, covered in soft, fluffy feathers.

"That's a **Velociraptor**," said Pip. "In movies, it looks giant and scary. Really, it's only the size of a **turkey**."

Juno giggled so hard he hiccupped. "A turkey with feathers!"

"Scientists think it really did have **feathers**," said Pip, "just like a bird has today."

"There's a famous T. rex skeleton," Pip added, "named **Sue**. Found in **South Dakota**, back in **1990**. One of the biggest ever found."

Milo grinned. "Sue sounds like a pretty cool name."

The T. rex stomped off into the ferns, not even looking their way.

Milo and Juno both let out their best dinosaur roars, RAWR, just for fun.

Juno let out a huge breath. "That was exciting!"

"And safe," said Pip, "the whole entire time."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: A Very Long Neck
chapters.text:
They walked out into a big, open field.

A long neck rose up, up, up — taller than their whole house!

"That's **Argentinosaurus**," said Pip. "Maybe the biggest dinosaur that ever lived. Over **100 feet long**, from nose to tail!"

Milo tried hard to imagine it. "That's like a hundred Milos, lying end to end!"

Juno giggled and fell over, dizzy just thinking about it. "Super duper long!"

Juno tried to spread his arms as wide as the dinosaur's neck was tall. He could not even come close.

A little bird chirped nearby and landed on a low branch.

"Funny thing," said Pip. "**Birds today** came from dinosaurs, a long, long time ago. So dinosaurs never really left us. They just got small, and grew feathers, and learned to fly."

Juno pointed at the bird, mouth wide open. "That's a dinosaur?!"

"A tiny, chirpy one," said Pip, smiling.

Milo looked at giant Argentinosaurus, then back at the tiny bird. "From that, all the way to that?"

"Pretty wild, right?" said Pip, winking.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Terrible Lizard
chapters.text:
Pip led them to a cozy nest, full of round eggs.

"This is a **Maiasaura** nest," said Pip. "Dinosaur moms and dads took good care of their babies here. Just like your family takes care of you."

Juno peeked gently at the eggs. "Hi, baby dinosaurs!"

Milo smiled softly. "That's really sweet."

"Also," said Pip, "did you know the word **dinosaur** means **'terrible lizard'**? A scientist named **Richard Owen** gave them that name, way back in **1842**."

Juno repeated it proudly. "Terrible lizard!"

"They're not really terrible," Milo said, patting the air gently. "Just big."

Pip nodded, kneeling beside them. "About **66 million years** after this, something huge happened to the whole world. It changed a lot, and most dinosaurs went away. But remember the birds? A little bit of dinosaur is still flying around today, right outside your window."

Juno looked way up, searching the sky. "Hi, dinosaur birds!"

Pip wrapped them both in a warm hug. "You two were wonderful explorers today."

The red brick in Milo's pocket began to glow, bright and warm.

Juno gave the glowing brick a gentle pat. "Thanks for the ride," he said.

"Time to go home," said Pip, smiling.

"Bye, Pip! Bye, dinosaurs!" Juno waved both arms.

WHOOOOSH!

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Home Again
chapters.text:
The spinning stopped. Milo and Juno landed, soft, on their bedroom floor.

Their LEGO tower still stood tall, right where they left it.

Juno yawned a giant, wide yawn. "Dinosaurs are SO cool."

Milo picked up a flat green LEGO piece. "Tomorrow, I'm building a Stegosaurus. Spiky plates and everything."

Juno grabbed a round little brick. "And I'm building the egg nest, with all the babies!"

They set the glowing brick gently on the carpet. It gave one last, soft glow, then went quiet and still.

Milo tucked it carefully under his pillow.

Their shark toy watched from the shelf, grinning, like it had a secret of its own.

"Night, dino friends," Juno whispered.

Milo pulled the blanket up over them both.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: The very first dinosaurs scampered around about **230 million years** ago.
A **fossil** is an old bone that turned hard like a rock after being buried a long, long time.
A story says a farmer's dog once dug up a big dinosaur bone — fun to imagine, but **nobody is sure if it's true**.

**Stegosaurus** had bony plates down its back and **spikes on its tail** to swing at danger.
A **T. rex**'s teeth could grow up to **12 inches** long — longer than a book!
A real **Velociraptor** was only about the size of a **turkey**, not a giant movie monster.
Many dinosaurs, including Velociraptor, are now thought to have had **feathers**, just like birds.
One of the biggest T. rex skeletons ever found is nicknamed **Sue**, discovered in **South Dakota** in **1990**.
**Argentinosaurus** might be the biggest dinosaur ever — maybe over **100 feet long**.
**Birds today** came from dinosaurs long ago, so a little bit of dinosaur is still flying around.
**Maiasaura** dinosaur parents took care of their babies in cozy nests, just like families do today.
The word **dinosaur** means **'terrible lizard'**, a name given by scientist **Richard Owen** in **1842**.
