new_recurring.name: Pip the Paleontologist
new_recurring.rule: A kind, dusty-hatted bone detective who appears to guide the children through science and history adventures; calm, warm, always says 'we watch, we don't touch' about wild animals.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: The red brick gave one last glow on the bedroom carpet before Milo tucked it under his pillow, while he and Juno planned tomorrow's LEGO Stegosaurus and egg nest.

fact_pack.summary: Dinosaurs were a group of reptiles that lived on Earth for over 160 million years, long before humans existed. They came in sizes from as small as a chicken to as big as a school bus, and today we learn about them from fossils dug up all over the world.

facts.text: Dinosaurs first appeared about 230 million years ago, during the Triassic period.
Most non-bird dinosaurs went extinct about 66 million years ago at the end of the Cretaceous period.
Many scientists believe a huge asteroid struck Earth near modern-day Mexico, causing the mass extinction that ended the age of dinosaurs.
The word 'dinosaur' means 'terrible lizard' in Greek, coined by scientist Richard Owen in 1842.
Argentinosaurus may have been the largest dinosaur, estimated to be over 30 meters (100 feet) long.
Tyrannosaurus rex had teeth up to 30 centimeters (12 inches) long, including the root.
Velociraptor was actually about the size of a turkey, much smaller than shown in movies.
Many dinosaurs, including Velociraptor, are now believed to have had feathers.
Birds are considered modern-day descendants of theropod dinosaurs, so dinosaurs never fully disappeared.
The Stegosaurus had bony plates along its back and spikes on its tail called a 'thagomizer.'
Triceratops had three horns on its face and a large bony frill to protect its neck.
Fossils form when an animal's remains are buried quickly and minerals slowly replace the bone over thousands of years.
Mary Anning, an English fossil hunter born in 1799, discovered important marine reptile fossils near Lyme Regis.
The first scientifically named dinosaur was Megalosaurus, described by William Buckland in 1824.
'Sue' is the nickname of one of the largest and most complete T. rex skeletons ever found, discovered in South Dakota in 1990.
Pterosaurs could fly but were not technically dinosaurs; they were flying reptiles related to them.
Plesiosaurs and Mosasaurs lived in the oceans at the same time as dinosaurs but were not dinosaurs themselves.
Some dinosaurs, like Maiasaura, cared for their babies in nests, which scientists learned from fossilized nesting sites in Montana.
The Spinosaurus is believed to be the largest known carnivorous dinosaur, possibly longer than T. rex, and may have spent time swimming.
Dinosaur footprints, called trace fossils, have been found preserved in hardened mud in places like Texas and China.
The Gobi Desert in Mongolia and China is one of the richest places in the world for finding dinosaur fossils.
Some dinosaurs, like Microraptor, had four wings and could glide between trees.
Paleontologists are scientists who study fossils to learn how dinosaurs lived, moved, and ate.
A popular story says a farmer's dog once dug up part of a famous dinosaur fossil; this detail is likely exaggerated folklore rather than confirmed history.

Megalosaurus becomes first dinosaur formally named
Richard Owen coins the word 'dinosaur'
'Sue' the T. rex skeleton discovered in South Dakota
Mass extinction ends the age of non-bird dinosaurs (66 million years ago)

story.title: Theo and the Dino Server
story.subtitle: A Roblox Studio adventure 230 million years in the making

chapters.heading: Level 9: Continue?
chapters.text:
Theo lay on his bedroom carpet, laptop balanced on his knees. Roblox Studio glowed on the screen. He was building a jungle level with swinging vines and a moving log bridge. The house was quiet. He should have been asleep an hour ago.

Last night the screen had flashed a message: THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD. Theo had saved a screenshot of it. Tonight, instead, the screen flashed green all on its own.

CLICK. BZZZT.

A tiny green pixel popped up in the corner of the screen. It grew arms. It grew a grin.

"Player One," said Bit, his old eight-bit guide, voice squeaky as ever. "Miss me?"

"Bit!" Theo nearly dropped the laptop. "You're back."

"Guides like me don't retire," said Bit. "We just go idle for a while." He spun once, scattering pixels like confetti. "New server tonight. Old-school. Like, *really* old-school."

The screen folded outward, wide as a doorway, and the carpet under Theo's hands turned warm and soft, like real dirt.

"Where are we loading into?" Theo asked.

"Further back than any level we've ever run," said Bit. "Welcome to the Age of Dinosaurs."

A low hoot drifted out of some bushes that definitely had not been in Theo's bedroom five seconds earlier. Theo grinned anyway. "Please tell me there's a boss fight."

"There's a few hundred bosses," said Bit. "Let's go find the first save point before one of them finds us."

Theo's sneaker scuffed something half-buried in the dirt. He dug it out with two fingers: a golden coin, warm, like it had been waiting just for him.

"One for every level you clear," said Bit. "Same rules as always. Collect them all, and at the end they build into something."

"Level complete?" Theo asked, pocketing it.

"Not yet, Player One," said Bit. "First you've got to survive one."

chapters.heading: Level 1: Spawn Point, 230 Million Years Ago
chapters.text:
A rustle came from the ferns. Then another, closer.

Theo went still, the way he did on the soccer field when he needed to read a play before making one. "Bit. Are we being hunted?"

"Relax," said Bit, floating at eye level. "That's just the welcome committee."

Out stepped a creature barely bigger than a dog, fast on its feet, with a long tail for balance and a mouthful of small sharp teeth. It looked Theo up and down, decided he wasn't food, and trotted off into the undergrowth like it had somewhere better to be.

"First dinosaurs ever," said Bit. "This whole server went live about **230 million years ago**. Scientists needed a name for a slice of time that old, so they call it the **Triassic**."

"Two hundred thirty *million*," Theo repeated. "That number doesn't even feel real."

"Numbers get weird when you zoom out far enough," said Bit.

Theo crouched by a patch of dried mud and found a three-toed print pressed into it, perfect and deep. "Whoa. It's like it got saved on purpose."

"That's exactly what happened," said Bit. "Mud hardens, footprints lock in, and millions of years later people dig them up. They're called **trace fossils** — not bones, just the *trace* something left behind. People have found them preserved in places as far apart as **Texas and China**."

Theo thought of his own game back home, how every level needed a spawn point where new players first loaded in. "This is a spawn point," he said slowly. "This whole dinosaur game — started right here."

"Give the kid a medal," said Bit.

They pushed through ferns taller than houses, Theo scanning the ground for clues the way he'd scan a build for a bug. The forest thinned ahead, and a coin — heavy, warm, unmistakably real — dropped straight into his palm.

"Level complete," said Bit.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Beach at Lyme Regis
chapters.text:
The ferns vanished. Salt air hit Theo's face, and gray cliffs rose above a gray beach, waves crashing far off.

"New map," said Bit. "England. A lot later — but still way before either of us had a phone."

A girl in an old-fashioned dress crouched near the cliffs, chipping carefully at a rock with a small hammer. She looked about Theo's age, maybe a little older.

"That's Mary Anning," said Bit. "Born **1799**. While other kids her age were playing, she was out here hunting for **fossils** — the hardened remains of creatures that lived and died long, long ago, when rock and minerals slowly swap in for bone over thousands of years. She found some of the most important sea-reptile skeletons anyone had ever seen, right along this coast near a town called **Lyme Regis**."

Mary waved them over without even looking up. "Careful where you step. The cliffs drop things sometimes."

Theo knelt beside her. A curved shape poked out of the rock, ridged like a rib. "Is that a dinosaur?"

"Sea lizard," said Mary. "Not every giant bone belongs to a dinosaur. Some of the biggest things in the old oceans were reptiles that never once walked on land."

Theo tapped gently where she pointed, mimicking her rhythm — light, light, pause, light. It felt a bit like placing blocks carefully in Roblox Studio, one wrong move and you'd wreck the whole build.

A chunk of rock came free. Underneath: a perfect curve of bone.

"Nice hands," said Mary, grinning.

"People who study this stuff for a living are called **paleontologists**," added Bit. "Mary never got the fancy title back then. Didn't stop her from being one of the best."

Theo looked at the bone in his palm, then at the endless gray cliffs. "How much is still buried in there?"

"Loads," said Mary. "That's the fun part."

A coin rolled out of the broken rock and clinked against Theo's sneaker.

"Level complete," said Bit, and even he sounded impressed.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Name Game
chapters.text:
The beach dissolved into a cluttered study — shelves of bones, a crackling fireplace, and a man hunched over a giant jawbone that looked like it belonged to something out of a nightmare movie.

"William Buckland," said Bit. "**1824**. He's about to do something big."

Buckland held up the jaw to the firelight. "This beast," he announced to no one in particular, "shall be called **Megalosaurus**."

"First dinosaur ever given an official name," Bit whispered to Theo. "Like being the very first mob added to a game — everything after it gets compared to this guy."

A door banged open and another scientist strode in, younger, sharper-eyed. "Buckland. You're naming bones again."

"Richard Owen," said Bit. "Give it eighteen years, and he's going to do something even bigger."

The room flickered. Years spun by like a loading bar. Suddenly Owen stood at a podium in front of a crowd, holding up a sketch of a massive skeleton.

"I propose," Owen said, "that we group these creatures under one name. **Dinosauria.** It means 'terrible lizard' in old Greek." The year, Bit murmured, was **1842**.

"Terrible lizard," Theo repeated. "That's a pretty solid game title, honestly."

"Right?" said Bit. "Though half of them weren't even lizards, and a chunk of them had feathers, but nobody knew that yet. Naming things is step one. Getting them *right* takes longer."

Theo studied Owen's sketch — ribs, spine, a long tail curling off the page. It reminded him of blocking out a character model before adding the details. "You build the skeleton first," he said. "Then you fill in the rest later, when you know more."

"That," said Bit, "is exactly how this whole science works."

The crowd in the sketch applauded, tiny and silent. A coin dropped out of the podium and rolled to Theo's feet.

"Level complete," said Bit, saluting Owen as the room faded.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Giants
chapters.text:
The ground shook before Theo even saw anything. BOOM. BOOM. BOOM.

"That's not a jump scare," said Bit quickly, catching the look on Theo's face. "That's just footsteps. Big ones."

A neck rose out of the tree line, longer than a school bus is wide, and kept rising.

"Argentinosaurus," said Bit. "Might be the biggest dinosaur that ever lived — scientists think over **thirty meters** long, nose to tail. That's about **a hundred feet**. Roughly the length of ten cars parked bumper to bumper."

"That's not a dinosaur," Theo said. "That's a landmark."

Something roared behind them, and both of them spun. A different giant stomped into view, head the size of a car door, jaws cracked open.

"T. rex," said Bit, unbothered. "Chill — he already ate. Check out those teeth, though. Up to **thirty centimeters** long, counting the root. Roughly the length of a school ruler, jammed into one tooth."

Theo backed up anyway, soccer instincts telling him to always know his distance from anything that big. The rex ignored them completely and lumbered off toward the tree line.

"Over here," said Bit, nudging Theo toward a slower, spikier shape grazing nearby. "Stegosaurus. Big bony plates down its back, and check the tail — those spikes have an actual name. They're called a **thagomizer**."

"A *what*-omizer?"

"Thagomizer. Someone made the name up as a joke, and it just... stuck."

Near it, a three-horned face poked up from the grass, calm as anything. "Triceratops," said Bit. "Three horns on the face, and that big bony **frill** around the neck — basically a built-in shield."

Theo crept closer, the way he'd approach a wild animal in any game — slow, no sudden moves, hands visible. The Triceratops huffed once and went back to chewing. Theo grinned. "Friendly tank build."

A coin bounced off the frill and landed square in his hand.

"Level complete," said Bit. "And no, you may not ride it."

chapters.heading: Level 5: Feathers and Flyers
chapters.text:
Something small darted past Theo's ankles, quick as a soccer ball off a bad touch.

"Whoa — Velociraptor?" Theo spun, half-expecting a monster from a movie poster.

"Technically, yes," said Bit. "Realistically... look down."

The creature paused a few feet away. It was about the size of a turkey, covered in something that looked suspiciously like feathers.

"No way," said Theo.

"Way," said Bit. "Movies made them huge and scaly. Real Velociraptors were small, quick, and probably fluffy. A lot of dinosaurs are now thought to have had **feathers** — not just the small ones, either."

"So birds are just... little feathery dinosaurs that never got the memo it was over?"

"Closer than you'd think," said Bit. "A lot of scientists consider birds today to be living descendants of a dinosaur family tree. The game never actually ended. It just patched itself quietly, over millions of years, until it looked like a pigeon."

Overhead, something leathery and wide-winged glided between the trees.

"Ooh, dragon," said Theo.

"Pterosaur," corrected Bit. "Flying reptile, cousin to the dinosaurs, but not technically one itself. Close relative, different roster."

Down at the shoreline, a long shadow slid beneath the waves — something enormous, finned, unmistakably not a fish.

"Let me guess. Also not a dinosaur," said Theo.

"Mosasaur," said Bit, clearly delighted. "Sea reptile. Same era, totally different branch. The dinosaur family tree has a lot of cousins crashing the party."

Theo watched the little feathered raptor hop away into the brush, unbothered by any of it. "Okay," he said. "New rule for my game. Nothing is what the trailer makes it look like."

"Wisest thing you've said all night," said Bit.

A coin dropped out of the sky, feather-light, and landed in Theo's open hand.

"Level complete."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Nest Save
chapters.text:
The trees opened into a quiet valley, dotted with careful mounds of dried mud in long rows.

"Nests," said Bit. "Scientists found a whole field of them in **Montana**, from a dinosaur called Maiasaura. The name actually means 'good mother lizard.'"

A large, duck-billed dinosaur stood over one mound, gently nudging a hatchling back toward the others with its snout.

"She sticks around?" Theo asked. "I figured dinosaurs just hatched and bolted."

"Not all of them," said Bit. "These fossil nests showed scientists that some dinosaurs cared for their babies, brought them food, kept them close. Before that, nobody was totally sure."

Theo watched the hatchlings tumble over each other, clumsy as new players who hadn't learned the controls yet. One of them wandered too close to the edge of the mound, and the mother nudged it back without even looking, like she'd done it a thousand times.

"That's good parenting code," said Theo. "Automatic, no input needed."

"Dinosaurs ran some surprisingly solid scripts," agreed Bit.

They walked on, and the valley gave way to cracked, dusty ground, the kind that stretched for miles. "Gobi Desert," said Bit. "Mongolia and China. One of the richest fossil-hunting grounds on Earth. People are still digging up new finds here."

"And over in America," Bit went on, "back in **1990**, someone dug up one of the biggest, most complete T. rex skeletons ever found, in South Dakota. They nicknamed her **Sue**."

"There's a legend," Bit added, grinning, "that a farmer's dog found part of a famous dinosaur skeleton first. Might be true. Might just be a good story that got repeated until it sounded true. Nobody's totally sure — which, honestly, happens a lot in this line of work."

Theo crouched by the nearest nest, careful not to disturb the hatchlings. A coin sat nestled right beside them, like it had been laid there on purpose.

"Level complete," said Bit softly. "Last one before the big one."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Patch Note
chapters.text:
The sky changed first. It went a strange, bright color, like a loading screen that hadn't finished rendering.

"Bit," said Theo slowly. "What level is this?"

"The last one," said Bit, and for once he wasn't joking. "About **66 million years ago**. The end of this particular server — for most dinosaurs, anyway."

Far off, something streaked across the sky, bright and silent, and vanished behind the horizon.

"Scientists think a huge **asteroid** — basically a giant space rock — slammed into Earth, somewhere near what's now Mexico," said Bit. "It changed everything, fast. Most non-bird dinosaurs didn't make it through what came after."

Theo watched the light fade from the sky, waiting for the ground to shake, for something terrible to happen in front of him. Nothing did. The valley stayed calm, green, ordinary.

"Wait," Theo said. "We're not about to watch it happen, are we?"

"Nope," said Bit. "We're way too far off, and way too late. This level's already over. We're just here for the patch notes."

Theo breathed out, relieved. "Okay. So... that's just it? Game over?"

"Depends how you look at it," said Bit. "Big changeover, sure. But remember those feathery little guys back a few levels ago?"

A flock of small birds burst out of a nearby tree and scattered across the strange bright sky, completely unbothered by any of it.

"They made it through," said Bit. "Their whole family did. Turns out the dinosaurs never fully logged off. They just respawned smaller, with wings, and a much better flight update."

Theo watched the birds go, something clicking into place. "So every bird I've ever seen outside my window..."

"...is basically still playing the oldest game on Earth," said Bit. "Yeah."

The sky dimmed to a soft, ordinary blue. A coin dropped out of nowhere and landed in Theo's palm, the last one, heavier than all the rest put together.

"Level complete," said Bit. "For real, this time."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Respawn
chapters.text:
The valley folded up like a closing tab, and the carpet was carpet again. Theo's laptop sat open where he'd left it, screen glowing soft blue.

"Home server," said Bit, floating down to sit cross-legged on the keyboard, which should not have been possible for a pixel, but was.

Theo turned out his pockets. Eight golden coins clinked onto the carpet — the spawn point, the beach, the naming, the giants, the feathers, the nest, the patch note, and one he couldn't quite place.

"That last one's for showing up," said Bit. "Every Player One gets one."

The coins rolled together on their own, clicking into place like LEGO bricks finding their tubes, until they'd built themselves into a small golden trophy shaped like a three-toed footprint.

"Nice," said Theo, turning it over in his hands. "This is going straight on my desk."

"BZZZT," said Bit happily, which Theo had learned meant roughly the same thing as a high five.

Theo glanced at his laptop screen, at the half-built jungle level still waiting for him, logs and vines frozen mid-swing. "You know what I'm adding tomorrow?"

"Let me guess," said Bit. "Dinosaurs."

"A whole level," said Theo. "Spawn point, a dig site, a nest you have to protect, the works. Maybe even a thagomizer boss fight."

"Terrible name, great idea," said Bit, and for just a second, his pixel eyes looked a little watery, the way they always did right before a goodbye. "You always did build better than you played, Player One."

The screen flickered. A line of text crawled across it, green on black: SAVE COMPLETE. NEW BUILD UNLOCKED.

Bit winked out like a console powering down, leaving just the quiet hum of the laptop fan and a small golden trophy sitting on the carpet, very real, very solid, very much still there in the morning light that was starting to creep under the curtains.

Theo set the trophy on his desk, right next to his keyboard, and opened a new file.

Tomorrow, he had a level to build.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a level to build.

fact_pack.summary: Dinosaurs were a group of reptiles that lived on Earth for over 160 million years, long before humans existed. They came in sizes from as small as a chicken to as big as a school bus, and today we learn about them from fossils dug up all over the world.

facts.text: Dinosaurs first appeared about 230 million years ago, during the Triassic period.
Most non-bird dinosaurs went extinct about 66 million years ago at the end of the Cretaceous period.
Many scientists believe a huge asteroid struck Earth near modern-day Mexico, causing the mass extinction that ended the age of dinosaurs.
The word 'dinosaur' means 'terrible lizard' in Greek, coined by scientist Richard Owen in 1842.
Argentinosaurus may have been the largest dinosaur, estimated to be over 30 meters (100 feet) long.
Tyrannosaurus rex had teeth up to 30 centimeters (12 inches) long, including the root.
Velociraptor was actually about the size of a turkey, much smaller than shown in movies.
Many dinosaurs, including Velociraptor, are now believed to have had feathers.
Birds are considered modern-day descendants of theropod dinosaurs, so dinosaurs never fully disappeared.
The Stegosaurus had bony plates along its back and spikes on its tail called a 'thagomizer.'
Triceratops had three horns on its face and a large bony frill to protect its neck.
Fossils form when an animal's remains are buried quickly and minerals slowly replace the bone over thousands of years.
Mary Anning, an English fossil hunter born in 1799, discovered important marine reptile fossils near Lyme Regis.
The first scientifically named dinosaur was Megalosaurus, described by William Buckland in 1824.
'Sue' is the nickname of one of the largest and most complete T. rex skeletons ever found, discovered in South Dakota in 1990.
Pterosaurs could fly but were not technically dinosaurs; they were flying reptiles related to them.
Plesiosaurs and Mosasaurs lived in the oceans at the same time as dinosaurs but were not dinosaurs themselves.
Some dinosaurs, like Maiasaura, cared for their babies in nests, which scientists learned from fossilized nesting sites in Montana.
The Spinosaurus is believed to be the largest known carnivorous dinosaur, possibly longer than T. rex, and may have spent time swimming.
Dinosaur footprints, called trace fossils, have been found preserved in hardened mud in places like Texas and China.
The Gobi Desert in Mongolia and China is one of the richest places in the world for finding dinosaur fossils.
Some dinosaurs, like Microraptor, had four wings and could glide between trees.
Paleontologists are scientists who study fossils to learn how dinosaurs lived, moved, and ate.
A popular story says a farmer's dog once dug up part of a famous dinosaur fossil; this detail is likely exaggerated folklore rather than confirmed history.

story.title: Finn and Nell and the Humming Honey Jar
story.subtitle: A tiny, buzzy bedtime adventure about how honey gets made

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Jar That Hummed
chapters.text:
Finn licked the last crumb of honey toast. He tucked the sticky jar under his blanket. Shhh. Don't tell Mommy.

Nell held her yellow flower close. She sniffed it one more time before bed.

Then the honey jar began to GLOW. It glowed gold, like a tiny sun. It started to hum. BZZZZZZ.

"Finn! Look!" whispered Nell.

The lid popped off. Warm light spilled out, like syrup. A tiny bee zoomed up and landed on Finn's pillow.

"Hello, friends! I'm Buzzby," she said. "Want to see how honey gets made?"

"YES," said Finn. "I love honey."

Nell held up her flower. "Does it start with a flower like this one?"

"It sure does," said Buzzby. "Hold my wings. We're going to get small."

WHOOOOSH! The room spun gold and yellow. Finn and Nell shrank down, down, down, until they were just Buzzby's size.

They zipped out the window into the night garden. A huge yellow flower glowed under the moon.

"Watch this," said Buzzby.

A fuzzy bee landed on the flower. She unrolled a long, curly tongue, called a proboscis, like a bendy straw. She used it to sip sweet flower juice called nectar.

"SLUUURP," went the bee.

"Try it," said Buzzby.

Finn leaned down and sipped through his own curly straw-tongue. Sweet juice filled his mouth.

"It tastes like candy!" he said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Buzzing House
chapters.text:
The sweet nectar did not go in Finn's tummy. It went into a special bee pouch, called a honey stomach. It's not for eating. It's just for carrying nectar home.

"Feel that?" asked Buzzby. "Your bag is filling up."

Finn patted his fuzzy belly. "Like a backpack made of jelly!"

They flew toward a big tree. Inside was a hive, buzzing like a tiny city.

"This hive can have sixty thousand bees in summer," said Buzzby.

Nell's eyes went wide. "That's SO many bees."

"Most of them are girl bees," said Buzzby. "We do all the jobs. Flying. Cleaning. Making honey."

A big, round bee walked by, slow and calm.

"That's our queen," whispered Buzzby. "She's the busy mom of almost every bee here. She lays more than a thousand eggs. Every single day."

Finn blinked. "A THOUSAND? That's more than my toy cars."

"She never stops," said Buzzby proudly.

Nell waved at the queen. The queen didn't wave back. She was too busy laying eggs.

"That's okay," said Nell. "She's working hard."

Buzzby laughed. "Come on. Let's bring your nectar inside."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Great Nectar Pass
chapters.text:
Inside the hive, a worker bee waited by the door.

"Pass it here!" she said to Finn.

Finn didn't know how. Buzzby showed him. Bee to bee, mouth to mouth, they shared the nectar, like passing a cup of juice.

"EWWW," said Finn, then, "...actually, kind of cool."

Nell watched closely. "Why don't they just drop it in?"

"Sharing makes it better," said Buzzby. "Every time it passes along, a little bee spit mixes in. That spit is magic. It changes the sugar. It turns runny nectar into thick, sticky honey."

"Spit magic!" Nell said, giggling.

"Say it again," said Finn.

"SPIT MAGIC!" they both shouted.

Buzzby laughed so hard she wobbled on her own six legs.

"Keep passing," she said. "Honey takes teamwork."

Finn passed his nectar to a worker bee. She passed it to another, and another. Around the hive it went, getting sweeter each time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Six Little Walls
chapters.text:
At last, the nectar reached its new home: tiny rooms made of wax.

"Look!" said Nell. "They're shaped like little flowers!"

"Almost," said Buzzby. "Count the sides."

Nell counted on her fingers. "One, two, three... six! Six sides!"

"Clever girl," said Buzzby. "We call this honeycomb, lots of little six-sided rooms, snug as puzzle pieces."

Finn tapped one gently. "Where does the wax come from?"

"From us!" said Buzzby. She turned so they could see her fuzzy tummy. "Our bodies make tiny flakes of wax, right here. We chew it soft and build with it."

"You're a tummy builder!" said Finn.

"That's one way to put it," laughed Buzzby.

Worker bees spread nectar into the little wax rooms, filling them like tiny golden cups.

Nell pressed her nose close. "It smells like sunshine."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Big Fan Dance
chapters.text:
Rows of bees lined up beside the honeycomb. They faced the wet nectar and began to flap.

FLAP FLAP FLAP FLAP.

"What are they doing?" asked Finn, covering his ears.

"Drying it out," said Buzzby. "Nectar starts out watery. Fanning blows the water away, until it gets thick and sticky. That's how it turns into real honey."

Nell flapped her own arms. "Like this?"

"Faster," said Buzzby. "Our wings flap about two hundred times every single second. That's why we buzz."

Finn tried flapping fast. His arms got tired after two seconds.

"I'm not a very good bee," he said, giggling.

"You don't need to be," said Buzzby. "That's our job. BZZZZZZZZZ."

The whole hive buzzed together, a hundred tiny fans whirring at once. The nectar shimmered, getting thicker and darker, until it looked just like the honey in Finn's own jar at home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Lid for Later
chapters.text:
Once the honey was ready, a worker bee came with a tiny cap of wax.

CLICK. She sealed the little room shut, like a lid on a jar.

"Why put a lid on it?" asked Nell.

"To keep it clean and safe," said Buzzby. "And to save it. In winter, there are no flowers at all. No nectar to sip. So we eat the honey we saved up."

Finn thought of his snow boots at home. "Like packing snacks for a snow day!"

"Exactly like that," said Buzzby.

Nell watched row after row get capped, each one sealed tight and shiny.

"It's like a whole pantry of sunshine," she said.

"That's exactly what it is," said Buzzby, patting her round belly. "Good thinking, little bee."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Wiggle Waggle Dance
chapters.text:
A bee burst through the hive door, wiggling and waggling.

"What is SHE doing?" asked Finn, laughing.

"That's a scout bee," said Buzzby. "She found a great patch of flowers. Now she's dancing to tell everyone where it is. A little wiggle one way means go this direction. A longer wiggle means it's far away."

Nell copied the dance, wiggling her arms. "Like this?"

"Pretty close!" laughed Buzzby.

"But why visit flowers?" asked Finn. "Besides yummy nectar?"

"Good question," said Buzzby. "When we land, yellow dust called pollen sticks to our legs. We carry it from flower to flower. That helps flowers grow new seeds and fruit."

Nell looked at her yellow flower crown, dusted faintly gold.

"So flowers need bees," she said, "and bees need flowers."

"Best friends," said Buzzby, and did one more wiggle, just for fun.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: One Sweet Spoonful
chapters.text:
Buzzby led them to a quiet corner of the hive.

"Want to hear something wild?" she asked. "It takes twelve bees, working their whole lives, to make just one teaspoon of honey."

Finn gasped. "ONE teaspoon? That's what's on my toast every morning!"

"That's a LOT of bee work for your breakfast," said Nell.

"Here's another wild thing," said Buzzby. "If honey is sealed tight and kept dry, it never goes bad. Ever. Honey from a very, very long time ago could still taste sweet today."

"Forever honey," whispered Nell.

Just then, a gentle hand reached toward the hive, not to grab, just to check. A beekeeper in a big white hat and veil peeked at the honeycomb.

"That's a friendly beekeeper," said Buzzby. "They take just a little honey, and always leave plenty for us."

Finn waved at the beekeeper's glove. "Thank you for sharing!"

The beekeeper smiled, even though she couldn't hear him, and gently closed the hive.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Honey Jar
chapters.text:
"Time to go home," said Buzzby softly. "Hold my wings again."

WHOOOOSH! The gold light spun once more.

Finn and Nell grew bigger, and bigger, until they were back in their own pajamas, in their own warm room.

The honey jar sat on the nightstand, glowing gently one last time before going still and quiet.

"Will you come back, Buzzby?" asked Nell, through a yawn.

"Whenever the jar hums," said Buzzby, "I'll be buzzing nearby."

She gave one last loop in the air, then zipped back inside the jar. The lid clicked softly shut.

Finn snuggled under his blanket. "Honey is a LOT of work," he said sleepily.

"Twelve bees, one teaspoon," murmured Nell, already half asleep.

Finn smiled at his jar. "Thank you, bees."

Outside, the moon shone yellow, just like Nell's flower, resting now on the windowsill.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Finn. Goodnight, Nell. Sweet dreams, sweet bees.

true_facts.text: A bee drinks sweet flower juice, called **nectar**, through a long curly tongue called a **proboscis**.
Bees carry nectar home in a special pouch called a **honey stomach**, which is not for eating.
Bees pass nectar mouth to mouth, and a little bee spit mixes in to help turn it into **honey**.
House bees spread the nectar into tiny six-sided wax rooms called a **honeycomb**.
Bees fan the nectar with their wings to dry it out, turning watery nectar into thick, sticky honey.
Once the honey is ready, bees seal each little room with a tiny wax lid to keep it clean and safe.
Bees save up honey to eat in winter, when there are no flowers to visit.
A hive can have as many as **sixty thousand** bees living together in the summer.
Every hive has one **queen bee**, who lays more than a **thousand** eggs a day.
A **scout bee** does a wiggly waggle dance to tell other bees where to find good flowers.
It takes **twelve bees**, working their whole lives, to make just **one teaspoon** of honey.
As bees visit flowers, yellow dust called **pollen** sticks to their legs and helps flowers grow new seeds and fruit.
If honey is kept sealed and dry, it never goes bad, even after a very long time.
A gentle **beekeeper** checks the hive and takes just a little honey, leaving plenty for the bees.

new_recurring.name: Buzzby the Scout Bee
new_recurring.rule: A tiny, cheerful bee who appears whenever something in the children's room glows and hums. She guides Finn and Nell into shrink-down adventures, explains things simply, and always returns them home safely at the end.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Finn and Nell returned to their bedroom as the honey jar's gold glow faded to a quiet shimmer, with Buzzby tucked back inside and both children drifting off still murmuring about bees and teaspoons of honey.

fact_pack.summary: Honey bees turn flower nectar into honey through teamwork, chemistry, and a lot of wing-fanning to dry it out. A single hive can hold tens of thousands of bees, each with a job, from scout to nurse to guard, all working together to make and store their sweet, long-lasting food.

facts.text: Worker bees called foragers fly from flower to flower sucking up sugary nectar with a long tube-like tongue called a proboscis.
Nectar is stored in a special pouch inside the bee called a honey stomach, separate from the stomach used for eating.
Back at the hive, the forager passes the nectar mouth-to-mouth to a house bee in a process called trophallaxis.
As nectar is passed between bees, enzymes in their saliva break down complex sugars into simpler ones, which helps turn it into honey.
House bees spread the nectar into the six-sided wax cells of the honeycomb.
Bees fan the nectar with their wings to evaporate its water, thickening it from watery nectar into sticky honey.
Fresh nectar is about 70 percent water, but finished honey is only about 17 to 18 percent water.
Once the honey is ready, bees seal the cell with a thin cap of wax to keep it clean and preserved.
Bees make honey to store food for winter, when there are no flowers blooming and they cannot forage.
Honey bees live together in colonies that can hold 20,000 to 60,000 bees in summer.
Each hive has one queen bee, whose main job is laying eggs, sometimes over a thousand a day.
Most bees in a hive are female worker bees, who do all the foraging, nursing, cleaning, and honey-making.
Male bees, called drones, do not make honey; their only role is to mate with a queen from another colony.
Scout bees find good flower patches and tell other foragers the direction and distance by performing a waggle dance.
The waggle dance was studied and explained by scientist Karl von Frisch, who won a Nobel Prize in 1973 for decoding it.
It takes about 12 worker bees their whole lifetime to make just one teaspoon of honey.
To make one pound of honey, bees must visit roughly two million flowers.
Honey bees are important pollinators, carrying pollen between flowers as they collect nectar, which helps plants make fruits and seeds.
Honey never truly spoils if kept sealed and dry, because its low water content and natural acidity stop germs from growing.
Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, thousands of years old, that were still edible.
Beekeepers, called apiarists, care for hives in wooden boxes and gently collect extra honey without taking all of it, leaving enough for the bees.
Honey bees communicate with scent too, using a special smell called pheromones to recognize their hive and warn of danger.
A worker bee's wings beat about 200 times per second, which is what makes the buzzing sound.
Bees make beeswax from special glands on their abdomen, and it is this wax that forms the honeycomb structure.

story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick That Clicked
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip through the real history of LEGO

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo lay on his bedroom floor, snapping together a tiny LEGO shark.

Juno lined up her dinosaurs in a wobbly row.

"Bedtime soon," called Mom, from down the hall.

Milo reached into the bin for one more brick. It felt warm. It was humming. Buzzzzz.

"Juno, look," Milo whispered. "This brick is glowing!"

Juno scooted closer. "Ooooh. Like a firefly."

The brick wiggled. Two tiny arms popped out. Then a tiny yellow face.

"Hello!" said the brick-person. "I'm Clicky. I live inside every brick ever made."

Juno giggled. "You're silly."

"I'm also very old," said Clicky. "Want to see where bricks began?"

Milo grabbed Juno's hand. The little brick glowed brighter. WHOOOOSH!

The bedroom spun like a tornado of bricks.

When it stopped, they stood in a small wooden workshop. Sawdust floated in the air.

A man in an apron sanded a little wooden duck.

"That's Ole Kirk," said Clicky. "He's a carpenter — someone who builds things out of wood."

"In 1932, in a town called Billund, Denmark," said Clicky, "Ole Kirk started making wooden toys."

Milo looked around at ducks, trucks, and tiny wooden blocks. "He made ALL of this?"

"Every single one," said Clicky. "And he never stopped trying new ideas."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well
chapters.text:
Ole Kirk held up two wooden toys and frowned.

"I need a good name," he mumbled, "for my little company."

Juno tugged his sleeve. "What about... Dino Toys?"

Ole Kirk chuckled. "Close. In 1934, I picked two Danish words instead."

He painted them on a sign: LEG GODT.

"It means 'play well,'" said Clicky. "He squished it into one word: LEGO."

Milo tried saying it slowly. "Lee-go. Lay-go. LEGO!"

"Some people also noticed," Clicky added, "that in a very old language called Latin, 'lego' means 'I put together.' That's probably just a fun coincidence, not the real reason."

Juno frowned. "What's a coincidence?"

"Two things that match by accident," said Clicky, "like finding two matching socks you didn't even look for."

Juno held up her dinosaur and Milo's shark. "Like this! They both have teeth!"

Everyone laughed. Ole Kirk hung his new sign above the door.

LEGO. Play well.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Squishy Plastic Machine
chapters.text:
A strange smell drifted through the workshop. Hiss. Clank. Hiss.

"What is THAT?" asked Milo, holding his nose.

Clicky grinned. "In 1947, Ole Kirk got a brand-new machine."

It was big and metal, with a long nozzle on one end.

"It melts plastic," said Clicky, "then squishes it into molds, like squirting toothpaste into a toy-shaped tube."

Juno watched, wide-eyed, as melted plastic SPLOOSHED into a tiny duck-shaped mold.

CLUNK. Out popped a perfect plastic duck.

"Whoa," said Milo. "Can I try?"

Clicky nodded. Milo pulled the big lever. SPLOOSH! CLUNK!

Out came a plastic brick, square and bumpy on top.

"You just made history," said Clicky.

Milo held it up like a trophy. "I made history AND a toy!"

Juno clapped her hands. "Do mine next!"

SPLOOSH! CLUNK! Out popped a little plastic dinosaur. Juno hugged it tight.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Bricks With Bumps
chapters.text:
By 1949, the workshop was full of plastic bricks with bumps on top.

"These are called Automatic Binding Bricks," said Clicky.

Milo stacked two together. They wobbled. He sneezed, and the tower fell. ACHOO! CRASH!

Juno tried too. She stacked three. They tumbled down the same way. Clunk, clunk, clunk.

"They don't hold very tight yet," said Clicky. "Something is missing underneath."

Juno peeked under a brick. It was hollow, like an empty cup.

"Maybe something should go inside there," said Milo, "to grab onto the bumps below."

Clicky's tiny eyes lit up. "Milo, that is EXACTLY what happens next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Brick That Finally Clicked
chapters.text:
A young man knelt by the workbench, sketching circles.

"That's Godtfred," said Clicky. "Ole Kirk's son."

Godtfred drew little round tubes inside the bottom of a brick.

"These tubes," he said, "will hug the bumps on the brick below!"

Milo snapped two new bricks together. CLICK!

He pulled. They held tight.

"IT CLICKS!" Milo shouted, bouncing on his toes.

"In 1958, Godtfred made this exact brick," said Clicky. "He even got special papers, called a patent, saying it was his new idea."

Clicky pulled a brick out of his pocket. "This one is from your bedroom, Milo," he said.

Juno snapped it onto the brand-new 1958 brick.

CLICK! It fit perfectly.

"They're the same brick!" Milo gasped.

"Old bricks and new bricks always fit together," said Clicky. "That almost never changes."

Juno built a tiny tower. It did not fall. Not even once.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: A Whole Park Made of Bricks
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! The scene spun again. They landed outside, in bright sunshine.

Giant brick animals towered over them. A brick dinosaur. A brick lion. A brick windmill.

"In 1968, the very first LEGOLAND opened," said Clicky, "right here in Billund."

Juno gasped at the dinosaur, taller than her house. "It's a DINO made of BRICKS!"

Milo spotted a brick fin poking out of a pond. "Whoa, a shark too!"

A little train chugged past, full of giggling kids.

"Can we ride it?" Juno asked, already running toward the tracks.

"Just this once," said Clicky, laughing. "History can wait five minutes."

The train rattled around the whole park. Juno waved at the brick dinosaur as they passed. Milo waved at the shark.

Everyone cheered. CHOO CHOO!

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Bricks for Little Hands
chapters.text:
Inside a toy room, Clicky showed them a box of extra-big bricks.

"In 1969, LEGO made bricks just for little hands," he said. "They're called DUPLO."

Juno picked one up. It was big and chunky, easy to hold. "These are PERFECT for me!"

"They still click onto regular bricks," said Clicky, "big or small, they all fit."

Juno snapped a giant DUPLO duck onto one of Milo's tiny bricks. It worked!

Nearby, Milo spotted a shelf of little plastic people with round yellow heads.

"Those showed up in 1978," said Clicky. "The very first minifigures — tiny LEGO people with arms that move."

Milo picked one up. Its arms swung. Its hat popped right off.

"You can swap their hats and faces," said Clicky. "Make a new one every day."

Milo swapped a pirate hat onto a little spaceman. "Now he's a space pirate!"

Juno laughed so hard she snorted. "Space pirate! Space pirate!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Tiny Tires and a Giant Screen
chapters.text:
Clicky led them to a room stacked with tiny rubber tires. Thousands of them.

"LEGO makes so many of these little tires," said Clicky, "some people say it's one of the biggest tire-makers in the whole world. Just maybe not full-sized ones!"

Juno counted as fast as she could. "One, two, three... a HUNDRED!"

"Close enough," laughed Milo, scooping up a handful.

A big screen flickered on, showing brick people dancing and laughing.

"In 2014, a movie all about LEGO came out," said Clicky. "Everyone everywhere went to watch it."

Milo and Juno watched a tiny clip, giggling at every CRASH and WOBBLE on the screen.

Then the room began to spin again. WHOOOOSH!

Back they landed, soft as a pillow, right on Milo's bedroom floor.

The humming brick sat quiet in Milo's hand now, not glowing anymore.

"Thank you, Clicky," Milo whispered.

"Play well," Clicky whispered back, and the tiny face faded into the plastic.

Milo set the brick on his shelf, right next to his shark.

Juno yawned and hugged her little plastic dinosaur close.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

true_facts.text: Ole Kirk was a **carpenter** who started making wooden toys in **Billund, Denmark**, in **1932**.
In **1934**, he named his company **LEGO**, from the words **'leg godt'** — which means **'play well.'**
Long ago, in an old language called **Latin**, the word **'lego'** also means **'I put together'** — just a fun coincidence.
In **1947**, LEGO got a big new machine that could **melt plastic** and squish it into toy shapes.
In **1949**, LEGO made its first plastic bricks with bumps, called **Automatic Binding Bricks**.
In **1958**, **Godtfred** added little **tubes** inside the bricks, so they could click tight together.
A brick made in **1958** still clicks perfectly with a brick made today.
The first **LEGOLAND** park opened in **Billund** in **1968**, full of giant brick animals.
In **1969**, LEGO made big chunky bricks for little hands, called **DUPLO**.
The first tiny LEGO people, called **minifigures**, appeared in **1978**, with arms that move and hats that pop off.
In **2014**, a big **LEGO movie** came out, and everyone went to watch it.

new_recurring.name: Clicky
new_recurring.rule: A tiny yellow LEGO minifigure who lives inside every brick ever made. He wakes up when a special brick glows and hums, guides the children through real history, and always says 'Play well' as his goodbye.

bible_suggestions.ending_summary: Milo and Juno returned to Milo's bedroom with the now-quiet glowing brick, setting it on the shelf beside Milo's shark toy while Juno hugged her little plastic dinosaur, having traveled through the real story of LEGO with their new guide, Clicky.

fact_pack.summary: LEGO began as a small Danish carpenter's workshop in 1932 and grew into one of the world's best-loved toys, built around a simple plastic brick that clicks together and never goes out of style. Along the way the company survived a warehouse fire and a near-bankruptcy, while keeping every brick compatible with every other brick ever made.

facts.text: Carpenter Ole Kirk Christiansen founded the company in Billund, Denmark, in 1932, first making wooden toys and stepladders.
In 1934 Christiansen named his company LEGO, a shortening of the Danish phrase 'leg godt,' meaning 'play well.'
A popular story notes that 'lego' also happens to mean 'I put together' in Latin, though this seems to be a happy coincidence rather than the real reason for the name.
LEGO began working with plastic in 1947, becoming one of the first Danish companies to own a plastic injection-molding machine.
In 1949 the company produced 'Automatic Binding Bricks,' hollow studded plastic bricks that were the direct ancestor of the modern LEGO brick.
Ole Kirk's son Godtfred Kirk Christiansen redesigned the brick with hollow tubes underneath, and the new locking brick was patented on 28 January 1958.
A brick made in 1958 still fits perfectly with a LEGO brick made today because the tube-and-stud design has barely changed.
A 1960 fire destroyed the company's wooden-toy warehouse, and afterward the family decided to stop making wooden toys and focus only on plastic bricks.
In 1963 LEGO switched its brick material to ABS plastic, which resists cracking and keeps its color much better than the earlier plastic.
The first LEGOLAND theme park opened in Billund in 1968, right next to the original factory.
DUPLO bricks, sized just right for toddlers and still compatible with regular LEGO bricks, were introduced in 1969.
The LEGO Technic line, adding gears, axles and beams for more mechanical builds, launched in 1977.
The first LEGO minifigures, with movable arms and swappable heads and hats, appeared in 1978.
Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen, grandson of the founder, took over leadership of the company in 1979, keeping it in family hands for another generation.
Because so many tiny rubber tires are made for LEGO sets, the company is sometimes called one of the world's biggest tire producers by count, though it makes no full-size tires.
LEGO launched its first Star Wars sets in 1999, beginning a long line of licensed themes based on movies and games.
The Fortune Encyclopedia and other outlets named the LEGO brick a top 'Toy of the Century' around the year 2000.
In the early 2000s the LEGO Group ran into serious financial trouble and came close to bankruptcy.
Jorgen Vig Knudstorp became CEO in 2004 and led a turnaround that focused the company back on its core brick sets.
In 2014 The LEGO Movie brought LEGO characters to cinemas worldwide and became a major box-office success.
The LEGO Group is still headquartered in Billund, Denmark, on the same ground where Ole Kirk's workshop once stood.
The Kirkbi family, descendants of Ole Kirk Christiansen, remain the majority owners of the LEGO Group today.

story.title: Max and Sami and the Hundred-Year Brick
story.subtitle: One glowing brick, ninety-two years of history, and a tie nobody saw coming.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Brick in the Bottom of the Bin
chapters.text:
It was eleven at night, long past lights-out, and Max was losing.

Not the Technic crane build — that part was tied, piece for piece. He was losing the race to finish it first, and in Max's house, that counted. It had counted since they were little enough to need a stool to reach the table, and it was still counting now.

"Faster hands, Max," said Sami, snapping a gear onto her half of the crane. She always said that when she was ahead by even one piece.

Max dug through the bottom of their old parts bin for the last black axle — and his fingers found something else instead. A single red brick, scratched and dull, buried under years of spare gears and stray wheels.

It was warm. Bricks are not supposed to be warm.

"Sami. Look at this."

Sami leaned over just as the brick started to glow, a soft green pulse, like a heartbeat made of light.

CLICK.

The glow burst upward into a shape — a tiny figure, no taller than a minifigure, made entirely of light, wearing a flat cap like an old photograph come to life.

"Evening," said the figure. "Name's Click. I believe you two have questions. I happen to have answers, if you've got the ears for a long story."

Max grabbed Sami's wrist before either of them could say a word, and the bedroom folded away like a page turning.

They landed on a dirt road in front of a wooden workshop, smelling of sawdust and rain.

"Where—" Sami started.

"Billund, Denmark," said Click, straightening his cap. "The year is **1932**. Say hello to the fellow with the saw."

A tired-looking carpenter was fixing the leg of a stepladder, glancing now and then at a shelf of wooden ducks and trucks nobody in town could quite afford. "Ole Kirk Christiansen," Click said, nodding at him. "Started this whole business right here, making wooden toys and stepladders, the same year, out of the same workshop. He didn't know it yet, but you two are standing in the beginning of something enormous."

Max looked around at the empty shelf, the quiet road, the one carpenter. "This is it? This is the beginning of LEGO?"

"Big things start small," said Click. "Ask him what he's building."

Sami didn't wait to be told twice. She walked right up to Ole Kirk and asked.

He looked up, surprised anyone was asking. "Toys," he said. "Toys people can actually afford. I'll keep making them until one of them works."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Play Well (1934)
chapters.text:
Two years had passed in a blink of Click's light.

Same workshop, same carpenter, but now a freshly painted sign hung above the door.

"Help me read it," Ole Kirk said to a passerby, laughing at his own handwriting. "L-E-G-O."

"It's from *leg godt*," Click explained, as the boys squinted at the Danish letters. "Those two words mean 'play well.' He shortened them, mashed them together, and that's the whole company name, right there, in **1934**."

Sami pulled out the little notebook she always carried and sketched the sign exactly, loop for loop. "Play well," she repeated. "That's a good rule for anything, not just toys."

"Hang on," said Max, who had been quiet a suspicious amount of time. "I heard somewhere that 'lego' also means something in Latin. Like 'I put together.' That can't be a coincidence."

Click's light flickered, which was apparently how he shrugged. "Funny thing about that — it probably *is* a coincidence. Ole Kirk never spoke Latin and never claimed the name came from it. People just like pointing it out because it fits so perfectly. Good story. Shaky history. Both things can be true at once."

"So it's basically a happy accident," Sami said.

"The kind he'd have taken anyway," said Click. "He wasn't fussy about why a win happened. Only that it did."

Max looked almost disappointed not to have uncovered a secret. Sami looked delighted that the world had, for once, lined up two good things by pure luck.

"Can we see him actually make something?" Max asked. "Something that works?"

"Patience," said Click. "He's still thirteen years from his best idea. Wooden toys first. Hold on to your gears."

The workshop faded, the sign swinging once in a wind that didn't exist anymore.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Machine That Changed Everything (1947)
chapters.text:
The next stop smelled like hot metal and something sharper, almost like melted crayons.

A huge iron machine sat in the middle of a new factory floor, hissing steam, with gears bigger than Max's whole Technic set stacked together.

"This," said Click, "is one of the first plastic injection-molding machines in Denmark. Picture a giant glue gun: it melts plastic, squirts it into a mold, and spits out a perfect shape every single time. LEGO got its hands on one in **1947**, years before plastic toys were anything special."

Max was already circling it like it owed him money. "How does it know the shape?"

"The mold tells it," Click said. "Change the mold, change the toy."

A worker pulled a lever, and out popped a small, hollow, studded brick — not quite the one in Max's pocket, but close enough to recognize at a glance.

"By **1949**," said Click, "they were calling these Automatic Binding Bricks. They stacked. They didn't fall over if you breathed near them. They were the brick before the brick."

"Let me pull it," Max said, already reaching for the lever before anyone agreed.

Click didn't stop him, which Max decided to take as permission. He hauled the lever down. The machine clunked, hissed, and dropped a warm brick straight into his palm.

"I MADE THE BRICK!" Max shouted, holding it up like a trophy.

"Careful," said Sami, "that's basically a fossil — a leftover from way back in history. The great-great-grandfather of every brick in our bin."

"Then I'm the first person in history to drop one," Max said, nearly dropping it.

Sami caught it before it hit the floor. Competitive instincts, it turned out, did not help with butterfingers.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tubes Underneath (1958)
chapters.text:
Click led them into a brighter workshop, shelves stacked with bricks that still slid apart if you looked at them wrong.

"Problem," he said. "Stack them tall enough, sneeze near them, and the whole tower surrenders."

A man about Ole Kirk's age was turning a brick over and over, frowning at the flat, empty space underneath it.

"Godtfred Kirk Christiansen," said Click. "Ole Kirk's son. He's trying to fix the wobble."

Max leaned in, because wobble was a problem he understood. "You need something underneath to grip," he said. "Like a plug and socket."

Godtfred looked up — not at Max, since nobody in 1958 could see or hear a time-traveling kid, but close enough that Sami laughed.

"He's about to think of exactly that," said Click. "Hollow tubes, fitted under the brick, gripping the studs on the brick below. Tight enough to hold. Loose enough to pull apart. On **January 28th, 1958**, LEGO made it official and patented the design — which just means they registered it as their own invention, so nobody else could copy it."

Two bricks clicked together in Godtfred's hand. He pulled. They held.

"Try yours," Click said to Max.

Max dug the scratched red brick from his pocket — the very one that had started the whole night — and pressed it onto a brand-new brick fresh off Godtfred's table.

CLICK.

It held exactly like it should, sixty-six years apart, no different at all.

"IT STILL FITS!" Max shouted, loud enough that Sami clapped a hand over his mouth, laughing.

"That tube design barely changed since," said Click. "Which is why your ancient bin brick just made friends with one made before your grandmother was born."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Hard Night, and a Fresh Start (1960)
chapters.text:
Not every chapter in a story gets to be fun, and Click didn't pretend otherwise.

"**1960**," he said, quieter than before. "A fire went through the company's wooden-toy warehouse one night. Everyone got out safely — nobody was hurt. But the wooden toys that started this whole company? Gone."

Sami went still. "That's sad."

"It was," Click agreed. "But listen to what they did next, because it's the important part."

The family stood outside the next morning, looking at the ash where the wooden ducks and stepladders used to be stacked. Nobody was crying. They were already talking.

"We've got the plastic bricks," one of them said. "They're already selling. Let the wood go. Let's build the whole company on the brick instead."

"That's it," said Click. "One hard night, one clear decision. After that fire, LEGO stopped making wooden toys completely and bet everything on plastic bricks. Turned out to be exactly the right bet."

Max thought about every competition he'd ever lost to Sami, every time he'd wanted to quit instead of switching strategy. "So the fire didn't end them," he said slowly. "It just told them what to stop doing."

"Exactly the lesson," said Click. "Sometimes losing a thing shows you the thing you were supposed to keep all along."

Sami squeezed Max's arm, which was about as close as their competitive streaks ever came to a truce.

By the time the smoke had cleared in Click's story, the workshop smelled like fresh plastic again, not ash — a whole company deciding, together, what kind of company it wanted to be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Tougher Bricks and a Whole Park (1963–1969)
chapters.text:
"Next stop smells like fresh paint and hot asphalt," Click warned, and he wasn't wrong.

"**1963**," he said. "LEGO switched to a tougher plastic called ABS. Older bricks could crack or fade in sunlight over the years. ABS held its color and resisted cracking far better — which is why a fifty-year-old brick in your own bin still looks almost new."

"That explains the one in my pocket," Max said, turning it over.

They landed next outside gates painted in bright primary colors, with a miniature castle and a tiny version of an airport laid out across the grass.

"**1968**," said Click. "The very first LEGOLAND theme park, built right here in Billund, next door to the original factory. Whole cities built from bricks, life-size rides, the works."

Sami was already sketching the miniature skyline in her notebook, fingers flying across the page. "I want to build every single one of these when we get home," she said.

A toddler nearby was gnawing happily on a chunky, oversized brick nearly the size of her fist.

"**1969**," Click explained. "DUPLO. Same idea, bigger size, made for little hands too small for regular bricks — and yes, it still clicks onto a normal LEGO brick if you line it up right."

"Wait, so it's not a whole different toy," Sami said. "It's the same family, just sized for someone smaller."

"Nobody ever gets kicked out of the LEGO family for being little," said Click. "Or for being a hundred years old. The bricks don't care either way."

Max picked up a stray brick from the path and pressed his old red one against it out of habit. It held, obviously. He was starting to expect that by now, no matter how many years sat between any two bricks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Gears, Faces, and a Grandson (1977–1979)
chapters.text:
"This one's for you," Click told Max, and the air filled with the smell of oil and spinning gears.

"**1977**," he said. "LEGO Technic. Gears, axles, beams — real moving parts, not just blocks stacked up. Your whole crane build tonight? This is where that family tree starts."

Max picked up an axle from a nearby table like he'd found a long-lost cousin. "Finally," he said. "My people."

"Don't get too comfortable," Click added. "**1978** brings company too." He pointed at a factory line where small plastic figures rolled past, each with movable arms and a head you could pop off and swap.

"Minifigures," Sami breathed, scooping one up. She tried three different heads on the same little yellow body in about four seconds. "This is basically a costume party for tiny people."

"And in **1979**," Click went on, "a young man named Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen — Ole Kirk's grandson — took charge of the whole company. He'd grown up playing with these exact bricks. Wasn't some stranger showing up to run things. He was raised on the factory floor."

"That's like if I inherited the crane," Max said, suddenly thoughtful. "And also the rivalry."

"One more thing," Click said, grinning. "Because of how many tiny rubber tires LEGO makes for sets like yours, people sometimes joke that the company makes more tires than almost anyone on Earth — not full-size ones, obviously, just an enormous pile of very small ones."

Sami looked at the minifigure in her hand, then at Max's axle, then back at her notebook. "This place just keeps getting bigger," she said.

"That's the theme of the whole night," said Click.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Hard Years and the Comeback (1999–2004)
chapters.text:
Click's light dimmed slightly as they landed in a room full of boxes stamped with spaceships and desert robes.

"**1999**," he said. "First LEGO Star Wars sets. First time the company built toys from someone else's movie instead of only its own ideas."

"That seems like it worked," Max said, eyeing a shelf stacked floor to ceiling.

"It did, for a while," said Click. "By around **2000**, people were calling the LEGO brick one of the top toys of the entire century. Big trophies. Big headlines."

Then the light shifted, and the room changed — quieter, tenser, stacks of unsold boxes instead of empty shelves.

"Then the early 2000s happened," Click said. "LEGO had grown so fast, in so many directions, that it nearly ran out of money. Came close to shutting down completely. That's about as bad as it gets for a toy company."

Sami's eyes went wide. "What did they do?"

"**2004**," said Click. "A new boss named Jorgen Vig Knudstorp took over — the person now in charge of running the whole company — and he made a hard call. Stop chasing every idea. Go back to what works. The brick. Just the brick, done brilliantly."

Max understood that one instantly, the way he understood losing a build and starting over with a smarter plan. "Sometimes you win by doing less stuff, better," he said.

"That's the whole turnaround in one sentence," Click said. "You'd have made a decent LEGO executive."

"I'd have made a better one," Max said, and Sami threw a stray minifigure head at him, which he caught one-handed — a fact he would absolutely bring up again later, probably several times.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back to the Bin
chapters.text:
One more jump, soft as a page turning, and they landed in a crowded movie theater, dark except for the screen.

Tiny plastic heroes raced across it, a whole city built entirely from bricks.

"**2014**," Click said. "The LEGO Movie. Every brick character you've ever imagined, finally on a real screen, in actual theaters, everywhere."

Sami laughed at a joke on screen that Max didn't quite catch, which he decided not to mention.

"So where does that leave things now?" Max asked, as the theater melted into familiar dark.

"Billund," said Click simply. "The company's still headquartered right there, same town, same ground where Ole Kirk's workshop once stood. And the Kirkbi family — his descendants — still own most of it today. Still a family business. Just a much, much bigger one."

The dark folded itself into a very specific shape: a bedroom floor, scattered gears, a half-finished Technic crane.

They were home.

Click's light had faded to a small, steady glow, sitting back inside the scratched red brick in Max's palm.

"That's the whole story," Click said. "Ninety-two years, one brick at a time."

Max looked at Sami's half of the crane. Then at his own. Exactly even, piece for piece, same as when they'd started.

"Tie," Sami said, before he could argue otherwise.

Max opened his mouth, closed it again, and decided — for once — that a tie was a perfectly good place to land.

He set the red brick carefully on the shelf above their bed, right between the finished crane and tomorrow's pile of new pieces.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there would be more to build — and plenty more to argue over whose half was better.

true_facts.text: LEGO began in **Billund, Denmark**, when a carpenter named **Ole Kirk Christiansen** started making wooden toys and stepladders in **1932**.
In **1934**, Ole Kirk named his company **LEGO**, short for the Danish words *leg godt* — **'play well.'**
Some people say 'lego' also means 'I put together' in Latin, but that's probably just a fun coincidence, not the real reason for the name.
LEGO got one of the first plastic-making machines in Denmark in **1947**, a giant machine that melted plastic and squeezed it into brick shapes.
Godtfred Kirk Christiansen, Ole Kirk's son, redesigned the brick with hollow tubes underneath, and the new click-together brick was made official on **January 28, 1958**.
A brick made in **1958** still clicks perfectly onto a brick made today, because the tube design barely changed.
A fire burned down the wooden-toy warehouse in **1960** — nobody was hurt, and afterward the company decided to make only plastic bricks from then on.
In **1963**, LEGO started using a tougher plastic called **ABS**, so bricks stopped cracking and fading the way older ones did.
The first **LEGOLAND** theme park opened in **1968**, right next to the original factory in Billund.
**DUPLO** bricks arrived in **1969** — bigger bricks made for little hands, but still able to click onto a regular LEGO brick.
**LEGO Technic**, with gears and axles for building machines that actually move, launched in **1977**.
The first **minifigures**, with arms that moved and heads you could swap, showed up in **1978**.
Ole Kirk's grandson, **Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen**, took charge of the company in **1979** after growing up playing with the very bricks his family made.
The LEGO company is still based in **Billund**, on the very same ground where Ole Kirk's first workshop once stood.

story.title: Ada and the Magnet That Jumped
story.subtitle: A bedtime adventure about how magnets pull, push, and stick

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Magnet That Jumped
chapters.text:
Ada sat on her bedroom floor long after lights-out, sorting her fridge magnets into piles. Red ones here. Yellow ones there. One small gray magnet, shaped like a lumpy pebble, would not stay in line.

It scooted across the carpet all by itself. **WHOOSH.** It stuck to her toy robot's foot with a soft **CLICK**.

Two blue lights blinked open. "Oh!" said the robot. "Someone woke me up. I'm Bolt."

"Robots don't just turn on," said Ada.

"Mine does," said Bolt, "when a magnet gets close enough. Every magnet has two ends, called **poles** — a north pole and a south pole. That's where the pull is strongest."

Ada held up two magnets. One end snapped together. The other end pushed apart.

"Opposite poles pull. Same poles push away," said Bolt. "Try it!"

Ada flipped a magnet around. It bonked Bolt's nose. "OOF," said Bolt.

Ada giggled so hard she nearly woke the whole house.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Invisible Push
chapters.text:
"Magnets have a secret," Bolt said, holding up a horseshoe magnet. "A pulling-and-pushing space goes all around them, even where you can't see it. We call it a **magnetic field**."

"Show me!" said Ada.

Bolt sprinkled tiny bits of iron dust onto a sheet of paper, then slid the magnet underneath. The little bits jumped into curvy lines, looping from one end of the magnet to the other.

Ada's eyes went wide. "It's drawing with no one drawing!"

"The field was always there," said Bolt. "Now you can see its shape."

Ada tilted the paper. The lines bent and swirled like tiny rivers. She tilted it back. They swirled the other way.

"The field goes wherever the magnet goes," said Bolt.

"Then I'm never losing you," said Ada, and stuck Bolt to her pajama pocket with a happy **CLICK**.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Rock From Greece
chapters.text:
Bolt's chest popped open like a tiny door. "Hop in my memory room," he said. "I want to show you something old."

Suddenly they stood on a sunny, rocky hillside.

"Long, long ago," said Bolt, "people near a place called **Magnesia** found strange rocks that pulled on iron all by themselves. Nobody made them magnetic. They just were."

"Rocks that are already magnets?" Ada asked.

"We call them **lodestones**," said Bolt. "Some people even think that's where the word magnet came from."

Ada picked up a pretend rock and held it near a nail. It wobbled, then snapped to her hand.

"The Greeks thought it was magic," said Bolt.

"It kind of is," said Ada, grinning, and tucked the little rock into her pocket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Floating Needle
chapters.text:
Next, Bolt's door opened onto a wooden boat on a calm river.

"More than **2,000 years ago**," said Bolt, "people in China figured out something clever. They floated a sliver of lodestone on water. It always turned to point the same direction."

"Like an arrow that never gets lost," said Ada.

"That's a **compass**," said Bolt. "A tool with a magnet needle that always points north."

Ada spun around three times, dizzy, then held out her toy compass. The needle swung, and stopped, pointing straight past Bolt's blinking nose.

"It's not even looking at you," said Ada, "and it still knows which way is north!"

"That's the magic of magnets," said Bolt, "not pointing at robots. Pointing at the whole planet."
chapters.shout_line: IT KNOWS WHICH WAY IS NORTH!

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Giant Magnet Under Our Feet
chapters.text:
"Wait," said Ada. "Why does it always point the same way?"

Bolt's lights flickered proudly. "Because the whole Earth is a giant magnet."

"THE WHOLE PLANET?" Ada nearly fell over.

"Deep down," said Bolt, "there's hot melted metal, swirling around and around. That swirling makes the whole Earth act like one big magnet, with a north end and a south end."

"So my compass is pointing at..."

"Earth's north," said Bolt. "Always has. Always will."

Ada held her little magnet up high. "Hello, Earth," she whispered. "You're the biggest magnet I know."

Somewhere far below, she imagined the whole planet humming back.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Magnet You Can Switch Off
chapters.text:
Bolt's arm popped open to show wire wrapped in loops around a metal rod. "This," he said, "is an **electromagnet**. Wrap wire in loops, run electricity through it, and—"

He flicked a tiny switch. **CLICK.** The rod snapped to a paperclip.

He flicked it again. The paperclip dropped.

"You can turn it OFF?" Ada gasped. "Regular magnets don't do that!"

"Electromagnets like mine are in doorbells, in loudspeakers," said Bolt, "and in giant cranes that lift old, broken cars."

Ada flicked the switch herself, over and over. **CLICK. CLICK. CLICK.** Paperclip on. Paperclip off.

"Best toggle switch ever," she said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Not Everything Sticks
chapters.text:
"Does EVERYTHING stick to a magnet?" Ada asked, holding up a spoon.

"Try it," said Bolt.

The spoon stuck. So did a nail. A penny, a gold ring from Ada's jewelry box, and a shiny soda can did not.

"Iron sticks," said Bolt. "Gold, copper, and silver don't. Magnets are picky!"

Ada picked up Lodey, the little gray lodestone, and pretended to snap it in half.

"If you really cut a magnet in two," said Bolt, "you don't get a north half and a south half."

"What do you get?"

"Two whole new tiny magnets," said Bolt, "each one with its very own north and south, all over again."

Ada's jaw dropped. "Magnets just... make more magnets?"

"Magnets," said Bolt, "never run out of poles."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
"One more stop," said Bolt. His door opened onto a quiet hospital hallway, then a silver train gliding just above its tracks, no wheels touching at all.

"Giant magnets help doctors take pictures inside people, with no cutting," said Bolt. "Giant magnets help some trains float and glide fast, too."

"What about animals?" Ada asked.

"Some birds and sea turtles," said Bolt, "seem to feel Earth's pulling-and-pushing field, to help them find their way on long trips across the world."

"Just like my compass," said Ada, yawning.

The door closed. Ada was back on her carpet, Bolt small and still beside her. Her fridge magnets lay scattered in a sleepy pile, bendy and soft, with magnet powder mixed right in.

She pressed Lodey onto the box. **CLICK.** It held.

"Goodnight, Ada," Bolt whispered. "Play well, little magnet."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ada. Play well, little magnet.

fact_pack.summary: Magnets are objects that pull on iron and a few other metals using an invisible force called magnetism. This pack explains why magnets attract and repel, how Earth itself is a giant magnet, and the people and discoveries behind our understanding of magnetism.

facts.text: A magnet has two ends called poles, a north pole and a south pole, where the magnetic force is strongest.
Opposite poles attract each other (north pulls south), while like poles repel each other (north pushes north away).
Magnetism comes from the movement of tiny particles called electrons inside atoms, which act like tiny spinning magnets themselves.
In magnetic materials like iron, nickel, and cobalt, groups of atoms called magnetic domains can line up in the same direction to create a strong overall magnetic field.
In most materials the atoms' tiny magnetic fields point in random directions, which is why most objects, like wood or plastic, are not magnetic.
A magnetic field is the invisible area around a magnet where its force can push or pull on other magnetic objects.
You can see the shape of a magnetic field by sprinkling iron filings near a magnet; they line up in curved lines from pole to pole.
The ancient Greeks discovered a naturally magnetic rock called lodestone near a region called Magnesia, which is likely where the word 'magnet' comes from.
The Chinese used lodestones to make the first compasses more than 2,000 years ago, helping travelers find direction.
Earth itself acts like a giant bar magnet because of swirling liquid iron deep in its core, and this is called Earth's magnetic field.
A compass needle points north because it lines up with Earth's magnetic field, with its north pole attracted toward the planet's magnetic north.
Confusingly, Earth's magnetic north pole actually behaves like a magnetic south pole, which is why opposite-pole attraction pulls compass needles there.
In 1820, Danish scientist Hans Christian Oersted discovered that electricity flowing through a wire creates a magnetic field, linking electricity and magnetism for the first time.
English scientist Michael Faraday showed in 1831 that moving a magnet near a wire could create electric current, an idea now used in generators that make our electricity.
An electromagnet is a magnet made by wrapping wire into a coil and running electric current through it, and it can be switched on and off.
Electromagnets are used in everyday things like doorbells, loudspeakers, electric motors, and giant cranes that lift old cars in junkyards.
If you cut a bar magnet in half, you do not get a separate north piece and south piece; each new piece becomes its own smaller magnet with both a north and south pole.
Heating a magnet to a very high temperature, called its Curie point, can make it lose its magnetism because the heat jumbles up its lined-up atoms.
Not all metals are magnetic: for example, aluminum, gold, copper, and silver are not attracted to ordinary magnets.
Some of the strongest magnets made today are called neodymium magnets, made from a mix of iron, boron, and the rare-earth metal neodymium.
Maglev trains use powerful magnets to float above their tracks and glide forward without touching the rails, reducing friction and allowing very high speeds.
Hospitals use giant, extremely strong magnets inside MRI machines to take detailed pictures inside the human body without any cutting.
Some animals, like birds, sea turtles, and some fish, are believed to sense Earth's magnetic field to help them navigate during long migrations.
Refrigerator magnets are usually made from flexible rubber mixed with magnetic powder, which is why they can bend without losing their stick.
