story.title: Nora and the Tile from Pompeii
story.subtitle: A bedtime journey into the Roman town that time forgot

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Tile That Glowed
chapters.text:
Nora sat cross-legged on her bedroom floor. Tiny tiles lay all around her. Red ones. Blue ones. One gold one, shaped like a leaf.

She was building a mosaic coaster. A mosaic is a picture made of tiny tiles glued together.

She pressed the last blue tile into place. It should have just sat there. Instead, it started to glow.

"Ow! Bright!" Nora blinked. The glow grew into a tiny shape. It had one painted eye and a crack down the middle.

"Hello," said the shape. "I am a tessera. That's just a fancy word for one little mosaic tile, like the ones in your hand."

Nora grinned. "You can talk?"

"Only at bedtime," said the tessera. "Want to see where tiles like me came from? Real ones. Very old ones."

Before Nora could answer, the room spun like a pinwheel. WHOOOOSH!

She landed on warm stone. Sunlight. Noise. Smells of bread and salt water.

"Welcome," said the tessera, "to **Pompeii**. A busy Roman town, near where the city of **Naples** is today."

People bustled past in sandals. Water trickled from a stone fountain on the corner.

"Thousands of people lived here," said the tessera. "As many as **fifteen thousand**. They had shops, bathhouses, theaters, and temples."

Nora looked down. The street had tall stepping stones poking up, with gaps on either side.

"Those are for crossing without getting your sandals wet," said the tessera. "Carts roll right through the gaps."

Nora hopped from stone to stone like hopscotch. "This town built its streets like a game!"

She didn't know yet. Pompeii was about to teach her far more than games.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Stone Arena
chapters.text:
A rumble rolled across the town. Nora froze. "Is that the ground?"

"No," laughed the tessera. "That is the crowd."

They followed the sound to a huge oval building, round like a giant stone bowl.

"This is the **amphitheater**," said the tessera. "A big open stadium for Roman games. People built it around **70 BC** — more than two thousand years before you were born."

Nora climbed onto a stone bench. Below, two **gladiators** practiced with wooden swords. A gladiator was a trained fighter who performed for crowds.

"Is it scary?" Nora asked.

"They are only practicing today," said the tessera gently. "No one is in danger. We're just watching."

Thousands of empty seats curved around them like a giant mosaic bowl.

"This is one of the oldest stadiums like this that anyone has ever found," said the tessera.

Nora pictured the seats full of cheering people, waving their arms, shouting names.

"It's like the oldest sports stadium in the whole world," she said.

"Close," said the tessera. "One of the oldest we know about."

Nora cupped her hands and shouted into the empty arena. Her voice echoed back three times.

"ECHO! ECHO!"

The tessera giggled, a tiny clinking sound, like two tiles tapping together.

"Come on," it said. "I want to show you something that smells a lot better than sweaty gladiators."

Nora laughed and followed, already wondering what was next.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Bread in the Oven
chapters.text:
A warm, yeasty smell drifted down the street. Nora's stomach rumbled. "Is that... bread?"

The tessera led her into a small bakery. A round stone oven sat in the corner, still warm after all this time.

Inside sat a loaf of **bread**, round and sliced into eight wedges, like a pizza.

"This loaf never got eaten," said the tessera softly. "But scientists found it, baked and ready, almost perfectly preserved. That means it stayed almost exactly the way it was."

Nora leaned close. "You can even see the baker's mark on top."

"That's right," said the tessera. "Everything here happened so fast that ordinary moments got frozen in place. Bread in ovens. Paint on walls. Even words scratched onto buildings."

"Frozen? Like ice cream?" Nora asked.

"Frozen in time," said the tessera. "Not frozen cold. Just... stopped. Like pressing pause on a very long movie."

Nora imagined a giant pause button, somewhere above the town.

"So this is basically a time capsule," she said. "Stuff from long ago, just sitting here, waiting."

"Exactly," said the tessera, its crack glowing proudly. "A whole town, paused."

Nora touched the edge of the oven, careful not to smudge any ash.

"I love time capsules," she whispered. "This might be the best one ever."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Paintings and Writing on the Wall
chapters.text:
Around the corner, a wall blazed with color. Reds, golds, deep blues — a painting stretched floor to ceiling.

"Whoa," Nora breathed. "Who painted that?"

"Artists, a very long time ago," said the tessera. "A painting made right onto wet wall plaster is called a **fresco**. Plaster is the smooth coating on a wall."

"It looks like people dancing," Nora said, studying the figures.

"Some call this one the **Villa of the Mysteries**," said the tessera. "Nobody is completely sure what the scene means. It might show a secret ceremony. That part is still a puzzle."

Nora loved puzzles. She traced the shapes with her finger, careful not to touch the actual wall.

Further down, letters were scratched into the plaster.

"Is that... writing?" Nora asked.

"**Graffiti**," said the tessera. "Messages people scratched or painted onto walls. Ads for shops. Even messages about who should get picked for town jobs."

"People wrote on walls two thousand years ago?" Nora laughed. "That's basically an old-fashioned text message."

"Pretty much," said the tessera. "Oh — and the town's own name might mean something too. Some think 'Pompeii' comes from an old word for **'five,'** maybe because five little villages joined together to build it."

"Five villages, one town," Nora said slowly. "Like five mosaic pieces making one picture."

The tessera's crack sparkled. "Exactly like that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Mountain That Watched
chapters.text:
Beyond the rooftops stood a tall green mountain, puffing a thin trail of smoke.

Nora pointed. "Is that a volcano?"

"Mount Vesuvius," said the tessera. "A volcano is a mountain with a secret: melted rock deep underground, pushing to get out."

"Is it going to erupt right now?" Nora asked, a little wobble in her voice.

"Not today," said the tessera kindly. "But a long time ago, it did. And it's still awake today. Scientists keep a close watch on it, because millions of people still live nearby."

Nora relaxed. "So someone's always watching it. Like a babysitter for a mountain."

"A very good way to put it," laughed the tessera.

They walked along the shore. Fishing boats bobbed on blue water.

"People here didn't know yet," said the tessera gently, "that one day, this mountain would change everything. But that's part of why we know so much about them now."

Nora looked back at the mountain. It looked peaceful. Almost sleepy.

"I hope the people got to leave," she said softly.

"Many did," said the tessera. "And because of what happened, we learned an enormous amount about how they lived. That's where we're headed next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Letter Writer
chapters.text:
Across the bay, a young man named **Pliny the Younger** stood watching, far from any danger.

"He wrote everything down," said the tessera. "Two whole letters, describing exactly what the mountain did."

"Like a reporter?" Nora asked.

"Exactly like a reporter," said the tessera. "He watched a huge cloud shoot up from the mountain, shaped like a tall tree. Then ash began to fall, far across the bay."

"Was he scared?" Nora asked.

"He stayed calm, and careful, and safe," said the tessera. "And because he wrote it all down so clearly, scientists still use his name today. They call this kind of fast, powerful eruption a **'Plinian eruption'** — after Pliny."

Nora's eyebrows shot up. "He got a whole kind of volcano eruption named after him? Just for writing a good letter?"

"A very good letter," said the tessera.

Nora imagined writing a letter so clear that people used her name forever. "I should write better letters," she said.

"You already write very good stories," said the tessera. "Maybe someday, someone will name something after you too."

Nora beamed, tucking that thought away like a tile in her pocket.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Ash Like a Blanket
chapters.text:
The sky over the bay turned strange, grayish-white, like a storm made of flour.

"On **August 24th**, in the year **79**," said the tessera, "ash and little bits of rock began falling from the sky, all over the town."

"That's so long ago," Nora said. "Almost two thousand years!"

"It kept falling," said the tessera, "until the whole town was buried. In some places, under as much as **twenty feet** of ash and rock. That's about as tall as two school buses stacked up."

Nora pictured it: streets, ovens, paintings, all disappearing under gray snow.

"That sounds sad," she said quietly.

"It is a little sad," said the tessera. "But it's also why we know so much. The ash covered everything so completely that it protected the whole town, like a blanket, instead of destroying it."

"A blanket that saves things instead of burying them for good," Nora said slowly.

"Exactly. And nearby, a smaller seaside town called **Herculaneum** got buried too, by a different kind of volcanic material. It even kept wooden furniture, and old scrolls of paper, safe."

"So the mountain didn't just end a town," Nora said. "It saved one."

"That's one good way to think about it," said the tessera softly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Digging It Up Again
chapters.text:
The scene shifted again. WHOOOOSH! Sunlight changed to softer, modern light.

Nora stood at the edge of a dig site. People in hats brushed dirt away from a stone wall with tiny brushes.

"These are **archaeologists**," said the tessera. "People who carefully dig up old things, to learn how people used to live."

"When did they find this place again?" Nora asked.

"People rediscovered Pompeii in **1748**," said the tessera. "Workers were digging nearby and found old walls and objects, buried for almost seventeen hundred years."

Nora watched a brush sweep sand from a tiny mosaic, just like hers.

"They still haven't found everything," said the tessera. "Only about two out of every three parts of the town have been dug up so far. New paintings and rooms keep turning up."

"So it's not finished," Nora said. "It's still a mystery."

"A very old mystery," said the tessera, "that people are still solving, today. Now, Pompeii is protected so carefully that **millions of visitors** travel from all over the world just to see it."

Nora smiled at the little mosaic in the dirt. It looked a lot like the one on her bedroom floor.

"I think," she said, "I'd like to be an archaeologist someday."

"I think," said the tessera, "you'd be a wonderful one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
WHOOOOSH! Color spun, then settled.

Nora blinked. She was back on her bedroom floor, mosaic tiles scattered around her knees.

The blue tessera tile sat quietly in her palm, glowing just a little, then going still.

"Tessera?" Nora whispered.

No answer. Just a tiny tile, warm from her hand.

She looked down at her half-finished coaster. In the corner, without even meaning to, she had pressed the tiles into a tiny spiral — just like the one on the old fountain in Pompeii.

Nora smiled and pressed one last gold tile into place. The coaster was finished.

She set it carefully on her nightstand, like a tiny time capsule of her own.

Tomorrow, she decided, she would ask her teacher if class could learn about Pompeii. Maybe even build a mosaic map of the whole town.

She pulled her blanket up to her chin, tiles glinting faintly in the dark.

Somewhere, under a mountain by the sea, a whole town was still waiting. Still keeping its secrets. Still being found, one little tile at a time.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Nora. Sleep well, little archaeologist.

new_recurring.rule: A tiny, cracked, one-eyed mosaic tile who glows gold and speaks only at bedtime. It can shrink the child and pull them into a real historical scene through a glowing tile, then returns them home and goes quiet until the next adventure.

request.care_notes: Focus on the archaeology, what scientists learned from the preserved city, and how volcanoes work. The story should not dwell on the eruption itself, describe people suffering, or emphasize death. Present it as a fascinating time capsule that helps us understand how people lived in ancient Rome.

fact_pack.summary: Pompeii was a busy Roman town near the Bay of Naples that was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. Ash and pumice covered the town so completely that it was preserved for almost 1,700 years, giving us an amazing snapshot of everyday Roman life.

facts.text: Pompeii was a Roman town in what is now southern Italy, near the modern city of Naples.
On August 24, 79 AD, the nearby volcano Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii in ash and pumice.
Before the eruption, Pompeii was a lively town of about 11,000 to 15,000 people with shops, bathhouses, theaters, and temples.
The eruption buried Pompeii under as much as 4 to 6 meters (13 to 20 feet) of volcanic ash and rock.
Many people in Pompeii escaped, but historians believe around 2,000 residents of the town died, with thousands more dying in nearby areas like Herculaneum.

A Roman writer named Pliny the Younger watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote two letters describing it in detail, which is why scientists call this kind of violent eruption a 'Plinian eruption'.
Pliny the Younger's uncle, Pliny the Elder, was a famous naval commander and author who sailed toward Pompeii to help people and died during the rescue attempt.
The eruption happened so fast that it froze the town in time, preserving bread in ovens, paintings on walls, and even graffiti on buildings.
Ash hardened around the bodies of victims, and later excavators poured plaster into the hollow spaces to make detailed casts showing their shapes and poses.
Pompeii was mostly forgotten for centuries until it was rediscovered in 1748, when workers digging in the area found ancient walls and artifacts.
Nearby Herculaneum, a smaller seaside town, was also buried by the same eruption but under a different kind of volcanic material that preserved even wooden furniture and scrolls.
Archaeologists have found colorful wall paintings called frescoes, including the famous 'Villa of the Mysteries' paintings showing mysterious rituals.
Pompeii had an advanced water system with public fountains and lead pipes bringing water throughout the town.
The town had a large amphitheater built around 70 BC, one of the oldest known Roman amphitheaters, used for gladiator games.
Archaeologists found a loaf of bread, still shaped and marked by its baker, preserved in a Pompeii oven.
A plaster cast of a dog, apparently chained and unable to escape, was found and is one of the most famous and sad discoveries from the site.
Pompeii's streets had raised stepping stones so people could cross without stepping in mud or water, while carts still passed through gaps in the stones.
Mount Vesuvius is still an active volcano today, and scientists continue to study and monitor it because millions of people live nearby.
Pompeii is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Italy's most visited archaeological parks, drawing millions of visitors each year.
Only about two-thirds of Pompeii has been excavated so far, and new discoveries, like freshly uncovered frescoes, are still being made.
Some buildings in Pompeii had advertisements and political slogans painted on their outside walls, an ancient form of public messaging.
The name 'Pompeii' likely comes from an ancient Oscan word 'pompe', meaning 'five', possibly referring to five original villages that joined together.

story.title: Isla and the City Under the Ash
story.subtitle: A midnight dig through Pompeii, 79 AD.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Lamp on the Shelf
chapters.text:
Isla was supposed to be asleep an hour ago.

Her site journal lay open instead, lit by a chipped clay lamp on the nightstand. She had bought it at a museum gift shop after a dusty tour of a Roman gallery — a stubby little thing with a spout where a wick would go. It did not actually burn. A small bulb flickered inside it, because, as the shopkeeper had said, kids kept trying to light the real ones.

Tonight the flicker came without the bulb.

The lamp guttered, like a true flame fighting a wind that wasn't there. Her window was shut tight. On the shelf above her desk, the little bronze owl bookend she'd bought the same day turned its head.

Isla did not scream. She was, after all, a person who solved mysteries for fun. "Owls don't do that," she said instead.

"Mine does." The owl's painted eyes caught the light and held it like a cat's. "Minerva. You've owned that lamp a month and never once asked who carried one like it before you."

"Who did?"

"Everyone, once," said Minerva. "Get your shoes. Pompeii is still warm."

The lamp's smoke thickened into a doorway, gray and curling, and Isla stepped through before she had time to decide whether this was sensible.

She came out onto a stone street, under a sun too bright for midnight. Buildings rose on either side, painted red and yellow, doorways open onto shops. The air smelled of bread and horses and something green cooking.

"We're not really here," Minerva said, landing on Isla's shoulder, surprisingly light for bronze. "Ghosts don't trip over Roman cobblestones. Watch, don't touch — nobody will see you, and nothing here can touch you back either."

Isla knelt instead of walking, because the street itself looked strange. Raised flat stones crossed it in a row, spaced like stepping stones over a river, with gaps just wide enough for cart wheels to pass between.

"Mud," Minerva said, before Isla could ask. "Pompeii's streets flooded when it rained, and nobody wanted wet sandals. Stepping stones let people cross dry, while carts still rolled right through the gaps."

"That's brilliant," Isla said. "That's basically a crosswalk with a loophole built in."

"This town was full of loopholes," said Minerva. "Welcome to **Pompeii**, a real town near the modern Italian city of **Naples**. Somewhere between **eleven and fifteen thousand people** lived here, packed into shops, bathhouses, and theaters. Some even think the town's name comes from an old word, *pompe*, meaning 'five' — maybe because five small villages once joined together to build one bigger town."

Isla turned in a slow circle, journal already in hand, pencil already moving. "Five villages that became one city. That's not a fact. That's a cold case."

"Everything here is a cold case," Minerva said. "That's rather the point of tonight."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Water From Everywhere
chapters.text:
Isla heard it before she saw it: water, trickling from every direction at once, like the whole town had sprung a leak.

She followed the sound down a side street and found a stone fountain built into a wall, water pouring steadily from a carved spout into a trough below. A woman filled a clay jug and walked off without a second glance, as if fountains just worked, which, Isla supposed, they did.

"Pompeii had running water before most of Europe had even thought to ask for it," said Minerva. "**Lead pipes** ran under these streets, carrying water down from the hills to public fountains like this one, and to bathhouses all across town."

"Lead pipes," Isla repeated, raising an eyebrow. "Bold choice."

"Romans were braver with their plumbing than their politics," said Minerva. "Follow the sound. There's more water where this came from."

Isla tracked the trickle three streets over, past shuttered shops and a sleeping dog, until the ground under her feet grew warm and the air turned damp. A building loomed ahead with steam curling from a gap in its roof.

"Bathhouse," Isla said, before Minerva could tell her. "I read about these. People didn't just wash here. They gossiped, worked out, argued about politics — basically the gym and the pub and the group chat, all in one building."

"Correct, and showing off," said Minerva, sounding almost proud. "Fountains sat on practically every corner, so nobody had far to walk for water. A town this size, growing this fast, needed it. Bathing wasn't a luxury here. It was Tuesday."

Isla pressed her hand toward the fountain's spout, forgetting for a second that her hand would pass straight through. It did, with no splash at all, just cool nothing.

"Right," she muttered. "Ghosts. Got it."

"Some lessons only need learning once," said Minerva, not unkindly.

Isla crouched instead, sketching the fountain's shape into her journal: the worn stone trough, the carved animal spout, the puddle nobody had bothered to wipe up in almost two thousand years. She noticed a groove in the stone, smoothed down by generations of jugs scraping the same spot, over and over.

"People used this exact fountain every single day," she said slowly. "Which means if I measured how worn the stone is, I could guess roughly how long it was used."

"Now you're thinking like someone who digs for a living," said Minerva.

"I *am* someone who digs for a living. Sort of. In my backyard. Mostly I find roots."

"Low season," said Minerva. "It happens to everyone."

A bell rang somewhere across town, deep and unhurried, and the street began to fill with people heading toward a different sound entirely: something closer to a crowd, and cheering.

"What's that?" Isla asked.

Minerva's painted eyes gleamed. "That," she said, "is where we're going next."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Oldest Stadium You Never Heard Of
chapters.text:
The crowd noise got louder, then turned into a roar, and Isla followed it to an enormous oval building with stone walls rising higher than her house.

"That," said Minerva, "is Pompeii's **amphitheater** — a big open-air stadium, oval-shaped, built so that everyone, even the people at the very top, could see what happened down in the middle."

"Like a stone Colosseum," Isla said.

"Older, actually. This one went up around **70 BC**, which makes it one of the oldest amphitheaters we know of anywhere. People came here for games — sporting contests, including gladiator matches — with crowds pulled from the whole town and beyond."

Isla climbed, unseen, up a worn stone staircase, counting rows as she went out of pure habit. Twenty, thirty, forty rows, curling around the whole oval like a wooden bowl made of stone.

"How many people fit in here?" she asked, slightly out of breath despite technically not having lungs that mattered anymore.

"More than the town itself held, some days," said Minerva. "People rode in from the farms and the smaller towns nearby just for a match. This was the biggest ticketed event for miles, and everybody wanted a seat."

At the top, Isla sat on sun-warmed stone and looked down at the oval floor, the crowd below her a blur of togas and shouting. She didn't ask Minerva to take her any closer. She had read enough about gladiator games to know she didn't need a front-row seat, and Minerva, to her credit, didn't offer one.

"What I want to know," Isla said instead, "is who cleaned up after. Forty rows of people eating, dropping things, definitely arguing about terrible seats."

"Somebody, presumably. History rarely credits the custodians."

"That's a travesty. The custodians are basically the first archaeologists. They're the ones who decide what gets left behind for people like me to find."

Minerva tilted her head, considering this with the patience of someone who had heard a great many eleven-year-olds have a great many good ideas at inconvenient volumes. "That," she said, "is an annoyingly sharp point for midnight."

A low groan rolled up from underground, more felt than heard, and the stone beneath Isla's hand gave the faintest shiver.

"What was that?" Isla's pulse ticked up, just slightly.

"Nothing that can touch you," Minerva said evenly. "This town sits on the old roots of a mountain. The ground here grumbles sometimes. Watch."

A few people below glanced at the sky, shrugged, and went straight back to the game. Nobody ran. Nobody even stood up. The tremor passed as quickly as it came, swallowed whole by the next roar of the crowd.

"They're used to it," Isla said.

"For now," said Minerva, in a tone Isla decided not to ask about just yet.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Walls That Talk
chapters.text:
Outside the amphitheater, Isla noticed something she'd missed on the way in: words. Painted words, everywhere, crawling up the walls like ivy.

"Is that... graffiti?" she asked, leaning close to a patch of red letters scrawled beside a doorway.

"In a sense," said Minerva. "Pompeii's walls were covered in painted messages — advertisements for upcoming games, the names of men running for local office, even jokes and insults scribbled by passersby. An ancient way of putting your opinion somewhere everybody would see it."

"So basically," Isla said, grinning, "the internet. On a wall. Except you can't delete it."

"Rather the opposite problem," said Minerva. "Nobody could delete it, so almost two thousand years later, we're still reading other people's old arguments."

Isla moved along the street, reading each painted slogan like a detective reading a ransom note. One begged passersby to vote for a man famous, apparently, for his honesty. Another advertised a gladiator match, complete with the names of the fighters, like a poster for a show that had already happened a thousand times before.

She stopped at a patch of wall where the paint looked newer than the rest, brighter, the plaster beneath it smoother and less cracked.

"This bit's been fixed," she said. "Recently. You can tell — the plaster doesn't quite match the rest."

"Good eye," said Minerva. "A strong earthquake shook this town some years back. Walls cracked, buildings needed patching up, and some repairs were still underway when we arrived tonight."

Isla frowned at the fresh plaster, something uneasy prickling at the edge of her thoughts. "They just rebuilt it. Like nothing happened."

"People mostly do," said Minerva. "A cracked wall gets plastered over. A frightening afternoon gets forgotten by dinnertime. That's not foolishness. That's just how a town keeps on living inside itself."

"But the ground already grumbled once tonight."

"It did," Minerva agreed. "Pompeii sat right beside a mountain the Romans mostly considered scenery. They grew grapes on its slopes. They built villas with a view of it. Nobody here called it dangerous. They called it home."

Isla looked up the street, past the rooftops, to where a green-sided mountain rose calm and ordinary against the sky — the kind of thing you'd stop noticing after a while, if you lived underneath it every single day.

"That's Vesuvius," she said. It wasn't quite a question.

"That's Vesuvius," Minerva confirmed.

Isla wrote the word in her journal, underlined it once, and did not ask the question sitting right behind her teeth. She had read enough mysteries to know when a story was circling toward its middle.

"Minerva," she said instead, closing the journal. "What day is it? Here, I mean."

The owl was quiet a moment, which from a bronze bird was its own kind of answer.

"**August the twenty-fourth**," Minerva said finally. "Of the year **79**. Tomorrow, if you'd like to call it that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Mountain Wakes
chapters.text:
Minerva didn't take Isla back to the street. Instead, the smoke-doorway opened onto a hillside across a wide stretch of water, a town called Misenum spread below them, boats bobbing in its harbor.

"Safer view," Minerva said. "Trust me."

A young man stood nearby, writing tablets balanced on his knee, staring across the bay with the fixed, scribbling attention of someone determined to get every detail exactly right.

"That's **Pliny the Younger**," Minerva said. "A young Roman who happened to be visiting his uncle that week. He watched what happened next from almost exactly where we're standing, and afterward he wrote it all down in two letters so careful that scientists still use his words today."

Across the bay, Vesuvius had changed. A column of ash and smoke rose from its top, climbing impossibly high, then spreading sideways at the summit like the top of an enormous tree.

"It looks like a pine tree," Isla murmured.

"That's almost exactly what Pliny wrote," said Minerva. "Scientists later started calling this kind of tall, violent eruption a '**Plinian eruption**' — named for him, because his letters described it so well that it became the word for this whole type of blast."

Isla's hands had gone very still around her journal. "Is everyone all right?"

"Watch what his uncle does," Minerva said, instead of answering directly.

Down in the harbor, an older man was shouting orders, and sailors were running to untie ships — not away from the bay, but toward it, toward Pompeii's side of the water, where the ash was falling thickest.

"**Pliny the Elder**," said Minerva. "A naval commander, and a man who studied the natural world for fun. When word came that people across the bay needed rescuing, he didn't sail away from the danger. He sailed his ships straight toward it, to pull people out."

Isla watched the little ships cut across the water, small and stubborn against that enormous gray sky. "That's either the bravest thing I've ever seen, or the worst plan in history."

"Possibly both," Minerva admitted. "Bravery often is."

The ash kept falling, for that whole long day and into the next, burying Pompeii under four to six meters of ash and broken rock — that's **thirteen to twenty feet**, enough to swallow a house right up to its roof.

Isla's throat tightened. "Did everyone get out?"

Minerva's answer came slow and honest, the way true things sometimes need to. "No. Many people in Pompeii did not survive that day. But some did — carried out by boats just like the ones you're watching now, by sailors willing to row toward smoke instead of away from it."

Isla didn't say anything for a while. She watched the little boats until they'd vanished into the gray, and the ash kept falling, soft as the worst snow imaginable, over a town she had been standing inside only an hour before.

"He went toward it," she said finally. "On purpose. To help people he'd never even met."

"That's generally what the word 'brave' is for," said Minerva.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Frozen
chapters.text:
The smoke-doorway opened again, and the roar of that long gray day was gone. In its place: silence, and a hillside of hardened ash where a town used to be.

"How long has it been?" Isla asked.

"Long enough," said Minerva. "Watch where you put your feet. We're not quite in 79 anymore, and we're not quite anywhere else, either. Call it the part of the story that happens in between."

The town reappeared beneath them in pieces, the way memory sometimes does — walls, then roofs, then rooms, as if the ash itself were deciding how much to show. Isla walked through a doorway into what had clearly been a bakery, flour dust still ghosting the counters, and stopped at the oven.

Inside it sat a round loaf of bread, still shaped by the hands that made it, a faint maker's mark pressed into its crust.

"That's bread," Isla said, very quietly. "That's actual bread. From that actual morning."

"The eruption moved fast enough to freeze the ordinary right alongside the extraordinary," said Minerva. "Bread in an oven. Paint still looking wet on a wall. Even words scratched into plaster by someone bored, mid-argument, mid-joke. All of it kept almost exactly as it was, like the town took one long breath and never quite let it out."

Isla moved to the next room, where a wall painting stretched floor to ceiling: figures in red and gold, caught in some kind of ceremony Isla couldn't quite puzzle out — a woman reaching, another turning away, something unspoken passing between them that eighteen centuries hadn't managed to fully explain.

"These are called **frescoes**," Minerva said. "Paintings made right into wet wall plaster, so the color sinks into the wall instead of just sitting on top of it. Some of the finest ones in this whole town are in a building people later nicknamed the **Villa of the Mysteries**, because nobody's entirely sure what the painted scene is even showing."

"A mystery," Isla said, "that's survived two thousand years, and nobody's cracked it yet."

"Correct."

Isla crouched and studied the painted woman's face, half-turned from the room, keeping some secret the ash had buried right along with everything else.

"I want to solve it," Isla said.

"Most people who study this town eventually say the exact same thing," said Minerva. "It's rather the job description."

Isla straightened, brushing invisible dust from knees that technically couldn't get dusty, and looked around at the quiet, ash-held rooms stretching in every direction, waiting.

"How much of this town has even been dug up?" she asked.

"Less than you'd think," said Minerva. "We'll get to that. First, there's somewhere smaller I want you to see. A neighbor, of sorts."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Other Town
chapters.text:
The next doorway opened onto a smaller town by the sea, close enough to Vesuvius to share its bad luck, far enough away to meet it differently.

"**Herculaneum**," said Minerva. "A smaller seaside town, buried by the very same eruption, on the very same day, by the very same mountain. But not by the same kind of ash."

Isla looked around. The buildings here felt oddly complete, wood doorframes still standing, a wooden bed frame visible through a window, even what looked like a scroll rack in a nearby library.

"Wood," Isla said, surprised. "Actual wood survived? In Pompeii everything wooden rotted away centuries ago."

"Different burial, different result," Minerva said. "Herculaneum wasn't buried by falling ash and pumice — light, bubbly rock that's almost airy enough to float — the way Pompeii was. It was covered instead by a scorching wave of volcanic material that sealed everything up tight almost instantly. No air left to let things rot. Furniture survived. So did scrolls."

Isla crouched by the scroll rack, where blackened, tightly rolled scrolls sat stacked like firewood. "Can you even read those?"

"Not easily," Minerva admitted. "They're baked solid all the way through, and for centuries nobody could safely unroll one without it crumbling to pieces. People today are still inventing clever new ways to read them without ever unrolling them at all."

"That's insane," Isla said, delighted. "That's a locked box nobody's fully picked yet."

"I did mention this town had excellent cold cases."

Isla walked slowly through the quiet street, comparing it against the one she'd stood in hours — or centuries — before. Same mountain, same single terrible day, two completely different kinds of leftover evidence.

"So if you wanted to understand everything about Roman life," she said slowly, thinking it through out loud, "you'd actually need both towns. Pompeii, for the walls and the paintings and the streets. Herculaneum, for the wood and the scrolls and the things ash usually eats first."

"Now you're doing actual science," Minerva said, sounding pleased in the dry, economical way she seemed to allow herself pleasure. "Two disasters, two different kinds of evidence, one clearer picture once you put them together."

Isla smiled, tucking that thought away like a coin into a pocket. "I like towns that keep secrets on purpose."

"These two didn't keep them on purpose," Minerva said. "They just happened to keep them *well*. There's a difference, and it's worth remembering, for a girl who likes mysteries as much as you do."

"Noted," Isla said. "Where to next?"

"Somewhere a very long time later," said Minerva, "where somebody finally started digging."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Found Again
chapters.text:
The doorway this time opened onto daylight Isla recognized — modern daylight, with tour buses parked along a road and a crowd of visitors in sun hats.

"We skipped a lot," Isla said.

"Centuries," Minerva agreed. "Pompeii vanished from memory for a very long time after it was buried. New towns grew up nearby. Grapes grew on the mountain again. Nobody quite remembered what lay underneath, until **1748**, when workers digging in the area struck ancient walls and found objects that made it very clear something old was down there."

"Just, what, by accident?"

"More or less. That's often how the biggest discoveries start. Somebody's shovel hits something it really shouldn't."

Isla walked among the ropes and signs, past excavated streets that matched, almost exactly, the ones she'd walked through hours before — fountains and stepping stones and all. Tourists leaned over railings, snapping photographs of the same bakery oven she had stood beside, the bread still sitting there, protected now behind glass.

"People are still finding things," Minerva said, nodding toward a roped-off section where archaeologists in sun hats brushed carefully at a half-uncovered wall. "Only about **two-thirds** of this town has been dug up so far. New rooms, new paintings, even new bits of graffiti, keep turning up."

"Two-thirds," Isla repeated. "So there's still a whole third of this place nobody's seen since the day it happened."

"A city-sized cold case, still open," said Minerva. "This whole site is protected now — a place the world has agreed matters enough to look after carefully. People call that a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. Millions of visitors come every single year, just to walk where you walked tonight."

Isla looked up at Vesuvius, green and quiet above the ruins, tourists posing for photos with it in the background like it was simply scenery.

"Is it still—"

"Still an active volcano, yes," Minerva said. "Scientists keep a close watch on it, because a great many people live near it today. It's resting. Mountains like this one don't retire."

Isla closed her journal, which had somehow filled with pages she didn't remember drawing — the stepping stones, the fountain, the amphitheater, the painted woman mid-turn. Proof, maybe. Or just a very good dream with excellent handwriting.

The smoke-doorway opened one last time, back into her own bedroom, the little clay lamp flickering gently on her nightstand like nothing at all had happened.

Minerva settled back onto the shelf, going still and bronze and ordinary again — except for the faint gray dust now clinging to one wing.

Isla touched it, and her fingertip came away the color of old ash.

"We'll go further next time," Minerva said, voice already fading toward bookend silence. "There's always another third."

Isla climbed into bed, journal still open to a sketch of a mountain she hadn't drawn herself, and already, she was making a list of questions for tomorrow.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there would be more questions than answers — just the way she liked it.

true_facts.text: **Pompeii** was a real Roman town near the modern Italian city of **Naples**.
On **August 24, 79 AD**, the volcano **Mount Vesuvius** erupted and buried Pompeii.
Before the eruption, Pompeii was home to somewhere between **eleven and fifteen thousand people**.
The eruption buried the town under **thirteen to twenty feet** of ash and broken rock.
**Pliny the Younger** wrote two letters about the eruption so detailed that this kind of blast is now called a **Plinian eruption**.
The eruption happened so fast it froze ordinary things in place, like **bread in an oven** and paint still looking wet on walls.
Pompeii was forgotten for centuries until it was rediscovered in **1748**, when workers digging nearby struck ancient walls.
The nearby town of **Herculaneum** was buried by the same eruption but by a different kind of volcanic material, which preserved **wood and scrolls**.
**Lead pipes** carried water under the streets to public fountains and bathhouses all over town.
Pompeii's big oval **amphitheater** was built around **70 BC**, one of the oldest known, and used for games.
A whole loaf of **bread**, still marked by its baker, was found preserved inside a Pompeii oven.
Pompeii's streets had **raised stepping stones** so people could cross without getting wet, while carts rolled through the gaps.
Pompeii is now a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**, visited by millions of people every year.
Only about **two-thirds** of Pompeii has been dug up so far, with new discoveries still turning up.

fact_pack.summary: Pompeii was a busy Roman town near the Bay of Naples that was buried by the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 AD. Ash and pumice covered the town so completely that it was preserved for almost 1,700 years, giving us an amazing snapshot of everyday Roman life.

facts.text: Pompeii was a Roman town in what is now southern Italy, near the modern city of Naples.
On August 24, 79 AD, the nearby volcano Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried Pompeii in ash and pumice.
Before the eruption, Pompeii was a lively town of about 11,000 to 15,000 people with shops, bathhouses, theaters, and temples.
The eruption buried Pompeii under as much as 4 to 6 meters (13 to 20 feet) of volcanic ash and rock.
Many people in Pompeii escaped, but historians believe around 2,000 residents of the town died, with thousands more dying in nearby areas like Herculaneum.

A Roman writer named Pliny the Younger watched the eruption from across the bay and wrote two letters describing it in detail, which is why scientists call this kind of violent eruption a 'Plinian eruption'.
Pliny the Younger's uncle, Pliny the Elder, was a famous naval commander and author who sailed toward Pompeii to help people and died during the rescue attempt.
The eruption happened so fast that it froze the town in time, preserving bread in ovens, paintings on walls, and even graffiti on buildings.
Ash hardened around the bodies of victims, and later excavators poured plaster into the hollow spaces to make detailed casts showing their shapes and poses.
Pompeii was mostly forgotten for centuries until it was rediscovered in 1748, when workers digging in the area found ancient walls and artifacts.
Nearby Herculaneum, a smaller seaside town, was also buried by the same eruption but under a different kind of volcanic material that preserved even wooden furniture and scrolls.
Archaeologists have found colorful wall paintings called frescoes, including the famous 'Villa of the Mysteries' paintings showing mysterious rituals.
Pompeii had an advanced water system with public fountains and lead pipes bringing water throughout the town.
The town had a large amphitheater built around 70 BC, one of the oldest known Roman amphitheaters, used for gladiator games.
Archaeologists found a loaf of bread, still shaped and marked by its baker, preserved in a Pompeii oven.
A plaster cast of a dog, apparently chained and unable to escape, was found and is one of the most famous and sad discoveries from the site.
Pompeii's streets had raised stepping stones so people could cross without stepping in mud or water, while carts still passed through gaps in the stones.
Mount Vesuvius is still an active volcano today, and scientists continue to study and monitor it because millions of people live nearby.
Pompeii is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of Italy's most visited archaeological parks, drawing millions of visitors each year.
Only about two-thirds of Pompeii has been excavated so far, and new discoveries, like freshly uncovered frescoes, are still being made.
Some buildings in Pompeii had advertisements and political slogans painted on their outside walls, an ancient form of public messaging.
The name 'Pompeii' likely comes from an ancient Oscan word 'pompe', meaning 'five', possibly referring to five original villages that joined together.

story.title: Ivy and the Rainbow Puddle
story.subtitle: A rainy-day adventure with Pip the raindrop

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Puddle Paint
chapters.text:
Ivy sat on her floor. She painted big circles. Red. Yellow. Blue.

Rain tapped the window. Tap, tap, tap.

She peeked outside. A puddle was glowing! It glowed every color.

"Ooh!" said Ivy.

She tiptoed to the door. She opened it wide.

A tiny drop popped up from the puddle. It had a swirly, rainbow shine.

"Hello, Ivy!" said the drop. "I'm Pip. Want to see how rainbows are made?"

Ivy grinned. "Yes, yes, yes!"

She held her paintbrush tight. Pip glowed bright. WHOOSH! The puddle pulled them both inside.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Sun and Rain Together
chapters.text:
They landed on a soft, fluffy cloud. Sun shined on one side. Rain fell on the other side.

Pip said, "Rainbows need two things. They need sun. They need rain. Both at once!"

Ivy looked at the sun. She looked at the rain. "Sun and rain, together!" she said.

Pip spun in a happy circle. "That's why rainbows pop out right after a rain shower, when the sun peeks out!"

Splish splash! The cloud bounced.

"I want to help make one!" said Ivy.

"Then come closer," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Inside a Raindrop
chapters.text:
Pip floated next to a tiny raindrop. It was round and clear, like a little glass ball.

"Watch," said Pip. "Sunlight goes inside the drop."

The light zoomed in. It bent, like a bendy straw.

Inside, it bounced off the back wall. Then it bent again on its way out.

Out popped every color! Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.

Ivy dipped her paintbrush in the drop. Colors swirled onto the bristles.

"It's like painting with light!" she giggled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Turn Around
chapters.text:
Pip and Ivy landed on a hill after the rain. The sun felt warm on her back.

"To see a rainbow," said Pip, "the sun must be behind you. The rain must be in front."

Ivy turned all the way around. Sun on her back. Soft mist in front.

She gasped. A big rainbow arched across the sky!

"I turned and I found it!" she said.

Pip bounced with joy. "You found the trick all by yourself!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Thinker Who Watched Light
chapters.text:
Next they floated to a cozy room with a lamp.

A kind old man with a long beard looked up. "This is Ibn al-Haytham," said Pip. "A long time ago, he watched how light travels."

He smiled at Ivy. "Light moves in a straight line, little painter. Until it meets a raindrop."

Ivy nodded. "Then it bends!"

"Just so," he chuckled.

Ivy waved goodbye. He waved back, his lamp glowing soft and warm.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Glass Ball Friend
chapters.text:
They floated into a room full of shiny glass balls.

A smiling man held one up to the sun. "I'm Kamal al-Din al-Farisi," he said. "I use glass balls to practice how raindrops bend light."

He tilted the ball. Colors spilled out, just like the raindrop had!

Ivy clapped. "A pretend raindrop!"

"A wonderful one," Pip agreed.

The ball spun, splashing light everywhere. SPARKLE!

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Prism Trick
chapters.text:
They landed in a sunny room with a man and a small glass shape.

"I'm Isaac Newton," he said. "This little glass shape is called a prism."

He held it to the sun. WHOOSH! White light turned into a rainbow on the wall.

"White light hides all the colors inside," he said.

Ivy's eyes went wide. "Just like the raindrop!"

He smiled. "Just like that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
WHOOSH! Pip and Ivy popped back through the puddle door.

Ivy was home on her floor. Her paintbrush was still in her hand.

Outside, the rain had stopped. The sun peeked out.

Ivy ran to the window. A soft rainbow glowed in the sky.

She picked up her brush and painted one more rainbow, right by her bed.

"Goodnight, Pip," she whispered.

A tiny sparkle glowed in her painting, and then it was still.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ivy. Paint bright, sleep tight.

true_facts.text: A rainbow starts when sunlight goes inside a tiny **raindrop**.
Inside the drop, the light **bends**, like a bendy straw.
The light **bounces** off the back wall inside the drop.
Then the light bends again and comes out as **colors**.
Rainbows need both the **sun** and the **rain**, at the same time.
That is why rainbows often pop out right after a **rain shower**.
To see a rainbow, the **sun** must be behind you.
The **rain** must be in front of you.

fact_pack.summary: Rainbows appear when sunlight passes through raindrops and gets bent, split into colors, and bounced back to our eyes. They are a science-and-wonder topic: a physics lesson dressed up as a beautiful arc in the sky, with plenty of fun details for kids to explore.

facts.text: A rainbow forms when sunlight enters a raindrop, bends, reflects off the inside back of the drop, and bends again as it exits.
This bending of light is called refraction, and it happens because light slows down and changes direction when it moves from air into water.
White sunlight is actually made of many colors mixed together, and raindrops separate them because each color bends by a slightly different amount.
The classic rainbow color order is red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet, often remembered with the name 'Roy G. Biv'.
Red always appears on the outer edge of a rainbow and violet on the inner edge because red bends the least and violet bends the most.
To see a rainbow, the sun must be behind you and rain (or spray) must be in front of you.
Rainbows are actually full circles, but we usually only see an arc because the ground blocks the bottom half.
From an airplane, people sometimes see a complete circular rainbow because there is no ground in the way.
Every person actually sees a slightly different rainbow, made from different raindrops, because the angle of light to your eyes is unique to your position.
A rainbow always appears in the part of the sky directly opposite the sun, centered on a point called the antisolar point.
Sometimes a fainter second rainbow appears above the main one, with its colors reversed, caused by light bouncing twice inside the raindrops.
The dark strip of sky between a primary and secondary rainbow is called Alexander's band, named after the ancient Greek philosopher Alexander of Aphrodisias who described it around 200 AD.
Rainbows can also form in mist, waterfalls, garden hose spray, and even moonlight, where they are called moonbows.
Moonbows are usually so faint that they look white or gray to human eyes, though cameras can capture their colors.
The scientist Isaac Newton showed in the 1660s that a glass prism could split white light into the same rainbow of colors, proving light itself contains all the colors.
The Persian scientist Ibn al-Haytham and later Kamal al-Din al-Farisi studied light and rainbows in raindrops centuries before Newton, around the 1000s and 1300s.
Many cultures have myths about rainbows, such as the Norse story of Bifrost, a rainbow bridge connecting Earth to the home of the gods.
In the Bible, the rainbow appears as a sign of a promise from God to Noah after a great flood.
Many cultures tell of a pot of gold at the end of a rainbow, especially in Irish folklore involving leprechauns, though a rainbow's end is never a real fixed spot since it moves as you move.
Because a rainbow depends on where the viewer stands, you can never actually walk up to or touch one.
Rainbows need both sunlight and water droplets at the same time, which is why they often appear during or right after a rain shower when the sun peeks out.
A rainbow's size in the sky is always about the same, spanning roughly 42 degrees from the antisolar point for the primary bow.
The rainbow flag, created by artist Gilbert Baker in 1978, uses rainbow colors as a symbol of pride and diversity.
Rainbows are studied in a branch of science called optics, which explores how light behaves, bends, and reflects.

story.title: Priya, Dev, and the Rainbow Made of Squirts
story.subtitle: A damp, colorful trip through sunlight and rain

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Squirt That Started It All
chapters.text:
Dev knelt on the carpet, water pistol loaded. Priya sat nearby, painting a sunset. Late sun poured gold through the window.

"Watch this," Dev said. He squirted a fine mist into the sunbeam.

A stripe of color popped onto the wall. Red, orange, yellow, green, blue. A tiny rainbow, right there.

Priya dropped her paintbrush. "You made a rainbow with a **water pistol**?"

The rainbow buzzed, then burst into a glowing dot with a tiny face.

"Hiya! I'm Lumi," it said. "I'm made of bent sunlight. Squirt me again, big guy."

Dev squirted again. The dot swelled into a shimmering doorway.

"To see a rainbow," Lumi said, "the sun has to be behind you, and rain — or spray — in front. You got both. Nice work, Dev."

Priya poked the door with her paintbrush. "Where does this go?"

"Into the rainbow," said Lumi. "Grab your brother. Let's go."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Inside One Single Raindrop
chapters.text:
The doorway swallowed them with a soft **WHOOSH**. They landed inside something round and wobbly, like a giant bubble.

"Welcome to one raindrop," said Lumi. "You're small enough to see inside it."

A beam of white light zoomed in through the curved edge. It bent sideways the moment it hit the water.

"That bending is called **refraction**," Lumi said. "Light slows down in water and turns, like a bike turning on wet grass."

The beam hit the back wall, bounced like a ball off a mirror, then bent again leaving the drop.

Priya watched closely, the way she watched paint spread on wet paper. "It bends twice. In, bounce, out."

"Every raindrop in the sky does that," said Lumi.

Dev squirted a tiny spray at the drop wall, just to test it. Nothing happened. Lumi laughed so hard she wobbled.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Secret Colors Hiding in White
chapters.text:
Outside the drop, the white beam kept traveling. It hit a floating triangle of glass, like a tiny glass kite.

"Watch the white light," Lumi said. "It isn't just white."

The glass triangle, called a **prism**, split the beam into a stripe of colors: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, purple.

"A scientist named **Isaac Newton** did this exact trick with a prism, back in the **1660s**," said Lumi. "He proved white sunlight is really every color, mixed together."

Priya gasped. "IT'S HIDING ALL THE COLORS!"

"Sort of backwards from mixing paint," grinned Lumi, "but yes."

"Why's red on the outside, purple on the inside?" asked Dev.

"Red bends the least. Purple bends the most," said Lumi.

Priya lined up her paint tubes to match the order. "Got it. Easy."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Rainbow That's Actually a Circle
chapters.text:
Lumi swooped them up above the clouds. Cold wind rushed past, but somehow it didn't feel cold.

"Look down," said Lumi.

Below spread a complete circle of color, a perfect glowing ring.

"RAINBOWS ARE CIRCLES?" Dev shouted.

"Always," said Lumi. "You only see an arc because the ground blocks the bottom half. Up here, no ground is in the way. Some airplane passengers even see this exact full circle."

Dev pointed his water pistol at the ring, as if he could squirt it bigger. "Can I keep it?"

"Nobody can," said Lumi gently.

Priya laughed. "Dev wants to bottle a rainbow."

"I would," Dev said, very seriously.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Two Kids, Two Different Rainbows
chapters.text:
They landed on a grassy hill, sun behind them, soft rain ahead. A rainbow arched overhead.

"Priya, stand here. Dev, stand there," said Lumi.

They moved a few steps apart.

Priya's rainbow sat slightly left. Dev's sat slightly right. Same sky, same rain, two different rainbows.

"Everybody sees their very own rainbow," Lumi explained. "It depends exactly where your eyes are standing."

Dev ran toward his rainbow, arms out. It stayed exactly the same distance away.

"Nobody can walk up to a rainbow," Lumi called. "It moves whenever you move."

Dev flopped onto the grass, out of breath. "Rude rainbow."

Priya cracked up. "That's the best kind of rude."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Rainbow's Shy Cousin
chapters.text:
A second, fainter stripe of color appeared above the first. Its colors ran the opposite way, purple on the outside this time.

"That's a **double rainbow**," said Lumi. "Light bounces twice inside some drops instead of once. The colors flip."

"Flipped like a pancake," said Priya.

"Exactly," said Lumi.

Night fell fast. A pale, ghostly arch glowed over the hill, almost no color at all.

"That's a **moonbow**," said Lumi. "Same trick, but moonlight instead of sunlight. Moonlight's too dim for our eyes to catch all the colors, so it looks almost white."

Dev squirted a fine mist up into the moonlight. A whisper-pale arc flickered, there and gone.

"See?" said Lumi. "Shy little thing."

"I MADE A MOONBOW!" Dev beamed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Old Stories About the Sky's Arch
chapters.text:
Lumi led them to a cozy patch of fog that glowed like a movie screen. Pictures began to shine inside it.

"People have told stories about rainbows forever," said Lumi. "Long ago, the Vikings called one **Bifrost**, a glowing bridge up to the home of their gods."

Priya grabbed her sketchbook and started drawing a bridge made of colored light.

"In another old story," said Lumi softly, "after a big flood ends, a rainbow shows up in the sky. It's a sign of a promise, that good times are coming back."

"That's a nice way to end a tricky story," said Priya.

"In Ireland," Lumi grinned, "some say there's a pot of gold where the rainbow ends. That one's just a fun old tale, not a true fact."

Dev's eyes went huge. "Can we find it?!"

"Nobody ever has," said Lumi. "A rainbow's end isn't a real spot. It moves when you move."

Priya drew a tiny cartoon guarding an empty pot, tongue sticking out. "Joke's on the legend."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Carpet
chapters.text:
The fog screen folded up like a blanket. Lumi spun, and the doorway reappeared on the bedroom wall.

"Time to go home," said Lumi. "Squirt me whenever you want to visit again, Dev."

"Every single day," Dev promised.

They stepped through. **WHOOSH**. Carpet. Paintbrush. Water pistol, still a little damp.

On the wall, a small rainbow glowed, fading slowly like a nightlight.

Priya picked up her sketchbook. She'd drawn a bridge, a leprechaun, and seven careful stripes of color, in the exact right order.

Dev checked his water pistol. Still half full. "Tomorrow," he announced, "I'm making a rainbow at breakfast."

"Tell your cereal milk I said hi," Priya said, grinning.

Dev threw a pillow at her. She threw it right back.

Outside, the real sun was setting, gold and soft.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Priya. Goodnight, Dev. Keep squirting rainbows into your dreams.

story.title: Milo, Juno, and the Brick That Found the Sharks
story.subtitle: A splashy, CLICK-y trip to the bottom of the sea

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
Milo lay on his bedroom floor. He built a tiny LEGO shark.

Juno sat beside him. She lined up her dinosaur toys in a neat row.

"Dinosaurs are the best," said Juno.

"Sharks are even older," said Milo.

Then the red brick on the shelf began to glow. It glowed bright red. It went **CLICK**.

"It's doing the thing again!" said Juno.

The brick grew warm. It grew big. A door of light opened in the carpet.

**WHOOOOSH!** Milo and Juno zoomed down, down, down. They landed with a splash in blue water.

A friendly shark swam up. He had a big smile and shiny gray skin.

"Hello!" he said. "I'm Splash. I show kids around the ocean."

"Are your bones hard like mine?" asked Milo.

"Nope!" said Splash. "My skeleton is **bendy**. Bendy like the top part of your ear. Not hard bone at all."

Milo wiggled his own ear. "Whoa. Bendy bones!"

Juno wiggled her ear too. "Bendy like noodles!"

Splash laughed a bubbly laugh. "Close enough, Juno. Follow me, friends. I'll show you something amazing."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: So Many Sharks!
chapters.text:
Splash swam past rocks and bubbles. Bubbles went **POP, POP, POP**.

"Guess how many kinds of sharks live in the sea," said Splash.

Milo thought hard. "Ten?"

"More than five hundred kinds!" said Splash.

Juno's eyes went wide. "That's SO many!"

"Big ones, small ones, flat ones, spotty ones," said Splash. "All kinds of shapes and sizes."

"Were there sharks when dinosaurs were alive?" asked Juno.

"Sharks came first," said Splash. "Long, long before dinosaurs. More than four hundred million years ago. Before trees even grew tall."

Juno gasped a big gasp. "Sharks are OLDER than dinosaurs?"

"Yes!" said Splash. "Sharks have been swimming a very, very long time."

Milo gave Juno a high five. "Your dinosaurs are old. But sharks win!"

Juno giggled and clapped her hands. "Okay, okay. Sharks win this one."

"Sharks win, sharks win!" she sang, kicking her feet in the water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
A huge shadow passed over them. It blocked out the sun.

Juno grabbed Milo's hand. "Is that a monster?"

"No," said Splash, smiling wide. "That's a whale shark. The biggest fish in the whole sea."

The whale shark glided by, slow and calm. It was longer than a school bus.

"Does it eat big fish?" asked Milo.

"Nope," said Splash. "It eats tiny floaty bits called plankton. It opens its huge mouth. It gulps water. Then it swallows the tiny bits. Nothing big at all."

Juno let go of Milo's hand. "A giant who eats tiny snacks?"

"Exactly," said Splash.

Milo grinned. "That's like a giant who only eats crumbs."

Juno laughed so hard she snorted. "Crumbs for a giant! Crumbs for a giant!"

The whale shark gave one slow, gentle flick of its tail. Then it swam on, big and gentle and quiet.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Megalodon's Giant Tooth
chapters.text:
They swam down to a sandy patch. Something huge and white lay in the sand.

"Is that a tooth?" asked Milo.

"A megalodon tooth," said Splash. "Megalodon was a giant shark. Bigger than a bus!"

Juno picked it up. It was as long as her whole hand.

"Can we see one?" asked Juno. "A real live megalodon?"

"Not anymore," said Splash gently. "Megalodon isn't around anymore. It lived a long, long time ago. Now we only find its teeth, hiding in the sand."

"That's a little sad," said Milo.

"It is," said Splash. "But the tooth tells us the story. That's how we know megalodon was real, even though we never saw one."

Juno held the tooth up high, like a trophy. "A dinosaur-shark!"

Splash chuckled. "Close enough, Juno. Close enough."

Milo tapped the tooth softly. "I'm going to build one just like this. Out of LEGO."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Teeth, Teeth, Everywhere
chapters.text:
Splash opened his mouth wide. Rows and rows of teeth shined inside.

"Whoa!" said Milo. "So many teeth!"

"Sharks grow new teeth all the time," said Splash. "When one falls out, another moves up to take its place."

"Like me losing a tooth?" asked Milo.

"Kind of," said Splash. "But sharks do it their whole life. Thousands and thousands of teeth, over and over!"

Juno poked Splash's skin gently. "Your skin feels funny. Like sandpaper!"

"That's because of teeny tiny bumps," said Splash. "Little scales shaped like tiny teeth. They help me zoom through the water fast."

Milo stroked the skin too. "Rough, but cool."

Splash did a fast little zoom through the water. **WHOOOOSH!** "See? Smooth and speedy."

Juno clapped. "Do it again, do it again!"

Splash zoomed in a circle, and they both cheered.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Snouts, Heads, and Walking Fins
chapters.text:
"Watch this," said Splash. He wiggled his nose.

"Sharks can feel tiny zaps," he said. "Other animals make tiny bits of electricity. Sharks feel it through little holes in their snout, even in the dark."

"Like a secret power!" said Milo.

Then a strange shark swam by. Its head was shaped like a hammer.

Juno pointed. "That shark's head is funny!"

"That's a hammerhead," said Splash. "Its wide head spreads its eyes far apart. That helps it see all around, like looking both ways at once."

"Can sharks walk?" asked Juno.

"Some can!" said Splash. "The epaulette shark uses its fins like little legs. It walks across the rocks when the water gets low."

Milo tried walking like a shark, flopping his arms like fins.

Juno copied him, giggling. "I'm a walking shark! Look at me walk!"

They flopped and walked together until they both tumbled into a pile of bubbles.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
They swam up to a lady in a diving suit. She smiled behind her mask.

"This is Eugenie Clark," said Splash. "Everyone calls her the Shark Lady."

"Why?" asked Milo.

"She spent her whole life studying sharks," said Splash. "She showed everyone sharks are curious. She even taught sharks little tricks."

"Sharks can learn tricks?" said Juno. "Like my dinosaurs in my games!"

"Just like that," said Splash, laughing.

"Sharks help the ocean too," said Splash. "They eat the sick or weak fish. That keeps all the other fish happy and healthy."

"So sharks are ocean helpers," said Milo.

"The best kind," said Splash.

Eugenie Clark waved at them through the water. "Keep being curious, you two."

Milo and Juno waved back big, splashy waves. Juno waved with both hands.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Again
chapters.text:
"Time to go home," said Splash. "Hold the brick tight."

Milo pulled the glowing red brick from his pocket. It pulsed warm and red.

"Goodbye, Splash!" said Juno.

"Goodbye, friends," said Splash. "Come back and play well in the sea again."

**WHOOOOSH!** The water spun into light. Milo and Juno zoomed up, up, up.

They landed softly on the bedroom carpet. The brick gave one last **CLICK** and went still.

Milo looked down. Next to his LEGO shark sat a shiny LEGO tooth, shaped just like megalodon's.

"A keepsake!" said Milo.

Juno yawned a big, dinosaur-sized yawn. "Sharks win tonight."

Milo tucked the tooth brick next to his shark model. Outside, the moon shone bright and round.

They climbed into bed, still smelling a little like the sea.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Juno. Play well.

Bull sharks tolerate both salty ocean water and fresh river water, and have been found swimming far upriver.

story.title: Jack and Ellie and the Mermaid's Purse of Sharks
story.subtitle: A splashy swim through four hundred million years of sharks.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Purse
chapters.text:
Jack lined up seashells in a row on the rug. Ellie held a small black pouch with curly strings, like a tiny bag.

"It's a mermaid's purse," she said. "Maybe a mermaid forgot it."

Jack grinned. "That's not quite a mermaid's purse. Well, sort of. A **shark** laid it, not a mermaid."

Ellie gasped. "Sharks don't carry purses!"

"Some sharks lay eggs inside a little case like this," Jack said. "People just call it a mermaid's purse because it looks like a tiny bag."

The pouch began to glow soft green in Ellie's hand. It hummed like a seashell held to your ear. **CLICK.** The glow swirled bigger and bigger, until the carpet looked like the top of the sea.

A small shark popped his head out of the glow, fins waving like little paddles. "Evening!" he said. "I'm Pip. Want to see four hundred million years of sharks before bedtime?"

Jack and Ellie looked at each other.

"YES," they shouted, at exactly the same time, which made them laugh, because they never agreed on anything.

Pip winked. "Then hold the purse. It's our ticket."

**WHOOOSH.** The green light swallowed the bedroom, and the carpet turned to cool, salty water.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Before the Dinosaurs
chapters.text:
They popped up in a strange blue sea. No boats, no towels, nothing but water and shapes swimming below.

"Where are the dinosaurs?" Ellie asked, looking around.

"Nowhere yet," Pip said. "Sharks showed up more than **four hundred million years ago** — before dinosaurs, before trees even grew on land."

Jack's mouth dropped open. "Before TREES?"

"Before trees," Pip said. "Sharks are some of the oldest swimmers there ever were."

A shape glided by, long and smooth, with no stiff bones at all. Jack watched it bend and curl, careful not to touch.

"We look, we don't touch," Pip reminded him gently. "Even friendly sharks like their space."

"Its body looks so bendy," Jack said.

"That's because sharks don't have hard bones," Pip explained. "Their whole skeleton is made of **cartilage** — the same bendy stuff as the squishy part of your ear. Give your ear a wiggle."

Ellie wiggled her ear and giggled. "Shark bones are EAR bones!"

"Not quite," Jack said, "but close enough to be funny."

Pip laughed so hard he did a little flip. "There are more than **five hundred** different kinds of sharks swimming around today," he said, "and we only just met one."

Ellie counted on her fingers and gave up at ten. "That's a LOT of sharks."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Giant Tooth
chapters.text:
A shadow bigger than their house drifted under the water.

Ellie grabbed Jack's sleeve. "Is that going to get us?"

"Nope," Pip said quickly. "That's not even swimming anymore. That was Megalodon, the biggest shark that ever lived. It's **extinct** now, which just means it isn't swimming anywhere today."

Ellie let go of Jack's sleeve, relieved. "So it's pretend?"

"It was very real once," Pip said. "We just can't visit it for real. Soft shark bodies don't last long in the ground, so almost everything we know about Megalodon comes from its teeth, which turned into **fossils** — shapes left behind in rock after a very, very long time."

Jack swam closer to a huge tooth stuck in the sandy floor, as long as his whole hand.

"That's a real Megalodon tooth," Pip said.

Jack held his hand next to it. "It's bigger than my hand!"

"Giant shark, giant tooth," said Pip.

Ellie poked Jack's arm. "Good thing you're not a snack."

"Good thing you're not either," Jack shot back, and they both cracked up, bubbles wobbling out of their mouths.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Tooth Factory
chapters.text:
**CRUNCH. CRUNCH.** Little white shapes floated past like confetti.

"Are those... teeth?" Jack asked.

"Yep," Pip said. "Sharks lose teeth all the time, and new ones just slide forward to take their place. Some sharks go through thousands of teeth in one lifetime."

Ellie scooped one up like a seashell. "Can I keep it?"

"Sharks don't mind losing a few," Pip said. "There's always another one coming."

Jack ran his hand along a passing shark's side, then pulled back fast. "Whoa, that felt like sandpaper!"

"Shark skin is covered in tiny bumps, like hundreds of little teeth all over its body," Pip said. "That rough skin actually helps it zoom through the water faster."

Ellie rubbed her own arm. "My skin is squishy, not sandpapery."

"Lucky you," said Jack. "Imagine brushing THAT every morning."

Pip laughed. "Sharks don't brush. The ocean does it for them."

Ellie held her tooth up to the light. "I'm naming him Toothy."

"You named a tooth," Jack said.

"Yes," said Ellie. "Toothy is coming home with us."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Hammer-Headed Hunter
chapters.text:
Something strange swam toward them, a shark with a head shaped like a hammer, wide and flat.

Ellie hid behind Jack's arm, just for a second. "That shape is so weird!"

"That's a hammerhead shark," Pip said. "Its head is wide so its eyes sit far apart. That gives it an extra wide view, almost like looking both ways at once."

Jack watched it swing its head side to side. "It's like it's shaking its head no."

"It's actually searching," Pip said. "Sharks have tiny dots on their noses that feel teeny-tiny electric sparks, even from animals hiding in the sand. That's how they find fish buried where you can't see them."

Ellie's eyes went huge. "It can feel SPARKS?"

"Tiny ones," Pip said. "Smaller than the spark from a balloon on your sweater."

"Could it feel ME?" Ellie asked.

"If you were buried in sand, maybe," Pip said, "but you're floating right here, safe and sound."

Jack grinned. "Ellie, race you. Last one to Pip is buried treasure!"

They kicked off together, laughing, while the hammerhead swung calmly on past, already somewhere else.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Pip Takes a Walk
chapters.text:
The water grew shallow and warm, full of coral bumps like a stone garden.

"Watch this," Pip said, wiggling out onto a flat rock using his fins like two little feet. "I'm an epaulette shark. I can walk across reefs and puddles with these."

"IT WALKS!" Ellie shouted, clapping.

Jack leaned in close. "Walking sharks. Why did nobody tell me this sooner?"

"I can hold my breath a long time too," Pip said, "longer than most fish could ever manage."

Nearby, another shark lay still on the sandy bottom, barely moving.

"Is it stuck?" Ellie asked.

"Nope, just resting," Pip said. "Nurse sharks can pump water over their gills while they lie still, so they don't have to keep swimming just to breathe."

Ellie spotted something leathery drifting near the coral, just like the pouch from her bedroom. "Pip, look! Another mermaid's purse!"

"That's a shark egg, growing safe inside its little case," Pip said. "Some sharks lay eggs just like that one. Others have live baby sharks, called pups, right away."

Ellie cradled it gently without picking it up. "Hello, baby shark."

Jack nudged her. "You're basically a shark babysitter now."

"I'm GREAT at babysitting," Ellie said proudly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Shark Lady
chapters.text:
A diver swam down toward them, trailing bubbles, notebook in hand.

"That's Eugenie Clark," Pip whispered. "Everybody called her the Shark Lady. She studied sharks for most of her life."

Jack swam closer, careful not to touch. "What did she find out?"

"She proved sharks are curious," Pip said, "and that they can even learn tricks, like pressing a target for a snack."

"Sharks can learn tricks?" Jack said. "Like a dog?"

"Sort of," Pip said, "just with more fins and fewer treats."

Ellie tugged Pip's fin. "Are sharks going to eat us?"

"Almost never," Pip said. "People hardly ever get hurt by sharks. It's much more often the other way around, sharks getting hurt by people."

"That's sad," Ellie said.

"It is," Pip agreed, "which is why people like Eugenie worked so hard to help others understand sharks instead of being scared of them."

Jack floated up near the Shark Lady and gave a small wave. She waved back before swimming off into the blue.

"Sharks keep the whole ocean balanced," Pip added, "by eating just enough of the right fish to keep everything healthy. That's why we need them around."

"Like referees," Jack said.

"Exactly like referees," said Pip.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home Before Bedtime
chapters.text:
One last shape floated toward them, bigger than a school bus, spotted like a starry sky.

Ellie shrank back, then peeked again. "Is THAT one safe?"

"Very safe," Pip said. "That's a whale shark, the biggest fish in the whole ocean, and it only eats tiny bits of food floating in the water, smaller than rice."

Jack floated beside it, careful and calm. "It's enormous and it's gentle. That's the best combination."

"Some whale sharks live to be a hundred years old or more," Pip said. "Longer than almost any other fish."

Ellie waved at it from a little distance, the way Pip had shown them. The whale shark gave a slow, lazy blink and swam on.

"Time for bed, you two," Pip said, the green glow curling back around them.

"Already?" Jack groaned.

"Already," said Pip. "Bedtime finds you, same as it always does."

**WHOOOSH.** The sea melted back into carpet, lamp light, and pillows.

Ellie looked down at her hand. The leathery little pouch sat there, closed soft and quiet, Toothy tucked right beside it on the rug.

"We should put Toothy somewhere safe," Jack said.

"Right next to the mermaid's purse," Ellie said, setting them both on the shelf.

Jack pulled the blanket up over both of them. "Four hundred million years in one bath night. Not bad."

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Jack. Goodnight, Ellie. Swim well.
