story.title: Leo and the Sleepy Night Train
story.subtitle: A gentle bedtime journey into why everybody sleeps

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Train
chapters.text:
Leo lined up his wooden train cars on the rug.

"Choo choo," he whispered.

His owl night-light blinked on the shelf. Its eyes glowed soft and gold.

Then something strange happened. The little toy train began to hum. It glowed bright green, just like the owl's eyes.

"Hello, Leo," said a voice. It was the owl! "I'm Oliver Owl," he said. "Climb aboard the Sleepy Express. Tonight we find out why everybody sleeps."

The train grew bigger, big enough to ride. Leo hopped on, excited, not scared.

"All aboard for dreamland!" said Oliver.

WHOOSH! Off they chugged into the night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Dancing Eyes
chapters.text:
The train rolled into a quiet little room.

A boy slept in a cozy bed. "Watch his eyes," whispered Oliver.

Under his eyelids, his eyes went flick, flick, flick!

"Long ago, in **1953**, two scientists watched a sleeping boy just like him," said Oliver. "They saw his eyes dance back and forth. That is how they found dream sleep!"

Leo giggled. "His eyes are dancing!"

"That is when dreams happen," said Oliver.

TOOT TOOT! The train tooted happily, and they chugged on into the night.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Round and Round
chapters.text:
The tracks began to loop, round and round.

"This is called a sleep **cycle**," said Oliver. "A cycle is like a loop of track."

"Sleep goes round and round too," he said. "Quiet sleep, then dream sleep, again and again. About every **ninety minutes**, all night long."

Leo watched the train circle the loop, just like his own train set at home.

"Just like my train set!" he said.

"Exactly like that," said Oliver, smiling.

The wheels clacked happily. CLICKETY-CLACK, CLICKETY-CLACK!

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Floppy Noodles
chapters.text:
The train stopped beside a cozy meadow.

Sleeping bunnies lay in a soft, floppy pile.

"During dream sleep," said Oliver, "your brain is busy, busy, busy. But your body goes floppy, like a wet noodle."

Leo flopped his own arms and giggled. "Floppy noodle!"

"That way," said Oliver, "you cannot act out your dreams while you sleep. Safe and snuggled, floppy and still."

The bunnies twitched their noses in their sleep.

Leo waved a floppy noodle arm back, and the train rolled gently on.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Growing Helper
chapters.text:
Next, the train passed a garden of tall sunflowers.

"Deep sleep is extra important," said Oliver. "During your deepest, quietest sleep, your body makes a special growing helper."

"It helps you grow bigger and stronger, bit by bit, every single night."

Leo looked at his own hands. "Will I grow big like Papa?"

"If you sleep well, you sure will," said Oliver, nodding.

The sunflowers seemed to stretch taller, reaching toward the moon.

Leo sat up a little straighter, proud and sleepy.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Tunnel of Tiny Blinks
chapters.text:
The train entered a tunnel. It got quite dark inside.

Leo's tummy did a little flutter.

"It is alright, Leo," said Oliver softly. "This dark is just sleepy dark. Cozy and safe."

He pointed to a tiny light ahead. "That is your brain's own tiny clock," he said. "It hides right behind your eyes."

"It tells you when to feel sleepy, and when to wake up bright and ready."

The tiny light blinked like a friendly firefly.

Leo breathed out slowly. The flutter melted away.

WHOOSH! They popped out into starlight again.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Sleepy Animal Friends
chapters.text:
Next stop: a meadow full of sleepy animals.

A brand-new baby owl slept nearby, in lots of tiny naps. "Brand-new babies sleep almost all day long," said Oliver.

A dolphin swam past with one eye open. "Dolphins rest half their brain at a time," said Oliver. "The other half stays awake, watching for danger."

A giraffe snoozed standing up. "Giraffes barely sleep," said Oliver. "Sometimes only two hours a day!"

A little bat hung upside down, snoring softly. "Bats sleep and sleep," said Oliver. "Almost all day long!"

Leo counted on his fingers. "So many different sleepy friends," he said, smiling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: One Sleepy Day
chapters.text:
The train rolled past a big round clock in the sky, shaped like a pie.

"Did you know," said Oliver, "if you add up all your sleepy nights, they make a whole day?"

"A whole day?" said Leo, surprised.

"Yes," said Oliver. "Out of every **three days** of your whole life, you spend **one whole day** snoozing."

Leo wiggled his toes. "That's a lot of sleeping!"

"And it is wonderful," said Oliver. "Sleep helps you in so many ways."

The pie-shaped clock winked, and the train puffed onward, toward home.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Sorting the Train Cars
chapters.text:
At last, the train slowed down. It rolled right back onto Leo's rug.

"One more secret," said Oliver. "While you sleep, your brain sorts today's memories, like sorting train cars onto the right tracks. That is how you remember what you learned!"

Leo looked at his own train set, cars lined up neat and tidy.

"Just like that!" he said, pointing.

Oliver fluttered back onto the shelf. His eyes glowed soft and gold again.

"Sleep well, little engineer," he said. "The Sleepy Express will be waiting, every night."

Leo climbed into bed, cozy and warm, and closed his sleepy eyes.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Leo. All aboard for dreamland.

story.title: Arjun and the Nightwatchman of Sleep
story.subtitle: A comic book, a cricket pun, and the real science of shut-eye.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Five More Minutes
chapters.text:
Arjun lay on his bedroom floor, flashlight in one hand, comic book in the other, three pages into *The Nightwatchman Annual*.

"Five more minutes," he whispered to nobody, the way he did every single night.

Then the panel he was reading flickered green, then black, like a TV losing signal.

A voice rose off the page. "Still awake, are we?" A figure stepped out of the comic, cape made of stitched quilt, cowl shaped like a crescent moon. "Name's the Nightwatchman. In cricket, that's the batter sent in late in the day, to survive until stumps so the real stars can bat fresh tomorrow. Tonight, I protect something better than a scoreboard. I protect your sleep."

Arjun sat up so fast his comic slid off his knees. "You're real?"

"Real enough. First stop — Chicago, **1953**."

The floor dropped away, and Arjun landed in a quiet lab. A boy about his own age slept on a cot wired to blinking machines. A young scientist named **Eugene Aserinsky** leaned close, watching the boy's eyelids twitch fast, like he was watching a tennis rally with his eyes shut.

"He's not waking up," Aserinsky whispered to his teacher, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, "but his eyes are moving like mad."

Arjun tried it himself, eyes shut, flicking them side to side. Nothing happened — but the Nightwatchman grinned. "That twitchy-eye sleep got a name: **REM sleep**, short for 'rapid eye movement.' First proof that dreaming sleep is its own busy, different kind of sleep."

"IT BLINKS!" Arjun shouted, pointing at the sleeping boy, and the Nightwatchman had to shush him before they woke the whole lab.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Clock Behind Your Eyes
chapters.text:
They landed in a hallway of glass jars and diagrams, inside a drawing of a human brain blown up to the size of a bus.

"Follow the wires," said the Nightwatchman, pointing at a cluster of cells glowing like stadium floodlights, tucked right behind where Arjun's eyes would be. "That's the master clock. It tells your whole body when to feel sleepy and when to feel awake."

Arjun squinted at it. "Does it actually tick?"

"Close enough. It runs on something called **circadian** time — old words meaning 'about a day' — because it resets roughly every **twenty-four hours**, same as a day on a calendar."

Arjun thought of his own stopwatch, the one he used timing his bowling run-up. "So my body's got its own built-in stopwatch?"

"Better. In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the actual genes that keep that clock ticking, hiding inside tiny flies."

"Flies have clocks too?"

"Flies, dolphins, giraffes, your grumpy uncle. Everybody's got one."

Arjun gave the glowing cluster a respectful nod, like greeting a teammate. The lights pulsed back, almost like they nodded too.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Sleepy Chemical
chapters.text:
The hallway melted into a chilly laboratory that smelled like lemon cleaner. Beakers lined every shelf, each holding a liquid that glowed faint silver.

"This is **1958**," said the Nightwatchman, nodding at a man in a white coat hunched over a dish. "That's **Aaron Lerner**. He and his team were hunting for the exact chemical that makes animals — and people — feel drowsy."

Arjun watched Lerner lift a tiny vial toward the light. "Did he find it?"

"Right there. A sleepy-time chemical called **melatonin**, pulled from a pea-sized part deep in the brain called a gland — basically a little factory that makes stuff your body needs. Your own brain makes melatonin every night, usually once it gets dark."

"So that's why I get sleepy when Mom turns off the lights?"

"Bingo. And why staring at a bright screen before bed can trick the factory into thinking it's still daytime." The Nightwatchman nudged the flashlight tucked under Arjun's arm. "Even this."

Arjun clicked it off, just to see what would happen. Nothing happened. But it felt like the right move anyway.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Eleven Days Awake
chapters.text:
Next stop: a school gymnasium strung with handmade science-fair banners, **1964**.

A teenager with heavy eyelids stood at a folding table, surrounded by reporters and a worried-looking doctor. A sign behind him read ELEVEN DAYS.

"Meet **Randy Gardner**," said the Nightwatchman. "Seventeen, from San Diego. For a school project, he stayed awake about **eleven days** straight — one of the longest stretches anyone's ever managed without sleep."

Arjun's eyes went wide. "Eleven days? That's basically forever."

"It is forever, to a brain. By the end he was forgetting words mid-sentence." The Nightwatchman's voice dropped, serious. "Doctors who studied him afterward were clear: nobody should ever try to beat that record. Going without sleep wrecks your mood, your focus, your memory — fast."

Arjun watched Randy sway slightly, people making sure he was all right. "Is he okay now?"

"Slept it off, good as new. Scientists learned a lot from him. But some experiments you admire from a safe distance — you don't repeat them." The Nightwatchman tapped his cowl. "Same way you don't bat without pads just because somebody once did."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Animal Innings
chapters.text:
The scene spun into ocean blue, then grassland gold, then a cave hung with upside-down shapes.

"Quick tour," said the Nightwatchman. "Every fielding position needs a different player. Sleep's the same — every animal does it differently."

Below them, **bottlenose dolphins** glided in slow circles, one eye shut, one eye open. "They sleep with half their brain at a time," the Nightwatchman said, "so one side keeps watch while the other rests — like a slip fielder who never fully looks away. Seals do it too."

On the grassland, a towering **giraffe** dozed standing up, head drooping for only a minute before snapping back awake. "Giraffes sometimes nap less than **two hours** a whole day, in tiny bursts," said the Nightwatchman. "Busy outfield, that one."

Then the cave: tiny bats hung still, wrapped in their own wings. "These guys are the opposite. Some small bats sleep up to **twenty hours** a day. Practically professional nappers."

Arjun laughed. "I want their job."

"You'd sleep through the whole match."

Arjun watched the dolphins circle once more, half-awake, half on duty, and felt oddly proud of his own two eyes, shut tight every night, both at once.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Ninety-Minute Overs
chapters.text:
Back in the brain-sized hallway, the Nightwatchman unrolled a long scroll covered in wavy lines, like a heartbeat monitor having an argument with itself.

"This is one whole night," he said. "Sleep comes in rounds, like **overs** in cricket — a set number of balls, then a pause, then more. Except these rounds last about **ninety minutes** each, back and forth between quiet sleep and busy, dreaming **REM sleep**."

"Busy how?"

"During REM, your brain's almost as switched-on as when you're awake — solving problems, replaying your day. But your muscles go completely limp, so you can't actually jump up and act any of it out."

Arjun pictured himself dream-batting a century and flailing his real arms at the wall. "Good system."

"And the deepest, quietest round — right before REM kicks in — is when your body pumps out the most **growth hormone**, the stuff that helps you actually get taller and stronger." The Nightwatchman tapped Arjun's shoulder, roughly at eyebrow height. "Probably why you keep outgrowing your cricket whites."

Arjun grinned and straightened up an extra inch, just to see if it had worked already.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Night Rinse
chapters.text:
One last room: a cluttered attic, shelves stacked with boxes labeled MONDAY, TUESDAY, all the way to a box marked TODAY, still half-open.

"Every night," said the Nightwatchman, lifting the lid off TODAY, "your brain sorts the day's stuff into boxes you can find later. Turning it into **long-term memory**. Sleep on your cover drive practice, and tomorrow it sticks better."

Arjun thought about the shots he'd hit in practice that afternoon, how badly he wanted to remember exactly how his wrists had turned.

"There's also a cleanup crew." The Nightwatchman swept an arm, and tiny glowing streams washed through the attic floor, like water finding cracks. "A nightly rinse called the **glymphatic system** — it flushes the gunk out of a tired brain while you sleep, so you wake up clearer."

"My brain gets a car wash?"

"Every single night. Free of charge."

Arjun watched the glowing water swirl around the TODAY box, tucking his cover drive safely inside, and felt, for the first time all night, genuinely ready for the lid to close.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Stumps
chapters.text:
The attic dissolved, and Arjun landed back on his own bedroom carpet, comic book splayed open on his knees exactly where he'd left it, flashlight dark beside him.

The Nightwatchman's shape faded back into the final panel, cape folding into stitched quilt lines, cowl flattening into ink. "Stumps," he said — cricket's word for when the day's play officially ends. "Time to let the real players rest up for tomorrow."

"Five more—" Arjun started, out of pure habit.

"You've had eleven days' worth of facts for one night," said the Nightwatchman, voice already fading into paper. "Let the clock behind your eyes do its job."

Arjun closed the comic, clicked off the flashlight for real this time, and pulled up the blanket. Somewhere behind his eyes, he figured, a little cluster of cells was clocking in for the night shift, and somewhere deeper, a quiet factory was brewing something sleepy, right on schedule.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a match to field — and a cover drive to remember.

story.title: Noah and the Eleven-Day Leaderboard
story.subtitle: One phone, nine levels, and the science of lights-out.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Boy Who Blinked (1953)
chapters.text:
It was 1:14 a.m., and Noah's phone brightness was down to what he privately called stealth mode, the setting that kept the glow from leaking under his door. One earbud buzzed with the same four bars of a song he'd looped nine times, because nine felt lucky and sleep was for people with worse playlists. He thumbed past a game update, a video he'd already watched twice, and a battery icon blinking red like it was personally offended.

Then the screen did something it had never done. The brightness ignored him, the display flickered green-on-black like an old computer terminal, and a new icon dropped onto his home screen like loot: a single eye, slowly blinking. No name. No app store listing. Just the eye, and under it, pixel letters spelling PRESS START.

Noah pressed start. Obviously he pressed start; a mystery unlock button on his own phone was basically a Tuesday.

The screen swallowed him with a long **WHOOOOSH**, like a song skipping too fast to its ending, and he landed in a bare white room beside a glitching shape made of waveform bars pulsing to a beat he couldn't hear.

"Took you long enough," it said. "DJ REM. Tonight's set is why you're going to fall asleep eventually, whether your thumbs vote on it or not."

The bars rearranged into a grainy black-and-white clip: a sleeping boy, eyes flicking under closed lids like he was watching something only he could see. "**1953**," DJ REM said. "University of Chicago. A grad student named **Eugene Aserinsky** was watching his own sleeping son and couldn't stop staring at that. His supervisor, **Nathaniel Kleitman**, helped him prove it was real and repeatable — a whole stage of sleep nobody had named yet. They called it **REM**, for rapid eye movement."

"So a dad got curious and discovered a brain stage," Noah said, "because he wouldn't stop watching his kid sleep."

"Nosy parent, sleeping kid, eyes that wouldn't sit still. That's half of science right there."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The 90-Minute Loop
chapters.text:
A progress bar filled the white room, looping over and over like a buffering wheel that never finished loading.

"Every night runs on repeat," DJ REM said. "Cycles about **ninety minutes** long, back and forth between quiet non-REM sleep and that busy, dreaming REM stage you just met. Several loops a night, like replaying the same track with a different mix each time."

"And during REM," Noah said, remembering, "the eyes go wild."

"Eyes, sure. But here's the weird part: during REM your brain is almost as busy as when you're wide awake, dreaming in full color. Meanwhile your muscles go completely limp. Soft-locked. Your body can't act out whatever your brain's doing, so you don't go punching your pillow mid-dream."

A controller materialized in Noah's hands, a single glowing slider running along the progress bar. "Find me where REM kicks in," DJ REM said. "Two guesses."

Noah's first guess landed in the flat, quiet stretch — wrong, that was deep non-REM. He scrubbed the slider further along the loop, toward a spike where the line started jittering like a heart rate monitor during a boss fight. The bar lit up green.

"There. Second guess, nailed it."

"Not bad," DJ REM admitted. "Most people take three."

"I've got good hitbox instincts."

"Sure. Let's see if they hold up a few levels from now."

chapters.heading: Level 3: Respawn Stats
chapters.text:
The room went dark except for a single bar chart, climbing slowly in one spot and flat everywhere else, like an XP meter that only filled during loading screens.

"This is the deepest part of non-REM sleep," DJ REM said. "Your body dumps most of its **growth hormone** — the stuff that helps you actually grow — right here. It's a big reason kids your age need more sleep than adults do. You're mid-build."

Noah grabbed for a slider at the chart's edge, the obvious move for anyone who'd ever tried to speed-run a loading bar. "Can I push it faster? Get more of the good stuff quicker?"

The slider wouldn't budge. DJ REM didn't even look smug about it, which somehow made it worse. "No fast travel on this one. It happens at its own pace, every night, whether you rush it or not."

Noah let go of the slider and watched the little bar creep upward on its own schedule, stubborn and unbothered.

"Fine," he said. "Respawns on its own timer. I can respect a system that doesn't take bribes."

"That's the attitude," said DJ REM. "Most players waste a week trying to cheat this level before they figure that out."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Master Clock
chapters.text:
A single blinking light pulsed in a dark server room, cables running off it in every direction like it was in charge of something important.

"Meet your body's master clock," DJ REM said. "A tiny cluster of brain cells called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus** — say that five times fast — sitting right behind your eyes. It tells every other system when to wind down and when to wake up."

"That's a lot of syllables for one light switch."

"Scientists call the whole 24-hour schedule it runs **circadian**, from Latin words that basically mean 'about a day.' Your clock isn't perfectly exact — it's *about* a day, close enough to matter."

Noah studied the cables. One bundle glowed faintly blue, tracing back toward a small window shaped suspiciously like a phone screen. "Let me guess. That's the one messing with the clock at 1 a.m."

"You said it, not me," DJ REM said. "Keep shorting this clock on a regular basis — not one rough night, but months of it — and researchers find it tangled up with worse moods, worse focus, worse memory. Nothing dramatic. Just a slow leak."

"Noted," Noah said, in the tone of someone absolutely filing that away for later and not tonight. "Harsh, coming from an app that lives inside the phone."

"I contain multitudes," said DJ REM. "Next level."

chapters.heading: Level 5: Patch Notes from Stockholm
chapters.text:
A notification banner slid across the top of the room: UPDATE AVAILABLE.

"**2017**," DJ REM said, tapping it open. "Three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall**, **Michael Rosbash**, and **Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize**, basically science's biggest award, for finding the actual genes that keep that master clock ticking. Not just *that* you have an internal clock. *How* it runs, down to the code."

Three badges floated up, each labeled with a vague, decoy-sounding title. "Pick the real one," DJ REM said. "One guess."

Noah ignored the flashy badge about dream control and the one about super-speed and went for the plainest-looking one, reasoning the way he would in any patch-notes list: the boring entry is usually the real fix. He tapped it. It lit up gold.

"FOUND THE CLOCK GENES," it read.

"Correct," DJ REM said. "The realest patch notes in science. Fixed bug where nobody knew why everybody gets tired on a schedule."

"How long did that bug sit open?"

"Depends how you count it. Long enough that it took until 2017 to close the ticket properly."

Noah grinned. "I respect a slow, correct fix more than a rushed one."

"Spoken like someone who's been burned by a day-one patch."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Potion Lab
chapters.text:
The room shifted into a dim lab bench, three vials glowing faint silver in the dark like loot drops nobody had picked up yet.

"**1958**," DJ REM said. "A scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team managed to isolate the actual chemical that makes you sleepy. They pulled it out of a tiny part of the brain called the **pineal gland** — think of it as a built-in dispenser — in animals, and named it **melatonin**. Basically the body's own sleep-mode button, discovered decades before anyone put one on a phone."

Only one vial actually glowed warmer than the other two, the way the correct answer in a puzzle usually looks slightly different if you're paying attention. Noah reached for the warm one.

"That's melatonin," DJ REM confirmed as it clicked into a little holder on the bench. "The others are decoys. One's just glow-in-the-dark paint."

"You put glow-in-the-dark paint in a sleep lab. Bold."

"Keeps you sharp. Most players grab the brightest vial and lose points."

Noah held the real one up to the light. "So this is why I can't stay up forever no matter how good the show is."

"That's the dispenser doing its job," DJ REM said. "Working as intended."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Animal Server
chapters.text:
A lobby screen lit up with four character cards, like a character-select menu nobody had asked for.

"Bonus round," DJ REM said. "Match the stat to the animal."

First card: a bottlenose dolphin. "These guys sleep with only half their brain at a time," DJ REM said, "keeping one eye open to watch for danger or keep swimming. Some seals pull the same trick."

"So they never fully log off," Noah said. "Hardcore mode, permanently."

Second card: a giraffe. "Shortest sleeper of any big animal. Sometimes under two hours a day, in little naps, standing up."

"That's not even a full loading screen's worth."

Third card: a small bat, curled upside down. "Up to twenty hours a day. Sleepiest mammal on record."

"Absolute champion. Respect."

Fourth card made Noah laugh out loud: a fruit fly. "Even these show sleep-like rest," DJ REM said. "Suggesting sleep's been part of the game since life's earliest versions. Ancient mechanic."

"A bug has a bedtime," Noah said. "I don't know what to do with that information, but I'm keeping it."

"Keep whatever helps you remember the point: everything sleeps, just on wildly different settings."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Overnight Rinse
chapters.text:
Pipes ran along the ceiling, draining a thin dark fluid from a tank labeled BRAIN into a floor grate, quiet and unglamorous, like server maintenance running at 3 a.m.

"Two jobs happen overnight that nobody brags about," DJ REM said. "First: your brain sorts the day's stuff into long-term storage. Whatever you actually practiced — a riff, a combo, a line you kept messing up — gets filed properly while you're out. That's why you sometimes nail something *after* sleeping on it, not before."

Noah thought of the song he'd been stuck on for a week, and the run he'd finally cleaned the next morning after giving up the night before. "That's not luck. That's a save file syncing."

"Exactly that. Second job — the pipes. A nightly flush called the glymphatic system clears waste out of the brain while you sleep. A rinse cycle, basically, running while the system's offline for everything else."

Noah watched the dark fluid drain away, leaving the tank clean and glowing faint blue. "So skipping sleep is skipping maintenance."

"Skip it one night, you're fine. Skip it constantly, things pile up."

"Noted. Again."

"You keep saying that."

"I keep meaning it less than I should," Noah admitted.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Eleven-Day Run
chapters.text:
A leaderboard lit up the final room, one name blinking at the top: RANDY G. — SAN DIEGO.

"**1964**," DJ REM said. "A seventeen-year-old named **Randy Gardner** stayed awake for about **eleven days** straight, for a school science project. One of the longest stretches ever properly recorded."

"Eleven *days*." Noah stared at the number. "How did he even function?"

"Badly, toward the end. His mood dropped, his focus got sloppy, his memory started skipping like a scratched track. Scientists learned a lot from watching it happen. Doctors have been very clear ever since: nobody should try to break that record. Going without sleep wrecks your mood, your attention, your memory, fast."

A prompt blinked under the leaderboard: TRY TO BEAT RANDY'S SCORE? Y / N.

Noah looked at it for exactly one second. "Hard pass. I've got ranked matches this weekend. I need my aim, not a leaderboard nobody should be climbing."

"Correct answer," DJ REM said, and the leaderboard folded itself away like a tab closing. "You'll spend something like a third of your whole life doing this. Might as well be good at it instead of fighting it."

The white room dissolved in a soft **WHOOOOSH**, and Noah landed back on his bedroom floor, phone warm in his hand, the eye icon fading off his home screen like a session ending cleanly.

His playlist had quietly reordered itself. Track one, now, was something he didn't remember downloading, titled simply *Lights Out*.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there was a riff to nail and a rank to climb, and for once that felt like a reason to log off early.

During REM sleep the brain gets almost as busy as when you're awake, but your muscles go completely limp so you can't act out your dreams.

fact_pack.summary: Every person and almost every animal sleeps, though scientists still study exactly why. Sleep runs in repeating brain cycles that help the body grow, heal, and sort memories.

facts.text: In 1953, Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman at the University of Chicago discovered rapid eye movement (REM) sleep by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch under his eyelids.

During REM sleep the brain is almost as busy as when awake, but the body's muscles go limp so the sleeper cannot act out dreams.
The deepest non-REM stage triggers the most growth hormone release, one reason growing children need extra sleep.
A tiny brain region called the suprachiasmatic nucleus, just above where the eye nerves cross, works as the body's master clock for sleeping and waking.
'Circadian,' the body's roughly 24-hour clock, comes from Latin words meaning 'about a day.'
In 2017 the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine went to Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young for finding the genes that keep the circadian clock ticking.
The sleepy-time hormone melatonin was first isolated in 1958 by scientist Aaron Lerner's team, extracted from animal pineal glands.
Sleep helps the brain sort the day's experiences into long-term memories, so good sleep can help someone remember what they practiced or learned.
A nightly 'rinse cycle' called the glymphatic system flushes waste out of the sleeping brain.

Doctors do not recommend anyone try to break sleep-deprivation records, since going without sleep quickly harms mood, attention, and memory.
Newborns sleep about 14 to 17 hours a day in short bursts, nearly half of it in REM sleep.
Bottlenose dolphins and some seals sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger or keep swimming.
Giraffes are among the shortest sleepers of any large mammal, sometimes under two hours a day in brief standing naps.

story.title: Lena and the Ball That Remembers
story.subtitle: A backyard goalkeeper meets the history of the beautiful game

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Oldest Kick in the World
chapters.text:
Lena was still diving onto the grass at eleven o'clock, training saves against the fence like it was a real goal. Her gloves were damp. Her knees were green. She loved every second.

The ball in her hands had been her grandfather's — scuffed brown leather, one crooked stitch, heavier than any ball she owned now. She picked it up to head inside and felt it hum, like a tiny heartbeat under the leather.

"Okay," she told it. "That's new."

Gold thread glowed along the crooked stitch. A voice, low and crackly as old shoes on gravel, said, "Good hands, kid. Shame hands won't help you here."

"Did you just talk?"

"Name's Mundo. I've been kicked through every match that ever mattered. Want to see where this whole business started?"

Before she could answer, the backyard folded shut like a closing map. Cold mud squelched under her cleats. A crowd in long robes chased a leather ball across a dusty field, using only feet, chests, shoulders — never hands.

"Over **2,000 years ago**, in China," Mundo said, "people played a game called **cuju** — kickball. No hands. Ever."

Lena laughed, catching herself reaching out on instinct. "Even the goalkeeper?"

"Nobody keeps goal yet. You'll have to wait for that part."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Game Too Wild to Allow
chapters.text:
Mundo rolled her forward over a thousand years. Now it was mud streets, a whole town chasing one ball between two far-off church towers — the goal was literally the other side of the city.

Men shoved through market stalls, leapt fences, used fists and feet and whatever worked. A barrel tipped over. A chicken ran for its life.

"This is **mob football**," Mundo said. "Hundreds of players. No referee. No rules. Shops boarded their windows on match day."

Lena ducked a flying cabbage. "This is chaos."

"**King Edward II** thought so too. In **1314**, he banned it in London — too much yelling, too much smashed property."

"So how does this ever turn into soccer?"

"Somebody," said Mundo, "has to shrink the field."

Lena grinned, already picturing lines on grass, a proper net, a job just for her — standing between two posts, saying no. "Lines," she said. "You need lines. And a goal that isn't three miles away."

"Patience," said Mundo. "That part takes five hundred more years."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Man Who Wrote It Down
chapters.text:
Mundo set her down in a smoky London tavern, **1863**. Papers covered a long table. Men in waistcoats argued so loudly a candle nearly tipped over.

"Gentlemen," said one, dipping his pen, "we need **one** set of rules, not twelve different ones from every school in England."

"**Ebenezer Cobb Morley**," Mundo whispered. "About to invent your whole sport."

Fifteen years earlier, Lena learned, Cambridge University students had already tried something similar — the **Cambridge Rules of 1848**, an early attempt to get everyone playing the same game. It hadn't quite stuck.

This time, on **October 26, 1863**, Morley's group founded the **Football Association**, and he personally wrote the first official rulebook, the **Laws of the Game**. Rule one: no carrying the ball with your hands.

Lena's stomach dropped. "Wait — *no* hands? At all?"

Morley looked up like he'd heard her. "One exception," he said. "A single player, inside his own goal, may use his hands to keep the ball out."

Lena's whole chest lit up. "That's me. That's the goalkeeper."

"Born on paper, same night as the rest of the rules," Mundo said.

And the schoolboys playing this new "association football"? They liked nicknames. They shortened "assoc" into a word Lena already used every day: **soccer**.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Game Goes Everywhere
chapters.text:
"Hold on tight," Mundo said. "This part moves fast."

The tavern spun into a blur of fields, flags, roaring crowds.

**1872**: fog in Glasgow, Scotland. Lena found herself suddenly in goal, cap two sizes too big. Scotland's forwards bore down. She dove, fingertips on the ball — the scoreboard stayed frozen. The world's first official international match ended **Scotland 0, England 0**.

"My kind of game," Lena panted, grinning in the mud.

Mundo kept moving. A trophy rose overhead — the **FA Cup**, first played in **1871-72**, the oldest football competition still running anywhere on Earth. Then new teams shaking hands: **1888**, a man named **William McGregor** organizing the world's first football league in England.

Finally, Paris, **1904** — seven men signing papers, founding **FIFA**, the organization that would run football for the whole planet.

"Why does it need a world organization?" Lena asked, catching her breath.

Mundo's stitches glowed warm gold. "Because by now, everybody wanted to play. And when everybody wants to play the same game, somebody has to make sure they're all playing it the same way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Ban That Should Never Have Happened
chapters.text:
Mundo dropped her onto the sideline of a packed stadium, more fans than Lena had ever seen for any game.

On the field, a tall, fast striker shrugged off two defenders and smashed a shot into the net. The crowd went wild.

"That's **Lily Parr**," said Mundo. "Best player on the **Dick, Kerr Ladies** — one of the most popular football teams in England. Men's or women's."

Lena pumped her fist. "She's amazing!"

Then the crowd noise dimmed. The stadium emptied, boarded up.

"In **1921**," Mundo said quietly, "the people running football banned women's teams from using the grounds. For **fifty years**."

"Fifty?" Lena's jaw tightened. "That's not fair."

"No," Mundo agreed. "It wasn't."

But the field brightened again. Women lined up once more, cleats on fresh grass.

"**1971**," Mundo said. "The ban finally got lifted."

Then — flags, a different stadium, two decades later — a roar as a team in white and blue lifted a trophy overhead.

"**1991**," said Mundo. "China hosted the first official **Women's World Cup**. The **United States** won it."

Lena watched them celebrate, something fierce and proud rising in her own chest. "Good," she said. "Good."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The First World Cup
chapters.text:
Mundo carried her across an ocean to **Montevideo, Uruguay**, **1930**. A brand-new stadium roared loud enough to shake Lena's teeth.

"First-ever **World Cup**," Mundo said. "Thirteen teams came. Uruguay's hosting — and playing in the final."

On the field, Uruguay's forwards pressed forward against Argentina, end to end. The crowd screamed every time the ball came near goal.

Final whistle: **Uruguay 4, Argentina 2**. The stadium exploded. Fireworks, flags, a city that didn't sleep that night.

A man in a sharp suit stepped out to hand over a small golden trophy shaped like a winged figure.

"**Jules Rimet**," Mundo said. "FIFA's president. The whole World Cup was his idea — they even named the trophy after him for a while."

Lena touched the cool metal for just a second before a steward whisked it away. "It's smaller than I thought," she said.

"Most important things are," said Mundo.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: A Dog Named Pickles
chapters.text:
Decades flashed by. Mundo slowed them outside a London exhibition hall, **1966**.

"Watch this," Mundo said. "The World Cup trophy — gone. Stolen off its display stand, months before England hosted the tournament."

Lena gasped. "Did they get it back?"

"One week later," Mundo said, "a dog out for a walk started sniffing a garden hedge. His name was **Pickles**. He found the trophy, wrapped in newspaper, sitting right there."

Lena burst out laughing. "A *dog* solved it?"

"A dog solved it. Months later, England won the whole tournament anyway — their only World Cup title, to this day, in **1966**."

They flickered forward to **1970**, Mexico, blazing heat. A referee held up a small colored card.

"**Ken Aston**," said Mundo. "Looked at a traffic light and thought: red means stop, yellow means slow down. Football needed the same thing. Yellow and red cards, debuting right here."

One more flash: a Brazilian forward weaving past defenders like they were standing still.

"**Pele**," Mundo said. "The only player ever to win the World Cup on **three** different teams — **1958**, **1962**, **1970**."

Lena shook her head. "This sport has more plot twists than my favorite show."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Back on the Back Step
chapters.text:
The yard folded back into place, porch light humming same as before. Grass, fence, same green knees.

Mundo sat warm in her hands, stitches glowing faintly gold, fading slow like a sunset.

"That's a lot of history for one ball," Lena said.

"Every match you ever play adds to it," said Mundo. "Cuju, mob football, Morley's rulebook, Lily Parr, Pickles the dog — it's all still in here. In you, too, now."

Lena turned the ball over and found the crooked stitch glowing gold against her palm, cooler now, steady.

"Saturday," she said slowly, "I'm in goal. Same rule as 1863. Only one player on the whole field gets to use her hands."

"Better practice," Mundo said.

She dove once more into the grass, caught an imaginary shot clean against her chest, and grinned up at the dark sky.

story.ending_line: Saturday's match couldn't come soon enough.

story.title: Theo and the Game That Took Two Thousand Years to Build
story.subtitle: A Roblox builder learns the real patch notes behind soccer.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Cuju Court, Han China
chapters.text:
Theo's bedroom floor looked like a construction site. Pieces everywhere. His laptop glowed on the desk, Roblox Studio open to a half-built soccer stadium — floodlights, grass textures, a goal he'd rebuilt four times.

A week ago, the last message had said: THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD. Tonight was supposed to be that level. Instead he'd spent an hour staring at a blank penalty box, stuck.

He leaned back. "I don't even know where penalty kicks came from," he muttered. "Or any of it."

The screen flickered green.

Then came the squeak. "DID SOMEONE SAY *LEVEL*?"

Bit popped out of the laptop, all blocky green pixels, eyes blinking like an old console booting up. "Long time, Player One. BZZZT. Miss me?"

"Bit!" Theo grinned. "I'm stuck. I'm making a soccer game and I don't actually know where the rules came from."

"Lucky for you," Bit said. "Soccer has the longest cheat code in history. Ready to load Level One?"

The room dissolved into green static. When it cleared, Theo stood on packed dirt under a strange-colored sky. Men in long robes kicked a leather ball between two bamboo poles.

"Welcome," Bit squeaked, "to **China, over two thousand years ago**. This game is called **cuju** — it means 'kick ball.' It's one of soccer's oldest known ancestors."

A player bumped the ball off his shoulder, juggled it twice, then threaded it clean between the poles. The crowd roared.

Theo's eyes lit up. "That's basically a trick shot."

"Feel free to show them one," Bit said. "Try not to break history."

Theo stepped in. He flicked the ball up with his toe — his go-to move from actual Saturday practice — and chipped it through the poles. The crowd went wild. One player clapped him on the back so hard he nearly fell over.

A gold coin, pixelated and glowing, dropped out of the air into Theo's palm.

"LEVEL COMPLETE," said Bit, eyes crinkling. "One coin down. A lot more kickoffs to go."

chapters.heading: Level 2: Mob Football, Medieval England
chapters.text:
The green static cleared into a muddy street, houses leaning in close. A roaring crowd surged past, kicking — and sometimes punching — an inflated ball the size of a melon.

"Welcome to **England, 1314**," Bit said, ducking a flying boot. "This game's called **mob football**. Rules? None. Teams? However many people show up. Goal? Sometimes a whole village away."

A man crashed through a vegetable stall. Cabbages flew everywhere.

"That's not soccer," Theo said. "That's a riot with a ball."

"Pretty much," Bit agreed. "So many shops got smashed that **King Edward the Second banned it in London that very year**."

Theo ducked as the ball bounced his way. Instinct took over — he trapped it on his chest, like he'd done a hundred times at practice, and rolled it down to his foot.

The street went quiet. Everyone stared.

"Nobody's done that before," Bit whispered. "They just whack it."

Theo grinned and passed it gently to a kid his own age, who looked at his own foot like it had just learned a new trick.

"Quick detour," Bit said. The scene shimmered into a stone castle. "This is **Stirling Castle, in Scotland**. Hidden in its rafters, people once found a ball **from the 1540s** — maybe the oldest football on Earth."

"What's it made of?"

"A **bladder** — a squishy bag from inside a pig — blown up like a balloon and wrapped in leather." Bit shrugged. "Gross. Also genius. Nobody had rubber yet."

Theo wrinkled his nose, then laughed. "I'm never complaining about my ball again."

A second gold coin dropped into his hand, warm and glowing.

"LEVEL COMPLETE," said Bit. "Next stop: somebody finally writes rules down."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Cambridge Rules (1848)
chapters.text:
The green fog cleared into a university courtyard, autumn leaves everywhere. A dozen students argued near a ball, waving chalk like weapons.

"You can't carry it like that!"

"Says who? Your school allows it, mine doesn't!"

"Welcome to **Cambridge, England, 1848**," Bit said. "Every school's got its own rules. Some let you run with the ball. Some let you trip people. It's chaos."

Theo winced. "That's like five people editing the same Roblox game with no shared rulebook. Nothing works."

"Exactly the problem," Bit said. "These students are trying to write **one shared rulebook** — the **Cambridge Rules** — so any school can play any other school."

A student thrust a chalk-smudged paper at Theo. "You. New fellow. Settle it. Hands or no hands?"

Theo thought of every argument he'd ever settled between friends building together. "Pick one rule," he said, "and everybody follows it. Doesn't matter which, as long as it's the same for both sides."

The students blinked. Then nodded slowly, like it was the most obvious thing in the world.

"Write that down," one said.

Bit nudged Theo. "Not bad, Player One. You just helped patch soccer's very first bug."

It wouldn't be the last rulebook soccer ever needed. But it was the first one anybody wrote down on purpose.

A third gold coin landed in Theo's hand, buzzing faintly.

"LEVEL COMPLETE," Bit said. "The rulebook's getting closer. One more argument to settle."

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Football Association (1863)
chapters.text:
Candlelight flickered over a crowded table in a London pub. Papers everywhere. A tall man with a thick mustache read from a draft, pen in hand.

"On **26 October 1863**," Bit announced, "a group of Englishmen founded **the Football Association** — the FA. Right here, right now."

"What's that mean?" Theo asked.

"It means soccer finally gets ONE official rulebook, not a hundred different ones," Bit said. "And this man — " he pointed " — **Ebenezer Cobb Morley** — is about to write it down himself. The **Laws of the Game**."

Morley looked up, chewing his pen. "The trouble," he muttered, "is this business of carrying the ball by hand. Half of you want it. Half don't."

Theo leaned over the table, careful not to touch anything. "Just ban it completely. No hands, period. Easier to ref, easier to explain, nobody argues mid-game."

Morley studied him. "No hands. Clean." He wrote it down.

"That rule," Bit whispered, "is still exactly the same today."

A man in the corner laughed. "Association football, they're calling it. Ridiculous mouthful."

"Just say 'assoc,'" someone joked.

Bit leaned toward Theo. "Fast-forward twenty years — schoolboys shorten '**assoc**' into '**soccer**.' That's actually where the word comes from."

"Wait, soccer's basically a nickname?"

"Soccer's basically a nickname," Bit confirmed. "Still going strong."

Morley slid the finished paper across the table, ink still wet.

A fourth gold coin dropped, heavier than the others, like it knew it mattered.

"LEVEL COMPLETE," Bit said. "The rulebook's official now. Try not to get carried away. Literally."

chapters.heading: Level 5: First Trophies and the First Match
chapters.text:
Fog rolled across a Glasgow field, so thick Theo could barely see the far goal.

"Welcome to **1872**," Bit said. "Scotland versus England — the very **first official international match** in soccer history. A real game between two whole countries, not just two teams."

Players chased a barely visible ball through the mist. Whistles. Shouts. Nobody scored.

"They're going to tie zero-zero," Bit said. "Historic result. Deeply boring to watch."

Theo laughed. "Thanks for the spoiler."

"Spoilers are free when you're traveling through time."

A roar went up anyway when the final whistle blew — a 0-0 draw still felt huge, because nobody had ever tried a game like it before.

The fog cleared into a different scene: a packed stadium, banners waving, a shiny trophy held high.

"This," Bit said, "is the **FA Cup**, first played in **1871 and 1872**. It's the oldest football competition still running anywhere in the world. Over a hundred and fifty years later, teams are still fighting for it."

Theo stared at the trophy. "That's older than basically everything except dinosaurs."

"Everything's older than dinosaurs to you," Bit said. "You're ten."

A player spotted Theo in the crowd and, grinning, tossed him a spare practice ball. Theo controlled it on his thigh without thinking, then passed it back one-touch. The crowd cheered like he'd scored the winner.

"Smooth," Bit said. "Very smooth."

A fifth coin landed, spinning before it settled into Theo's hand.

"LEVEL COMPLETE," Bit said. "Soccer's got its first trophy. And its first bragging rights."

chapters.heading: Level 6: A League and a World Office (1888-1904)
chapters.text:
The scene shifted to a cluttered office, stacks of letters everywhere.

"**1888**," Bit said. "A man named **William McGregor** has an idea: instead of teams just arranging random matches whenever, what if there's a proper **league** — a set schedule, same teams, every season?"

Theo nodded slowly. "Like a season pass instead of random pickup games."

"Exactly. The **Football League**. World's first."

McGregor, hunched over his desk, looked up at exactly the right moment and smiled like he'd heard him.

The office dissolved into a grand room in a different city, flags on the walls.

"**Paris, 1904**," Bit announced. "Seven countries just founded **FIFA** — the group that runs soccer's rules worldwide. Think of it as soccer's head office."

Men in sharp suits shook hands around a table, signing papers with real ceremony.

"Seven countries? That's it?" Theo asked.

"Everybody starts somewhere," Bit said. "Now it's over two hundred."

One of the men noticed Theo watching and waved him over, sliding a blank sheet across the table. "Sign as a witness, young man."

Theo, feeling slightly ridiculous, signed his name under a row of important-looking signatures.

"You just witnessed soccer go worldwide," Bit said. "Not bad for a Tuesday."

A sixth coin dropped, spinning like a tiny planet before landing in his palm.

"LEVEL COMPLETE," Bit said. "Next up — some of the best players soccer's ever seen almost didn't get the chance to play."
chapters.shout_line: YOU JUST WITNESSED SOCCER GO WORLDWIDE!

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Game They Tried to Ban
chapters.text:
The next field was packed shoulder to shoulder, more people than Theo had ever seen at a single game.

"**England, the 1920s**," Bit said. "Women's soccer was massive back then. Tens of thousands of fans."

A player cut through three defenders like they weren't there, then rocketed a shot into the top corner.

"Who is THAT?" Theo said.

"**Lily Parr**," Bit said. "Star forward. Helped make her team, the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**, one of the most popular in England."

The crowd roared. Then, abruptly, the scene darkened.

"Here's the part that isn't fun," Bit said, quieter now. "England's soccer association decided women shouldn't play on its fields anymore. They banned it. Lily kept playing anyway, on whatever field she could find."

Theo's jaw tightened. "That's not fair."

"It wasn't," Bit said simply. "But it didn't stay that way forever. **Fifty years later, in 1971**, the ban was finally lifted."

The scene brightened. A new field. New players, new jerseys.

"And twenty years after *that*," Bit continued, "**in 1991**, the first official **Women's World Cup** was played, in China. The **United States** won it."

A player lined up a shot exactly where Theo always practiced his own penalties, and buried it top corner. The net rippled.

Theo found himself cheering louder than he had all night.

An older woman stood at the edge of the field, watching with the kind of grin that said *finally*. She caught Theo's eye and gave him a nod, like she knew the game would keep going now.

A seventh coin landed, warm, almost glowing gold-pink.

"LEVEL COMPLETE," Bit said quietly. "That one mattered."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The First World Cup (1930)
chapters.text:
Green static dropped them onto packed terraces under a blazing sun.

"**Uruguay, 1930**," Bit said. "The very first **FIFA World Cup**. Countries sending their best teams to one tournament, winner takes all."

"Who's playing?"

"Final's **Uruguay versus Argentina**," Bit said. "Host country versus their neighbors."

The stadium shook every time Uruguay touched the ball. When the final whistle blew, Uruguay had won, and the home crowd exploded like fireworks going off all at once.

A man in a sharp suit held up a small gold statue, gleaming even brighter than the coins in Theo's pocket.

"That's **Jules Rimet**," Bit said. "The FIFA president who pushed hardest to make the World Cup happen in the first place. They even named the first trophy after him."

Theo studied the little golden figure on top, arms raised, holding a ball. "It's tiny. I thought World Cup trophies were huge."

"This one's the original," Bit said. "Wait till you see what happens to it."

"That sounds ominous."

"It's soccer," Bit said. "Something always happens to the trophy."

A Uruguayan player spotted Theo's grin and tossed him the game ball as a souvenir — scuffed, heavier than Theo expected, nothing like the smooth ones he used at home.

An eighth coin dropped into his free hand, the metal faintly warm from the sun.

"LEVEL COMPLETE," Bit said. "Speaking of what happens to that trophy..."

chapters.heading: Level 9: World Cup Legends
chapters.text:
The green fog this time didn't settle into one place — it kept flickering, scene after scene, like someone mashing the fast-forward button.

"**London, 1966**," Bit said, as a headline spun past: TROPHY STOLEN. "Someone actually stole the World Cup trophy, right off display."

"They just... took it?"

"For about a week," Bit said. "Then a dog named **Pickles** found it, wrapped in newspaper, under a hedge."

"A DOG found the World Cup?"

"Good dog," Bit agreed.

The scene snapped to a roaring stadium, England's players lifting that same trophy. "**England hosted the 1966 World Cup — and won it.** Their only title, so far."

Flicker. A new stadium, yellow jerseys everywhere, one player gliding past defenders like they were standing still.

"**Pele**," Bit said. "Brazilian forward. The only player in history on **three World Cup-winning teams — 1958, 1962, and 1970**."

Theo watched him slip the ball through a defender's legs without even looking down. "That's not fair. That's cheat-code soccer."

"Brazil's won it **five times total**," Bit added. "Still the record."

Flicker. A referee pulled two small cards from his pocket, one yellow, one red, and held them up at a confused player.

"**1970 World Cup**," Bit said. "Referee **Ken Aston** got the idea watching a traffic light change. Yellow means careful. Red means you're out."

"That's such a simple idea," Theo said.

"The best ones always are," Bit said.

One last flicker: a brand-new, bigger trophy, gleaming under stadium lights.

"**1974**," Bit said. "Brazil got to keep the *original* trophy for good, after that third title. So FIFA made a **new World Cup Trophy** — the one still used today."

The montage slowed, then stopped. Theo stood blinking, trying to process an entire half-century in about ninety seconds.

"That was a lot," he said.

"History moves fast when you're not the one living through it," Bit said, and dropped a ninth coin into Theo's hand.

"LEVEL COMPLETE. Last stop — home."
chapters.shout_line: A DOG FOUND THE WORLD CUP!

chapters.heading: Level 10: Home Pitch
chapters.text:
The green fog thinned one last time, and Theo's bedroom floor reappeared under his feet — same carpet, same half-built Lego goalpost, same laptop glowing on the desk.

Nine gold coins sat in his open palm, each one pulsing faintly.

"Watch this part," Bit said.

The coins lifted off his hand, spinning together, melting into one shape — a small glowing trophy, not unlike the one Jules Rimet once held up in the sun.

Theo turned it over in his hands. "A thousand years of soccer. In my pocket."

"Give or take," Bit said. "You helped settle an argument in Cambridge, fixed a rule in London, and witnessed FIFA get founded. Not a bad Tuesday."

"I still don't know how to build the penalty box," Theo admitted.

Bit's pixel eyes went a little glassy, the way they always did right before a goodbye. "Maybe you don't build the rule first," he said. "Maybe you build the moment — then the rule writes itself. That's basically what everybody you met tonight did."

The laptop screen flickered. Letters appeared, green on black:

LEVEL COMPLETE. THE PITCH IS YOURS NOW.

Theo set the little trophy on his desk, right next to the keyboard, and looked back at his half-finished stadium on screen. The penalty box didn't look so impossible anymore.

"Same time tomorrow?" he asked.

"BZZZT," Bit said, already fading into static. "Always, Player One."

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a penalty box to build.

story.title: Mia and the Midnight Pitch
story.subtitle: Nine stops through the history of the world's game

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Kickoff at Midnight (Han China, roughly 200 BCE)
chapters.text:
Mia was supposed to be asleep two hours ago. Instead she was flat on her bedroom floor, laptop propped against a pillow, staring at a spreadsheet of her own team's shots from Saturday's game.

She was trying to calculate something called **expected goals** — a number that guesses how likely a shot was to go in, based on where it was kicked from and how many defenders were in the way. Her coach called it overkill. Mia called it Tuesday.

On her shelf, propped between a trophy and a stack of math textbooks, sat an old leather soccer ball. She'd bought it at a thrift store for three dollars because it looked like it had survived a war. Its stitching was cracked, its color somewhere between mud and regret.

Tonight the cracks were glowing green.

Mia sat up slowly. The seams on the ball were rearranging themselves, stitching into thin lines like the markings on a pitch. Her laptop screen flickered, went black, then lit up the same shade of green.

"Okay," she said to the empty room. "That's new."

The ball rolled off the shelf by itself, bounced once on the carpet, and spoke in a voice like gravel and an old radio. "Finally. Someone who does her homework."

Mia did not scream, mostly because she was too busy staring. "You're a ball. You're talking."

"I'm a lot of things," said the ball. "Tonight I'm your ride. Call me Cuju."

"That's not a normal name for a soccer ball."

"It's not a normal soccer ball," said Cuju. "It's also the oldest name soccer ever had. Over **2,000 years ago**, kids in Han dynasty China played a kicking game called **cuju** — literally 'kick the ball.' No hands, a leather ball stuffed with feathers, and a net strung between two poles. People had already figured out the main idea before anyone had written down a single rule."

The green light swallowed the room, and the floor dropped away like the world's weirdest elevator.

They landed on packed dirt under a wide gray sky, a crowd of players in loose tunics chasing a ball between their feet. One boy flicked it up with his heel, kept it in the air with his knee, and grinned like he'd invented gravity.

Mia watched the rhythm of it — foot, knee, foot, pause — and felt something click in her chest, the same click she got watching a perfect give-and-go. "That's a juggle," she said. "That's literally a warm-up drill. We're doing the same thing they did two thousand years ago."

"Give the girl a trophy," said Cuju, sounding genuinely pleased. "Nobody invented this game. It got invented over and over, everywhere, because kicking a round thing at a target is just a good idea. Tonight I'm going to show you the version that stuck."

Mia tucked her laptop under one arm out of sheer habit. "Lead the way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The King Who Banned the Streets (1314)
chapters.text:
The next thing Mia smelled was mud, and a lot of it.

They stood at the edge of a medieval English street, except "street" was generous — it was a churned-up battlefield of elbows, shouting, and at least forty grown men chasing one object nobody could clearly see.

"Meet mob football," said Cuju. "Whole villages against whole villages. No ref, barely any rules, and the ball could end up a mile from where it started."

A man in fine robes picked his way around the edge of the chaos, holding a scroll like it might bite him. He was reading a proclamation to anyone who'd listen, which, given the noise, was nobody.

"That's a royal herald," said Cuju. "In **1314**, **King Edward II banned the sport in London** entirely. Too many broken windows. Too many broken shins. The man's basically trying to cite a public menace, and the public menace is currently climbing over a fence."

Mia watched the mass of players swerve, a dozen men falling into a hedge like dominoes. "This isn't a game. This is a sample size of one chaotic event."

"Funny you say that," said Cuju. "The herald's trying to convince the king's men this needs stopping, and he's got no numbers. Just vibes and a torn sleeve."

Mia, who had never in her life seen a problem that didn't want a chart, grabbed the herald's scroll before she could think better of it. On the back she scratched a quick tally — players down, fences broken, one dog that had clearly had enough — using a stick of charcoal Cuju produced from, generously, nowhere.

The herald blinked at the numbers. "Fourteen incidents. In one match." He looked almost grateful. "The king will want to see this."

"Everything's easier to argue with a number next to it," Mia told him.

They left as the game dissolved into a shoving match near a bakery stall, nobody hurt worse than a muddy shirt.

"One more thing," said Cuju, as the scene faded. "Centuries later, someone cleaning out **Stirling Castle** in Scotland found a ball stuffed in the rafters — leather, stitched by hand, maybe from the **1540s**. Pig's bladder inside for bounce. It might be the oldest football still in existence."

"They just left a ball in the ceiling for five hundred years?"

"Somebody's little brother was definitely blamed first," said Cuju. Mia laughed hard enough that a passing sheep gave her a judgmental look.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Cambridge, and the Birth of a Rulebook (1848–1863)
chapters.text:
They landed in a wood-paneled room that smelled like candle wax and stubbornness.

Around a long table sat a dozen young men from different schools, each absolutely certain his school's version of football was the correct one. Someone was arguing that hacking — kicking an opponent in the shins — was a totally reasonable part of the game. Someone else looked like he wanted to leave.

"**1848**," said Cuju. "Cambridge University. Every school in England plays football a little differently, which is a nightmare if you ever want to play someone from a different school. So these guys tried to write down one shared rulebook — the **Cambridge Rules**. It didn't fully stick, but it was the first real attempt."

"They couldn't even agree on whether kicking people was allowed," Mia said. "This is the worst committee meeting in history."

"Wait for the sequel."

The scene shifted fifteen years forward to another meeting, smaller and sharper. One man stood at the head of the table, pen in hand, writing with the unbothered confidence of someone finishing an argument he'd already won in his head.

"Ebenezer Cobb Morley," said Cuju. "On **October 26, 1863**, in London, he and a handful of club representatives founded the **Football Association** — the FA. Their biggest rule: no more picking the ball up and running with it. That version went off to become rugby. This version became soccer. Morley personally sat down and wrote the first official **Laws of the Game** — the rulebook everything else grew out of."

Mia leaned over Morley's shoulder, reading upside down as he wrote. "You're really doing this. One ruleset. For everyone."

"Someone has to," Morley said, without looking up. "Otherwise every match starts with twenty minutes of arguing before anyone's kicked anything."

"Sounds like my group chat before practice," Mia muttered.

"One more thing you'll want for your trivia arsenal," said Cuju, as the ink dried. "Twenty years later, some schoolboys started calling the sport '**assoc**,' short for association football, because British schoolboys in the **1880s** loved shortening everything and adding '-er' to it. Assoc became **soccer**. You're welcome."

Mia stared at the ball. "That's — that's genuinely the dumbest and best word origin I've ever heard."

"History's full of those," said Cuju. "Try not to get attached. There's more."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Scotland 0, England 0 (1872–1888)
chapters.text:
The next field was real grass, a proper pitch, and a crowd that had actually bothered to show up.

"**1872**, Glasgow," said Cuju. "Scotland versus England. The first official international match in the sport's history. Two whole countries, one ball, and about four thousand people freezing in a field to watch."

Mia watched ninety minutes compress into a blur of passes, tackles, and one extremely enthusiastic man waving a Scottish flag. When the final whistle blew, the scoreboard — such as it was, a man with chalk — read **0–0**.

"That's it?" Mia said. "The first international match in history, and it's a scoreless draw?"

"Welcome to soccer," said Cuju. "Sometimes the story's in the fact that it happened at all, not in the score. Although" — the ball rolled a little closer — "I know a stats kid when I see one. Want to guess what fraction of matches in this sport end nil-nil, even now?"

"Don't tempt me, I will actually calculate this when I get home."

"That's the spirit."

The scene jumped forward. A stocky man with an impressive mustache was striding between club officials, clipboard in hand, clearly done asking nicely.

"**William McGregor**, **1888**," said Cuju. "Clubs kept arranging random one-off matches and nobody could plan a season around that. McGregor organized the first-ever **Football League** — a proper, scheduled competition, with every team playing every other team. It's the blueprint every league in the world still copies."

Mia watched McGregor hand a schedule to a skeptical club chairman, who studied it like it might be a trick. "He basically built the first fixture list. The thing my coach complains about every September."

"Someone had to invent the headache," said Cuju. "While we're here — the **FA Cup**, first played the year before this, in **1871–72**, is still running today. Oldest football competition on Earth. Outlasted empires. Outlasted several haircuts."

"Respect," said Mia, and meant it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Seven Countries, One Game (1904)
chapters.text:
Paris smelled like river and coffee, and the room Cuju led her into was crowded with men in stiff collars arguing in at least three languages at once.

"**1904**," said Cuju. "Soccer's gotten popular enough that it's crossed the English Channel and taken off across Europe. Problem is, every country's making its own rules again, same as the schoolboys at Cambridge, just bigger. So **seven countries** sit down in Paris and found **FIFA** — the organization that's still in charge of international soccer rules and the World Cup today."

"Seven countries," Mia repeated. "And none of them were England."

"England thought the whole idea was unnecessary," said Cuju. "They joined a year later anyway. Some things never change — showing up late and pretending you weren't invited."

Mia watched a French official slide a document across the table for signatures, each representative adding his name like he was signing something bigger than he fully understood yet — which, given what FIFA would eventually become, he was.

"This is wild," Mia said, watching another official from Belgium scrawl his name.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The World Cup (1930)
chapters.text:
The next stop happened in a stadium that felt too big for the world to fit inside. Flags hung from every angle, and a roar went up from the crowd that sounded like it came from somewhere deeper than regular human lungs.

"**1930**, Uruguay," said Cuju. "The first FIFA World Cup. Before this, soccer was popular everywhere — club leagues, international matches, all of it. But nobody had ever tried to gather every nation that could field a team and make them compete in one tournament. Until now."

Mia watched the opening match begin, the players moving with a kind of electricity that felt different from every other match she'd seen so far. "They know this is a big deal," she said.

"They know they're making history," said Cuju. "Thirteen teams showed up. Only four Europeans bothered to make the journey to South America. But they came. And **Uruguay won**, playing at home, which nobody's complaint about if you're the host."

Mia leaned against the rail, taking in the stadium. "This is the template, isn't it. This is what every World Cup after this is trying to be."

"Give the girl another trophy," said Cuju. "The tournament happens every four years now. Still does. Still dominates every calendar in every country that plays soccer."

They watched the final whistle blow on Uruguay's victory, the crowd exploding like fireworks had forgotten they were supposed to be quiet about it.

"One more thing," said Cuju, as the noise faded. "That first World Cup ball, made in Uruguay — nobody knows where it ended up. It's lost to history. But the moment it kicked off, something shifted in the world. Soccer stopped being a sport and became a religion."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Women's Soccer Takes the Pitch (1972–1996)
chapters.text:
The field was smaller than Mia expected, and the crowd was smaller still, but the energy crackled with something sharp.

"**1972**," said Cuju. "Title IX in America — a federal law that basically said if a school offered sports for boys, they had to offer sports for girls too. High schools didn't know what hit them. Suddenly thousands of girls were playing soccer because it was finally, legally, their right to."

Mia watched girls in vintage uniforms run a pitch that looked nothing like the manicured stadiums she'd seen before. "This is chaos," she said, but she was smiling.

"This is building," said Cuju. "The women's national team in the United States got its first coach in the '80s. They had no money, no sponsorships, no stadium. Just ambition and a ball."

The scene shifted forward. A women's team in red, white and blue was walking into a massive stadium in California, and the crowd — thousands of them — was on their feet.

"**1996**, Atlanta Olympics," said Cuju. "The first women's soccer tournament at the Olympics. America versus China in the final, and **40,000 people** showed up to watch."

Mia watched Mia Hamm — a player with the same first name — score on a header, the stadium losing its mind. "They're allowed to just... do this. In front of people."

"They fought for decades to be allowed to," said Cuju. "That's Mia Hamm, by the way. One of the greatest players ever. Thought you should know you share a name with someone who changed everything."

Mia felt something click in her chest. "So when people ask me why I care so much about the spreadsheets and the stats..."

"Tell them Mia Hamm didn't get to play because of vibes," said Cuju. "She got to play because women fought for data, funding, and representation. You're doing the same work."

story.ending_line: You're doing the same work.

true_facts.text: In Han dynasty China, roughly 2,000 years ago, children played a game called cuju, literally meaning 'kick the ball,' using a leather ball stuffed with feathers and a net strung between two poles.
In 1314, King Edward II banned football in London due to broken windows, broken shins, and the sport being considered a public menace.

A ball found stuffed in the rafters of Stirling Castle in Scotland, dating to around the 1540s, is possibly the oldest football still in existence, made of leather and stitched by hand with a pig's bladder inside.
In 1848, Cambridge University attempted to create the first shared rulebook for football, called the Cambridge Rules, to standardize the sport across different schools.

On October 26, 1863, Ebenezer Cobb Morley and representatives founded the Football Association in London and wrote the first official Laws of the Game, establishing that players could not pick up and run with the ball.
The term 'soccer' originated in the 1880s when British schoolboys shortened 'association football' to 'assoc' and added '-er' to create 'soccer.'
On March 5, 1872, Scotland and England played the first official international football match in Glasgow, ending in a 0–0 draw, with approximately 4,000 spectators in attendance.
In 1888, William McGregor organized the first-ever Football League, a scheduled competition where every team played every other team, establishing the blueprint for leagues worldwide.
The FA Cup, first played in 1871–72, is the oldest football competition still in existence today.
In 1904, seven countries founded FIFA in Paris, the organization that governs international soccer rules and the World Cup, with England joining a year later.
The first FIFA World Cup took place in 1930 in Uruguay, with thirteen teams competing, only four from Europe, and Uruguay winning the tournament on home soil.
In 1972, Title IX in America mandated that schools offering sports for boys must also offer sports for girls, leading to thousands of high school girls playing soccer legally for the first time.
In 1996, the first women's soccer tournament at the Olympics was held in Atlanta, with the United States facing China in the final and drawing 40,000 spectators.
