story.title: Maya and the Race to the Moon
story.subtitle: A splashy, beepy, starry bedtime adventure with Barnacle the seal.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Beep From Space (1957)
chapters.text:
Maya sat on the edge of the bathtub. Her little red boat bobbed in the water. She dipped one finger and made a wave.

It had been one whole week since Barnacle waved his flipper from the water, after the last rivet on the humming bridge went in. Tonight, the old radio on the shelf crackled. The screen went black. Then it flickered green.

BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.

"That's not my bath song," Maya whispered.

A whiskered nose popped up out of the tub. "All aboard, Maya!" said Barnacle, shaking water off his fur. "That beep is almost seventy years old."

"Seventy years? From a radio?" Maya's eyes went wide.

"Not a radio. A little round ball, flying way past the clouds." Barnacle grinned his gap-toothed grin. "It's called a **satellite** — a machine that flies in a big circle around Earth, like a ball on a very long string. That circling is called an **orbit**."

On **October 4, 1957**, he said, the Soviet Union shot a shiny ball called **Sputnik 1** into the sky. It was only **58 centimeters wide** — about the size of a beach ball. It did not sing or talk. It just went *beep... beep... beep...* and people all over the world heard it on their own radios.

"Like we're hearing it now," Maya said.

"Exactly like now," said Barnacle. "Want to go see it fly?"

Maya grabbed her boat. She pushed it in a big circle around the tub, just like an orbit. The water glowed green and swirled like a tiny whirlpool.

"SPLOOSH!" Maya shouted, and the whole bathroom folded up like a paper boat.

When it unfolded, Maya and Barnacle were floating — actually floating — above a glowing blue Earth, with a little silver ball beeping along beside them.

"Welcome," said Barnacle, "to 1957."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Laika's Big Loop (1957)
chapters.text:
A bright rocket roared up from the ground below them. WHOOSH! Smoke puffed out in round white clouds.

"Who's riding that one?" Maya asked, leaning close to look.

"A dog," said Barnacle. "Her name was **Laika**."

Maya gasped. "A dog went to space?"

"On **November 3, 1957**," Barnacle said, "Laika became the first living creature to ever **orbit** Earth — the first one to fly all the way around in a big circle."

Maya watched the tiny capsule — that's the little metal pod a space traveler rides inside — zoom around the curve of the Earth.

"Is she scared?" Maya asked.

"She's brave," said Barnacle gently. "People all over the world cheered for her. She became famous everywhere, in every language."

Maya pressed her hand against the cold window of their floating bubble and drew a circle in the fog with her finger, right where Laika's capsule looped around the planet.

"There," she said. "Now she has a friendly circle to fly in."

Barnacle chuckled. "That's the nicest flight plan I've ever seen."

They watched the little capsule swing all the way around, following Maya's drawn circle exactly. For one small, cozy moment, the whole cold sky felt like a bathtub full of friends.

"Okay," Maya said, satisfied. "What's next?"

"Next," said Barnacle, "everybody on the other team wakes up."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: NASA Wakes Up (1958)
chapters.text:
Back on the ground, lights switched on in a hundred windows at once. People ran outside in their pajamas, pointing at the sky.

"They just heard the beep," Barnacle explained. "It scared them. They thought, if the other team can fly a ball around Earth, what else can they do?"

"So what did they do?" Maya asked.

"They built their own team," said Barnacle. "On **October 1, 1958**, the United States started a brand new space group called **NASA**."

A little silver rocket zipped past them, smaller than Sputnik, wobbling slightly.

"That's **Explorer 1**," Barnacle said. "It launched on **January 31, 1958**. It found something nobody expected — an invisible ring of energy wrapped around the Earth, like a giant hula hoop made of sparks. Today we call it the **Van Allen belt**."

Maya watched the ring shimmer faintly around the planet, like heat over a hot sidewalk.

"It's like Earth has its own hula hoop!" she said.

"A hula hoop nobody can see," Barnacle agreed, "and it keeps some of space's zappy stuff away from us."

Maya pulled a little notebook from her pocket — she always kept one, for drawing boats, and apparently now, planets too. She sketched the ring around her circle of Earth and labeled it in big wobbly letters: GIANT INVISIBLE HULA HOOP.

"Perfect," said Barnacle. "Science needs more drawings like that."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Yuri's Giant Circle (1961)
chapters.text:
A new rocket thundered past, bigger than any before. Maya covered her ears. WHOOOOSH!

"Who's flying now?" she shouted over the roar.

"A person, this time," Barnacle said. "On **April 12, 1961**, a Soviet pilot named **Yuri Gagarin** became the very first human being to fly in space."

Maya's mouth fell open. "A real person? All the way around?"

"All the way around, once," said Barnacle. "It took him about **108 minutes** — less time than one of your long car rides."

Maya tried to imagine it: looking down at the whole blue Earth, all in less time than a car ride to the beach.

"Count us down," Barnacle said. "Every good launch needs someone to count."

Maya cleared her throat. "Three! Two! One!"

Somewhere below, cheering erupted as Gagarin's capsule landed safely.

Not long after, a new voice crackled through their glowing bubble — a president's voice, calm and sure.

"On **May 25, 1961**," Barnacle explained, "President **John F. Kennedy** stood up and dared his whole country to land a person on the Moon — and bring them home safe — before ten years were up."

Maya's eyes lit up like fireworks. "That's like daring someone to swim across the whole ocean!"

"Bigger," said Barnacle. "The Moon is about a quarter million miles away."

Maya grinned and paddled her arms through the air like she was swimming there herself. "I dare us too, then," she said. "Let's go see if they made it."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Alan's Quick Hop (1961)
chapters.text:
Another rocket lifted off, smaller and quicker than Gagarin's had been. Up it went, then — almost right away — it curved back down.

"That was fast," Maya said. "Did it break?"

"Nothing broke," Barnacle laughed. "That's **Alan Shepard**, the first American in space. On **May 5, 1961**, he rode a little capsule called **Freedom 7** up and right back down again. He didn't go all the way around Earth like Gagarin did. It was a quick hop, not a big loop."

Maya thought about the times she jumped off the dock into the lake — up, splash, done — compared to swimming all the way across it.

"So his was the jump," she said, "and Yuri's was the swim."

"That," said Barnacle, "might be the best way anyone has ever explained it."

They watched Shepard's little capsule splash down into the ocean far below, bobbing gently like Maya's own red boat in the bathtub.

"He's floating just like my boat does," Maya said happily.

"Space capsules and bathtub boats," said Barnacle, "have more in common than you'd think."

Maya gave a little wave down at the tiny capsule, even though nobody down there could possibly see her.

"Nice hop," she called out anyway. Barnacle chuckled and nudged their glowing bubble onward, toward the next beep in the sky.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Valentina's Forty-Eight Loops (1963)
chapters.text:
"Wait," Maya said suddenly, floating upside down just to see what it felt like. "Were there any girls who went up?"

Barnacle's whiskers twitched into a smile. "Funny you should ask. On **June 16, 1963**, a Soviet space traveler named **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space."

"Was she a pilot too?" Maya asked.

"She'd worked in a factory before that," said Barnacle, "and loved parachute jumping for fun. Then she rode a capsule called **Vostok 6** around Earth — not just once, like Yuri."

"How many times?" Maya asked, bouncing a little in the air with excitement.

Barnacle paused dramatically. "Forty-eight times around the whole planet."

Maya's jaw dropped. "Forty-EIGHT?!"

"Forty-eight," Barnacle repeated happily. "More loops than anyone before her."

Maya pulled out her notebook again and drew a girl in a round space helmet, with little loop after loop after loop circling behind her, like a long jump rope wrapped around the Earth.

"She's my favorite so far," Maya announced.

"Mine too," said Barnacle. "Don't tell the others."

Maya giggled and tucked her drawing carefully into her pocket, right next to the hula-hoop sketch from before. Her notebook was getting crowded with space pictures now, right alongside her usual boats.

"Keep drawing," Barnacle said warmly. "History likes being remembered."

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Alexei's Swim in Space (1965)
chapters.text:
A hatch popped open on a floating capsule nearby, and out drifted a puffy white shape, tied to the ship by a long cord.

"Is he okay?" Maya asked quickly, grabbing Barnacle's flipper.

"He's wonderful," Barnacle said. "That's **Alexei Leonov**. On **March 18, 1965**, he became the very first person to float outside his spaceship. We call that a **spacewalk** — floating outside, tied on by a cord, like a leash, so you never drift away."

"How long did he float?" Maya asked.

"About **ten minutes**," said Barnacle.

Maya watched Leonov tumble slowly, arms out, legs out, turning in lazy circles.

"That looks just like floating on my back in the pool," she said.

"Space has no water," Barnacle said, "but no gravity either, so it feels a little like swimming. Just much, much quieter."

Maya kicked her legs through the air, pretending to swim right alongside Leonov. She did a slow-motion backstroke, giggling as her hair floated up around her face.

"Careful," Barnacle laughed. "You'll get a reputation as the best swimmer in orbit."

"I already am," Maya said proudly, still paddling along beside the little floating cosmonaut, both of them turning slow, happy circles against the dark.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Earthrise (1968)
chapters.text:
Their glowing bubble drifted closer to the Moon, gray and quiet and covered in bumps.

"Look back," Barnacle whispered.

Maya turned around — and gasped. There, rising over the Moon's gray edge, was Earth itself: blue, swirly, and small enough to cover with her thumb.

"In **December 1968**," Barnacle said softly, "astronauts flying on **Apollo 8** became the first people ever to travel all the way around the Moon. One of them, **William Anders**, took a photograph of exactly this."

"What's it called?" Maya asked, barely breathing.

"**Earthrise**," said Barnacle.

Maya didn't say anything for a moment. She just looked at her whole entire home, hanging there in the black, smaller than her thumbnail.

Then, quietly, she pulled out her notebook one more time and began to draw — not a boat this time, and not a girl in a helmet, but a small round Earth rising over gray Moon dust.

"That's the best one yet," Barnacle said, peeking over her shoulder.

"It's the only one that's home," Maya said simply.

Barnacle didn't make a joke this time. He just floated beside her, quiet and warm, while she finished her drawing of the whole wide world.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: One Giant Leap, One Big Handshake (1969–1975)
chapters.text:
A silver rocket stood taller than anything Maya had ever seen, pointed at the sky like a pencil.

"That's the **Saturn V**," Barnacle said. "**363 feet** tall — taller than the Statue of Liberty."

Maya tipped her head all the way back. "That's SO tall!"

It thundered off the ground, and this time, it was headed for the Moon itself.

"On **July 20, 1969**," Barnacle said, "astronaut **Neil Armstrong** climbed down a little ladder and became the very first person to ever step on the Moon."

Maya watched a dusty gray boot print press into the ground below them.

"He said something, didn't he?" she asked.

"A giant leap for mankind," Barnacle said. "His friend **Buzz Aldrin** joined him down there, while **Michael Collins** circled above, alone, in their ship **Columbia**."

"Three friends, three jobs," Maya said. "Just like us and Barnacle."

One rocket later, something did go wrong — on **Apollo 13**, in 1970, an oxygen tank had a problem on the way to the Moon. But the crew and the engineers back home worked together and fixed it, and everyone came home safely.

"See?" Barnacle said gently. "Even in space, teams take care of each other."

The last rocket of their journey carried two very different crews — one American, one Soviet. On **July 17, 1975**, their ships gently came together in orbit, locking together like puzzle pieces. The astronauts and cosmonauts floated through a little tunnel and shook hands.

Maya grinned. "That's the best ending."

"The whole Space Race," Barnacle said, "ended in a handshake."

The green glow swirled around them once more, gentle as bathwater. SPLOOSH! — and Maya was back on the edge of the tub, her little red boat still bobbing beside her knee. The radio sat quiet and dark on the shelf.

Barnacle's whiskered nose peeked up one last time. "All aboard, Maya," he said softly, "for one more good night's sleep."

He gave a small flipper-wave and slipped under the water, leaving only gentle ripples behind.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. All aboard for dreams — sleep tight, little space sailor.

facts.text: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the US and USSR to achieve spaceflight firsts, lasting roughly 1957 to 1975.
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beach-ball-sized satellite that became the first man-made object to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was about 58 centimeters wide and sent out a simple radio beep that people around the world could pick up on ordinary radios.
On November 3, 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 carrying a dog named Laika, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States created NASA, which began operating on October 1, 1958.
The first US satellite, Explorer 1, launched January 31, 1958, and discovered the Van Allen radiation belt.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once aboard Vostok 1 in about 108 minutes.
On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space aboard the Freedom 7 capsule, though his short flight did not orbit Earth.
On May 25, 1961, President Kennedy challenged the US to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before decade's end.
On June 16, 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, floating outside his Voskhod 2 capsule for about ten minutes.
On January 27, 1967, astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died in a fire during a launch pad test of Apollo 1.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
Buzz Aldrin joined Armstrong on the Moon while crewmate Michael Collins orbited alone above in the command module Columbia.
In 1970, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but the crew safely returned to Earth after engineers improvised a fix.
Between 1969 and 1972, twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon across six successful Apollo landing missions.
The Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo astronauts to the Moon stood 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
Soviet chief designer Sergei Korolev secretly led the USSR's rocket program, and his identity was kept a state secret until after his death in 1966.
Wernher von Braun, who earlier built rockets for Germany, led the NASA team that developed the Saturn V rocket.
The Space Race ended in a spirit of cooperation on July 17, 1975, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.

story.title: Theo and the Space Race Server
story.subtitle: A Roblox builder's journey from a beeping satellite to a handshake in orbit.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Beep From Nowhere (1957)
chapters.text:
Theo was still awake at 11:14 p.m., and his rocket would not fly straight.

He had spent an hour in **Roblox Studio** — the program where he builds his own games — trying to make a tiny pixel rocket lift off a launchpad. Every time he pressed play, it tipped sideways and smashed into a palm tree.

"Ninety-nine more tries," he muttered, and reached for the mouse again.

That was when his screen went black, then green, then black again. A soft beep came out of the speakers — not a game sound. A real one. Steady. Patient. Like something was knocking.

An avatar popped onto the screen that Theo had never built. It wore a scuffed space helmet and had pixels for a face.

"Finally," the avatar said. "Do you know how long I've been trying to get your attention? You left your speakers on."

"Who are you?"

"Call me Pixel. I live in the server behind every game you've ever built — don't ask how, it's complicated, like trying to explain lag to a parent. I heard that beep and figured you'd want to know where it's from."

"What beep?"

Pixel turned up the sound. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP. Steady, mechanical, lonely.

"That," said Pixel, "is the actual sound of **Sputnik 1** — the world's first satellite, a machine that circles a planet instead of landing on it. The Soviet Union launched it on **October 4, 1957**. It was about **58 centimeters wide** — roughly the size of a beach ball — and it just beeped, over and over, so that ordinary radios on Earth could pick it up."

Theo sat up straight. "People on Earth could actually hear it?"

"Anyone with a radio. Scientists, farmers, kids your age. The whole planet tuned in to listen to a beeping ball flying over their heads."

Pixel held out a glowing dial, like an old radio tuner stitched out of light. "Want to hear it the way they did? Find the right frequency. Consider it a server you have to join."

Theo had never tuned a radio in his life, but he'd spent two years learning exactly how signals worked in his own games — pinging a server until it answered. He turned the dial slowly, past hisses and crackles, until the beep locked in, clean and clear.

BEEP. BEEP. BEEP.

"You joined the server," Pixel said, sounding impressed. "Not bad for someone who still can't land a rocket."

"It's a *work in progress*," Theo said.

The screen behind Pixel opened like a loading window, and through it Theo could see a cold launch pad, floodlights, a rocket standing in fire and smoke.

"That's the actual launch," Pixel said. "You caught its signal decades late, but a beep doesn't care what year it's arriving in. Want to see where this story goes? I warn you — it gets a lot bigger than a beach ball."

Theo grinned at his broken rocket game, still crashed on the screen. "Load it up."

chapters.heading: Level 2: Laika and the Belt Nobody Could See (1957–1958)
chapters.text:
Pixel's green loading screen flickered again, and this time it smelled, faintly, like static electricity.

"After Sputnik," Pixel said, "the Soviets didn't stop. One month later, on **November 3, 1957**, they launched **Sputnik 2** — and this time, something alive rode inside it."

"Alive like what?"

"A dog named **Laika**. She was the first living creature to ever circle the Earth. People everywhere followed her mission on the news. She became famous around the whole world."

Theo pictured a dog looking out of a tiny window at the planet below, and decided that was the single greatest thing a dog had ever done. "She beat every dog ever. Forever."

"Here's the part that stings a little," Pixel said. "The Americans were watching Sputnik go up, and up again, and they panicked. So on **October 1, 1958**, the United States started a brand-new space agency: **NASA**. Still around today. Still launching things."

"Wait, the whole agency happened just because the Soviets launched a beeping ball and a dog?"

"Pretty much. Being second is a great motivator." Pixel pulled up a map glowing with dotted lines — an orbit path, like something from a strategy game. "NASA's first satellite went up on **January 31, 1958**. It was called **Explorer 1**. I need a favor. Can you plot its path? You've debugged worse than this."

Theo had spent dozens of hours finding bugs in his own rocket scripts, watching numbers for the one that didn't belong. He traced Explorer 1's glowing orbit line across the screen, following it around the planet — until one stretch spiked, jagged and strange, like corrupted code.

"There," Theo said, pointing. "Right there. Something's off."

Pixel lit up. "You found it on your first try. That spike is real. Explorer 1 flew through a part of space nobody knew existed — a wide ring of invisible energy circling the Earth, made of tiny charged particles **trapped** by the planet's own magnetism. Scientists named it the **Van Allen radiation belt**, after the man who figured out it was there."

"So the first American satellite didn't just launch. It found something nobody had ever seen."

"A whole invisible ring around your own planet," Pixel said. "And you spotted the glitch in under a minute. I've seen professional testers take longer."

Theo leaned back, pleased with himself, and the launch pad screen flickered toward a new scene — a small capsule, a man in a silver suit, and a date that made Pixel grin like it already knew this part was good.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The First Lap (1961)
chapters.text:
A low rumble shook the speakers, like sound leaking through a locked door.

"Four years after Sputnik," Pixel said, "a human finally rode a rocket into space." The loading screen opened onto a tiny metal capsule balanced on top of a bigger rocket than Theo had ever drawn.

"On **April 12, 1961**, Soviet pilot **Yuri Gagarin** climbed inside **Vostok 1** and blasted off. He circled the whole Earth one time, in about **108 minutes**, and became the first human being ever to fly in space."

"A hundred and eight minutes," Theo repeated. "That's barely longer than a movie."

"Less time than your last soccer tournament, actually," Pixel said. "Want to call it like a match? I'll start the clock when he launches. You tell me when he should be landing."

Theo had sat through enough overtime periods to know exactly how long minutes could stretch when everything mattered. He watched the glowing capsule arc away from Earth, tracking a timer ticking up in the corner of the screen. He counted silently, the way he counted down penalty kicks in his head before they happened.

"One hundred eight," he called out, right as the number hit. The capsule's parachute bloomed open on screen.

"Dead on," said Pixel. "Gagarin smiled the entire flight, by the way. Grinned like he'd just scored the winning goal."

"He kind of did."

The screen flickered to a smaller capsule and a different flag. "Three weeks later, on **May 5, 1961**, an American named **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space, aboard a capsule called **Freedom 7**."

"Did he go all the way around too?"

"Nope. His flight was shorter — up, and straight back down, never making a full lap the way Gagarin had. Still brave. Still first for his country. Just not the same event."

Theo frowned, thinking it over. "So Gagarin got the full match, and Shepard got a penalty shootout."

Pixel considered that. "That's annoyingly accurate. I'm stealing it."

The loading screen dimmed, and somewhere behind it Theo could hear the ghost of applause — cheering crowds from two different countries, both certain they were winning the same race.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Dare and the Record (1961–1963)
chapters.text:
Pixel's screen flashed red, like a countdown clock snapping to life.

"In **1961**, the American president, **John F. Kennedy**, made an actual promise in public," Pixel said. "He said the United States would land a person on the Moon and bring them home safe — before the decade ended."

"Before the decade ended," Theo repeated. "So by when exactly?"

"**May 25, 1961** was when he said it. Figure it out."

Theo did the math the way he worked out server reset timers: count forward, don't round. "If a decade ends at the end of 1969, that's eight years. Eight years to go from nothing to landing on the actual Moon."

"No pressure," Pixel said. "You've had longer deadlines for smaller builds."

"I've had longer deadlines for a *spawn room*."

Pixel grinned, pixel teeth and all. "That's the dare the whole country took on. Meanwhile, the Soviets weren't finished setting records either." The screen shifted to a woman in a bright orange flight suit, climbing into a capsule with practiced calm.

"Her name is **Valentina Tereshkova**," Pixel said. "She used to work in a factory. On **June 16, 1963**, she became the first woman in space, flying aboard **Vostok 6**. She circled the Earth **48 times** before she came home."

Theo whistled. "Forty-eight laps. That's not a flight, that's a whole season."

"She trained for it like one, too." Pixel pulled up a roster of names, like a lineup screen before a match. "The Soviets picked her out of dozens of trained candidates. I want you to guess what made her stand out, before I tell you."

Theo studied the short list of facts Pixel had posted — fitness, discipline, steady hands under pressure. He thought about the kids on his own soccer team who never panicked no matter the score.

"The person who stays calm when everything's loud," Theo said. "That's who you want taking the shot."

"That's exactly it," Pixel said. "Calm under pressure. That's the whole scouting report."

The loading screen folded itself into a new scene — a man in a bulky white suit, floating untethered against total black, a thin cord the only thing tying him to his ship.

"Buckle in," said Pixel. "This next one happens outside the spacecraft."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Man Who Floated, and the Man No One Could Name (1965)
chapters.text:
The screen showed a man in a white suit, floating free in space, nothing beneath him but black.

"On **March 18, 1965**, Soviet cosmonaut **Alexei Leonov** opened his hatch and pushed off from his ship," Pixel said. "He became the first human to ever float outside a spacecraft — what people call a **spacewalk**. He stayed out there about **ten minutes**, tied to his capsule by one thin cord."

"Ten minutes floating in actual space," Theo said. "What if the cord snapped?"

"It didn't. He got back inside, hatch closed, mission logged as a total success." Pixel said it fast, the way you'd report a goal that already happened — nothing left to worry about.

Theo exhaled. "Okay. Good. Ten out of ten, no notes."

Pixel pulled up a new window — a dusty file folder, every important word inside it blacked out, like a redacted file in a spy game.

"Here's something strange," Pixel said. "The person who designed almost every rocket the Soviets launched — Sputnik, Gagarin's ship, Leonov's ship, all of it — nobody outside the program was allowed to know his name. Not during his whole career. The Soviet government kept him a total secret."

"Why would you hide the person who built everything?"

"That's your mystery to solve. One clue at a time." Pixel dropped a line of text: *brilliant, driven, worked for years without public credit.* "Guess the kind of person that describes."

Theo thought about the builders he admired most in Roblox Studio — the ones whose games everyone played without ever learning their usernames. "Someone who cares more about the thing getting built than about getting famous for it."

"Close enough to the truth," Pixel said, and let the blacked-out name fade into view: **Sergei Korolev**. "That's him. Chief designer. Nobody outside the Soviet space program knew his name until after he died, in **1966**. He never got to see a single public photo of himself connected to his own work."

Theo sat with that a moment. It felt strange — someone building something enormous, something the whole world watched, and getting none of the credit while it happened.

"Meanwhile," Pixel went on, "the Americans had their own chief rocket builder, and everyone knew *his* name just fine. **Wernher von Braun** had built rockets years earlier, before he came to lead the NASA team that designed the giant rocket that would eventually fly to the Moon."

"So one country hid its best builder, and the other one put his name on everything."

"Different games, different rules," said Pixel. "Same goal."

The screen folded again, and this time it opened onto a view Theo had never imagined anyone actually seeing with their own eyes.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Photo Nobody Planned (1968)
chapters.text:
The new scene was a window — an actual window, round and small, set in the wall of a spacecraft.

"In **December 1968**," Pixel said, "three astronauts became the first humans to ever fly around the Moon. Not land. Just circle it, then come home. Mission called **Apollo 8**."

"That's still huge."

"It gets bigger. While they were circling, the Moon rolled past the window, and suddenly Earth came up over its edge — a small blue marble rising over a gray, cratered horizon."

Pixel handed Theo a glowing camera, the kind of tool from a building game's photo mode. "One of the astronauts, **William Anders**, grabbed a camera fast, fumbling with the settings, racing to catch the shot before the moment passed. Where do you point it?"

Theo had spent enough hours lining up the perfect screenshot in his own builds to know exactly what mattered: never center the obvious thing, always leave room for scale. He swung the camera so Earth sat small and whole in one corner, with the huge gray Moon filling the rest of the frame.

CLICK.

The picture that filled the screen was almost exactly the real one — Earth, tiny and blue and alone, floating above a dead gray horizon.

"That's it," Pixel said, quiet for once. "That's the actual photo. People call it **Earthrise**. It's one of the most famous pictures ever taken, and nobody on that mission planned to take it. They were just circling the Moon, looked out a window, and saw their entire planet for the first time as one small thing, floating."

Theo stared at it longer than he meant to. "Everyone you've ever met is somewhere in that dot."

"Every single person," Pixel agreed. "Every soccer field. Every server you've ever built on. All of it, in one blue speck."

"That's actually kind of a lot of pressure for one photo."

"It changed how a lot of people thought about the whole planet," Pixel said. "Not bad for a camera grabbed in a hurry."

The loading screen rippled, and this time what came through was bright white light, bouncing off dusty gray ground, and the shape of a ladder leading down.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Giant Leap (1969)
chapters.text:
A rocket filled the entire screen, and it kept going, past where Theo expected it to stop.

"This is the **Saturn V**," Pixel said. "The rocket that finally carried astronauts to the Moon. It stood **363 feet tall**."

"How many of me is that?" Theo asked.

"Let's just say it's taller than the Statue of Liberty. Look it up when you're not mid-launch."

"Worth it," Theo said.

Pixel let the rocket thunder upward off the screen, fire and smoke rolling sideways across the launch pad, until it shrank to a dot and vanished. The view jumped to a small spindly spacecraft drifting toward a gray, pitted surface.

"**July 20, 1969**," Pixel said. "Apollo 11. Two astronauts, **Neil Armstrong** and **Buzz Aldrin**, landed on the Moon in a little ship called the lunar module. A third astronaut, **Michael Collins**, stayed up above in the main spacecraft, called **Columbia**, orbiting alone, waiting to bring everyone home."

"That's rough. He came all that way and didn't even get to walk on it."

"Somebody has to hold the ship steady," Pixel said. "Not every important job gets a parade."

The hatch on the little lander opened. A boot, white and bulky, stepped down a ladder rung by rung, and pressed into gray dust that puffed up and settled, slow and strange, in the Moon's weak gravity.

"Armstrong stepped out first," Pixel said, "and said it was one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."

Theo watched the boot print sit there in the dust, not blowing away, not fading — nothing to disturb it on a world with no wind at all.

"Between **1969** and **1972**," Pixel went on, "twelve different American astronauts walked on the Moon, across six separate successful landing missions. Armstrong was just the first."

"Twelve people have literally walked on the Moon," Theo said slowly, like he was trying to make the number sit still in his head. "And I can't even land a rocket on a flat launchpad in my own game."

"You'll get there," Pixel said. "They also crashed test rockets for years before any of this worked. You're keeping excellent company."

Theo looked at the footprint again — quiet, permanent, sitting exactly where it had been left, waiting, it seemed, for absolutely nothing to disturb it.

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Trouble Fix (1970)
chapters.text:
Pixel's screen flickered amber instead of green, like a warning light instead of a loading bar.

"Not every mission went according to plan," Pixel said. "In **1970**, **Apollo 13** was flying toward the Moon when an oxygen tank exploded inside the spacecraft."

Theo tensed. "Exploded? Were they okay?"

"Shaken, not hurt. But it crippled their main spacecraft, and suddenly three astronauts, far from home, had a badly damaged ship and not much time."

"What did they do?"

"They didn't panic, and neither did the engineers back on the ground. Everybody started working the problem together, piece by piece, using only what the astronauts already had on board."

Pixel pulled up a cramped little cabin, cluttered with gear, nothing extra anywhere. "Here's your job. Picture you're building with the Roblox parts already in your inventory — no new pieces allowed, mid-build, something critical just broke. What's the first thing you check?"

Theo thought about every time a script of his had crashed mid-game, forcing him to work only with what was already placed. "You don't start over. You check what's still working, and you build the fix out of that."

"That's exactly the plan they ran," Pixel said. "They used only what was already on board, improvised a fix from spare parts and sheer stubbornness, and steered the crippled ship on a longer, slower path back toward Earth."

"Did it work?"

"The crew made it home safe. All three of them. Splashed down in the ocean, recovered, completely fine." Pixel said it plainly, the way a final score gets read out after the game is long over and nobody's still worried about the result.

Theo let out a breath he hadn't noticed holding. "So the scariest mission is also the one with the happy ending."

"Sometimes those go together," Pixel said. "A good team doesn't need a perfect flight. It needs a plan for when things go wrong."

The amber light faded back to its familiar green, calm again, like a server finally stable after a rough patch.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Handshake in Orbit (1975)
chapters.text:
The last scene opened on two spacecraft, slowly easing toward each other against a black sky, like two players finally meeting up in the same server.

"After everything," Pixel said, "all those firsts, all that racing — it didn't end in a race at all. On **July 17, 1975**, an American spacecraft and a Soviet spacecraft docked together in orbit. Their crews opened the hatch between them and shook hands, floating together above the Earth."

"After racing each other for almost twenty years?"

"After everything," Pixel said again. "Sputnik, Gagarin, Tereshkova, Leonov, the Moon, Apollo 13 — the whole stretch from **1957** to **1975** — and it ended with two crews shaking hands in the same spot in the sky."

Theo watched the two spacecraft link together, hatches opening, two sets of gloved hands reaching across. "That's a weirdly good ending for something that started as a competition."

"The best server merges usually do," Pixel said. "Different builders, different styles, same map in the end."

The green light dimmed, softer now, and the loading window folded itself smaller and smaller until it was just a screen again — Theo's screen, his actual bedroom, his unfinished rocket game sitting right where he'd left it.

Except it wasn't quite where he'd left it.

His little pixel rocket sat steady on its launchpad, nose pointed straight up, like it had been waiting patiently the whole time he was gone. Theo clicked play, half expecting the usual crash into a palm tree.

The rocket lifted off clean. Straight up, no wobble, no sideways tumble — just a smooth, perfect launch, all the way to the top of the screen, where the words **LEVEL COMPLETE** blinked once in friendly green.

Theo stared at it, then laughed out loud, quiet so he wouldn't wake anyone.

"Did you fix my script?" he asked the empty room.

Pixel's voice came back, faint now, already fading like a signal moving out of range. "Let's just say I left you the right parts in your inventory. The rest was always going to be yours."

The screen went dark, peacefully this time, no flicker, no static — just a small sleeping light in the corner of a quiet room.

Theo climbed into bed, already planning tomorrow's build, already certain the next launch would go even further.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, there was a whole Moon level left to build.

true_facts.text: The Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1** on **October 4, 1957** — the first satellite, a machine that just circles a planet.
Sputnik 1 was about **58 centimeters wide**, roughly beach-ball size, and sent out a steady beep ordinary radios could pick up.
On **November 3, 1957**, Sputnik 2 carried a dog named **Laika** into orbit — the first living creature to ever circle the Earth.
The United States started **NASA**, its space agency, on **October 1, 1958**.
NASA's first satellite, **Explorer 1**, launched **January 31, 1958**, and discovered an invisible ring of energy around Earth called the **Van Allen radiation belt**.
On **April 12, 1961**, **Yuri Gagarin** became the first human in space, circling Earth once in **Vostok 1** in about **108 minutes**.
On **May 25, 1961**, President **John F. Kennedy** promised the US would land someone on the Moon and bring them home safe before the decade's end.
On **June 16, 1963**, **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth **48 times** aboard **Vostok 6**.
On **March 18, 1965**, **Alexei Leonov** became the first person to float outside his spacecraft, staying out about **ten minutes**.
Soviet chief designer **Sergei Korolev** was kept a total secret, and the world only learned his name after he died in **1966**.
In **December 1968**, Apollo 8 astronauts were the first to fly around the Moon, and **William Anders** took the famous **Earthrise** photo of Earth rising over the Moon's horizon.
On **July 20, 1969**, **Neil Armstrong** became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
In **1970**, an oxygen tank explosion damaged Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but the crew used only what was on board and made it home safe.
The Space Race ended on **July 17, 1975**, when an American and a Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.

new_recurring.rule: A pixelated astronaut-helmet NPC who lives in the server behind Theo's games. Appears when a screen glitches black-then-green, opens 'loading windows' into real history, challenges Theo with in-game-style puzzles tied to each fact, and…

facts.text: The Space Race was a Cold War contest between the US and USSR to achieve spaceflight firsts, lasting roughly 1957 to 1975.
On October 4, 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, a beach-ball-sized satellite that became the first man-made object to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was about 58 centimeters wide and sent out a simple radio beep that people around the world could pick up on ordinary radios.
On November 3, 1957, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 carrying a dog named Laika, the first living creature to orbit Earth.
Shocked by Sputnik, the United States created NASA, which began operating on October 1, 1958.
The first US satellite, Explorer 1, launched January 31, 1958, and discovered the Van Allen radiation belt.
On April 12, 1961, Soviet cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, orbiting Earth once aboard Vostok 1 in about 108 minutes.
On May 5, 1961, Alan Shepard became the first American in space aboard the Freedom 7 capsule, though his short flight did not orbit Earth.
On May 25, 1961, President Kennedy challenged the US to land a man on the Moon and return him safely before decade's end.
On June 16, 1963, Soviet cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard Vostok 6.
On March 18, 1965, Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk, floating outside his Voskhod 2 capsule for about ten minutes.
On January 27, 1967, astronauts Gus Grissom, Ed White, and Roger Chaffee died in a fire during a launch pad test of Apollo 1.
In December 1968, Apollo 8 astronauts became the first to orbit the Moon, and William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.
On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 astronaut Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon, calling it a giant leap for mankind.
Buzz Aldrin joined Armstrong on the Moon while crewmate Michael Collins orbited alone above in the command module Columbia.
In 1970, an oxygen tank explosion crippled Apollo 13 on its way to the Moon, but the crew safely returned to Earth after engineers improvised a fix.
Between 1969 and 1972, twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon across six successful Apollo landing missions.
The Saturn V rocket that carried Apollo astronauts to the Moon stood 363 feet tall, taller than the Statue of Liberty.
Soviet chief designer Sergei Korolev secretly led the USSR's rocket program, and his identity was kept a state secret until after his death in 1966.
Wernher von Braun, who earlier built rockets for Germany, led the NASA team that developed the Saturn V rocket.
The Space Race ended in a spirit of cooperation on July 17, 1975, when American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit and their crews shook hands.

story.title: Eli and the Relay: Nine Frequencies to the Moon
story.subtitle: A night of static, signals, and one very old radio that should not work.

chapters.heading: Frequency Zero: A Signal With No Business Existing
chapters.text:
The soldering iron hissed against rosin, and the smell of hot metal hung in the garage long after Eli should have gone to bed.

He'd spent three weeks chasing one thing: the two-second chirp the International Space Station sends out when it passes over Ohio. Tonight the radio he'd built from a kit — coils, a tuning capacitor, a dial that stuck at twenty kilohertz — finally had a signal clean enough to hold.

Except it wasn't the ISS. It was slower. Older. A single flat tone, beeping on a loop like a metronome left running since before his parents were born.

"That's not a satellite I know," Eli said out loud, to nobody.

"That's because it isn't one of yours," said a voice out of the speaker — dry, a little bored, like it had been waiting for someone to notice. "Call me Relay. You found me on the leftover frequency of the first thing humans ever put in orbit."

Eli didn't drop the iron, which he considered an achievement. "The first what?"

"October 4, **1957**," Relay said. "The Soviet Union put up a metal ball about the size of a beach ball — **58 centimeters** wide — called **Sputnik 1**. It didn't do anything except beep. That beep came through on ordinary household radios, all over the planet, and it scared the United States out of its mind." It paused. "This was the Cold War — the two biggest powers on Earth racing each other, not with armies this time, but with rockets. Historians just call it the **Space Race**."

Eli ran the math in his head without meaning to — a beach-ball-sized object, moving fast enough to stay up, and ordinary radios on the ground catching its heartbeat from orbit. "People could actually hear it? On a normal radio?"

"Families sat by their sets just to listen," Relay said. "You're doing the same thing right now, seventy years later, in a garage, for free. Some signals never really stop."

Eli looked at his own little rig — coils and a cracked dial — and felt, for one second, like it was plugged into something much bigger than Ohio.

"Alright," he said. "Where else does this dial go?"

Something in the speaker almost sounded pleased.

chapters.heading: November 3, 1957: The Passenger
chapters.text:
The next signal came through rougher, full of pops, and underneath the static was a rhythm Eli recognized before Relay said a word.

Not a machine's beep. A heartbeat.

"Slow it down," Eli said, reaching for a dial that wasn't really there. "That's not electronics. That's biological."

"Good ear," said Relay. "On **November 3, 1957**, barely a month after Sputnik 1, the Soviets launched **Sputnik 2**. It carried a passenger — a dog named **Laika**. She became the first living creature to orbit the Earth."

Eli sat back on the workbench stool. "They sent a dog into orbit a month after the first satellite ever flew?"

"The engineers barely had time to sleep, let alone test everything they wanted to," Relay said. "But they got her up, and for the first time a heartbeat — not a beep — was circling the planet. People all over the world tracked her passes overhead, the same way you're tracking me now."

Eli thought about the dial stuck at twenty kilohertz, about how a signal this old had outlasted every radio that first heard it. He didn't say anything for a second. Then: "She was the first living thing to see Earth from up there. Before any person ever did."

"Before any person," Relay agreed. "You're allowed to think that's a big deal. Most people do."

Eli reached out and, with no real reason to, tapped the side of his radio twice — the way you'd pat something that had done well. The static crackled back at him like a reply.

chapters.heading: January 31, 1958: The Belt Nobody Saw Coming
chapters.text:
The next frequency buzzed with interference so dense Eli's receiver nearly gave up.

"That's not noise," he said, frowning at the meter. "That's a detector maxing out."

"Sharp," said Relay. "On **January 31, 1958**, the United States got its own satellite up — **Explorer 1** — answering Sputnik with the thing America actually had ready: a Geiger counter, a device that clicks faster the more radiation it detects."

"And it clicked itself silent," Eli guessed, "because there was too much to count."

"Exactly. Explorer 1 had just discovered a belt of charged particles trapped around the Earth by its own magnetic field — invisible, enormous, and nobody had known it was there. They named it after the scientist who figured out what the flatlined readings meant: the **Van Allen radiation belt**."

Eli grinned at the dial. "So the instrument was too good at its job to describe what it found. That's not a failure, that's data."

"Most scientists would agree with you," Relay said. "The shock of Sputnik had already pushed the US to stand up a whole new agency for exactly this kind of work. On **October 1, 1958**, it opened its doors: **NASA**."

"So one dog, one beeping ball, and one maxed-out Geiger counter built an entire space program," Eli said.

"When you put it that way," Relay said, "it sounds almost too easy. It wasn't."

Eli turned the dial again, already wanting to know what came next.

chapters.heading: April 12, 1961: One Hundred Eight Minutes
chapters.text:
This time the static resolved into a man's voice, calm, speaking a language Eli didn't know, under the roar of something enormous.

"You're catching the real broadcast of **April 12, 1961**," Relay said. "Soviet pilot **Yuri Gagarin**, aboard a capsule called **Vostok 1**, about to become the first human being in space."

Eli leaned toward the speaker like it might show him something. "How long was he up there?"

"One full orbit. About **108 minutes**, start to finish."

Eli did the physics without being asked — out loud, mostly for himself. "To stay in orbit you're not fighting gravity, you're using it. You go fast enough sideways that you keep falling around the planet instead of into it. That's the whole trick."

"That's the whole trick," Relay confirmed. "The Americans answered fast. Just **three weeks later**, on **May 5, 1961**, astronaut **Alan Shepard** became the first American in space aboard a capsule called **Freedom 7** — though his flight was shorter, straight up and down, and never reached orbit at all."

"So Gagarin went around. Shepard went up and came back."

"Different trick, same courage," Relay said. "And it rattled the US enough that on **May 25, 1961**, President **John F. Kennedy** stood up in front of Congress and dared his country to land a man on the Moon — and bring him home safely — before the decade was out."

Eli let out a breath. "That's not a speech. That's a deadline on the hardest physics problem anyone's ever tried."

"Which is exactly why people still quote it," Relay said.

chapters.heading: Two Firsts, Two Years Apart
chapters.text:
The static this time carried something lighter — almost a laugh, crackling through decades of interference.

"Two more firsts for you," Relay said. "On **June 16, 1963**, Soviet cosmonaut **Valentina Tereshkova** became the first woman in space, orbiting Earth aboard **Vostok 6**."

"She wasn't even a trained pilot first, was she?" Eli said, half-remembering something. "I thought she worked in a factory."

"She did. Then she applied, trained, and flew," Relay said. "Nearly two years later, on **March 18, 1965**, Soviet cosmonaut **Alexei Leonov** opened his hatch and became the first human to walk in space — floating outside his **Voskhod 2** capsule, tethered by a single cable, for about **ten minutes**."

Eli's physics brain snagged on the obvious problem before Relay could get there. "Ten minutes in a vacuum, in a suit that's the only thing keeping air around his body. What's actually holding that suit together under that pressure difference?"

"Layers of sealed fabric, built to keep the body's own air pressure in when there's none outside to push back," Relay said. "It worked. He got back in. The suit had actually puffed up so much from the pressure that he barely fit back through the hatch — but he made it."

Eli exhaled, relieved on behalf of a man who'd been fine for sixty years. "So the scary part already has an ending."

"It always does, in this story," Relay said. "That's rather the point of telling it."

chapters.heading: The Two Men No One Was Allowed to Name
chapters.text:
The dial caught something strange this time — not a launch, not a voice, just paper. Blueprints, somehow, coming through as sound, like Relay was reading engineering drawings out loud in static.

"Behind every launch you've heard tonight," Relay said, "was one man the Soviet Union never let the world name. **Sergei Korolev**, chief designer of their entire rocket program. His identity was a state secret — kept hidden even from most of his own country — until he died in **1966**."

Eli frowned. "They hid the guy who built the rockets?"

"Officially he didn't exist. Unofficially, every Soviet first you've heard tonight runs through his drawings."

"And on the other side?"

"**Wernher von Braun**, who had built rockets years earlier in Germany, and later led the NASA team that designed the **Saturn V** — the rocket that would eventually carry Americans to the Moon."

Eli looked at the two names sitting next to each other in his head: one hidden by his own government, one working in the open for a rival one, both chasing the same equations. "Same problem. Same math. Different flags."

"Rockets don't care which country does the arithmetic," Relay said. "They only care if you did it right."

Eli almost laughed. "That might be the most physics sentence anyone's ever said to me."

"I try," said Relay, and for once it didn't sound bored at all.

chapters.heading: The Photo Nobody Planned For
chapters.text:
Static resolved into something Eli had actually seen before — a photograph, grainy, coming through the speaker as a hum that somehow felt like an image.

"**December, 1968**," Relay said. "**Apollo 8** — the first crew ever to leave Earth orbit and circle the Moon. They weren't planning to take anything historic. Then one of them, **William Anders**, looked up from a window and saw the Earth rising over the Moon's grey horizon, and grabbed a camera."

"Earthrise," Eli said quietly. He'd seen the photo in a textbook — small blue marble, half-lit, hanging over a dead grey edge of rock.

"That one," Relay said. "Taken by someone who went to photograph the Moon and came back with a photo of home instead."

Eli thought about his own radio, built to catch one kind of signal, catching something else entirely instead. "That's basically what's happening to me right now."

"I'd noticed," Relay said. "It's not a bad kind of accident to have."

Eli looked at the photo a moment longer in his mind — one planet, framed by nothing, no borders visible from that far away — and understood, a little better than before, why people kept talking about it sixty years on.

chapters.heading: July 20, 1969: The Giant Leap
chapters.text:
The signal sharpened into something unmistakable: a countdown, old and crackling, followed by a roar that made Eli's little speaker rattle on the bench.

"The rocket under that roar," Relay said, "is a **Saturn V** — **363 feet** tall. Taller than the Statue of Liberty."

Eli glanced at the model rocket kit sitting half-built on his shelf, maybe four feet tall if he was generous, and tried to scale it up ninety times in his head. He gave up. Some numbers just need to stay numbers.

"**July 20, 1969**," Relay went on. "**Apollo 11**. Astronaut **Neil Armstrong** stepped onto the Moon's surface and called it one small step for a man, one giant leap for mankind."

"And he wasn't alone up there," Eli said, because he actually knew this part.

"No. **Buzz Aldrin** walked beside him on the surface, while a third astronaut, **Michael Collins**, orbited alone overhead in the command module, named **Columbia**, waiting to bring them both home."

"That's the job nobody puts on a poster," Eli said. "Flying solo around the Moon so the other two can land."

"Someone has to hold the orbit," Relay said. "Between **1969 and 1972**, twelve American astronauts would eventually walk on the Moon, across six successful landings. Armstrong and Aldrin were just the first."

Eli sat with that a second — twelve people, six missions, one giant rocket each time — and felt the scale of it land properly for the first time all night.

chapters.heading: Apollo 13: The Problem They Solved With What They Had
chapters.text:
The next signal cracked, hard, and for a second the speaker went to pure static.

"That's not interference," Relay said, quieter than before. "In **1970**, an oxygen tank exploded aboard **Apollo 13**, on its way to the Moon. It crippled the spacecraft hundreds of thousands of miles from home."

Eli's stomach tightened — the first real wobble of the night. "What happened to the crew?"

"They survived," Relay said immediately. "Engineers on the ground, working with whatever the astronauts actually had on board, improvised a fix to get them home safely. Every one of them made it back to Earth."

Eli let his shoulders drop. "So it's a story about a disaster where nobody dies. It's actually a story about fixing things."

"That's precisely why people still tell it," Relay said. "Not for the explosion. For the solution."

Eli thought about every half-finished project on his own workbench — soldered wrong, resistors backwards, fixed anyway with whatever was in the parts bin. "That's basically every good physics problem I've ever had. Something breaks, and you use what's actually in the room."

"Then you and three astronauts have more in common than you think," Relay said.

chapters.heading: July 17, 1975: Handshake in Orbit
chapters.text:
The last signal came through cleanest of all — two voices, speaking different languages, laughing at something Eli couldn't translate.

"**July 17, 1975**," Relay said. "An American spacecraft and a Soviet spacecraft docked together in orbit — locked hatches, matched airlocks — and the crews floated through and shook hands. After eighteen years of racing each other to every first there was, that handshake is generally where people mark the **Space Race** as having ended."

Eli sat back from the workbench. The garage was quiet again, just the hum of his own little radio, dial still glowing faintly on the number where it had first caught Sputnik's leftover beep.

"From a beeping ball to a handshake," he said. "Eighteen years."

"Give or take," Relay said. "You found all of it on a kit radio and a frequency that shouldn't have had anything left to hear."

A strip of paper fed slowly out of the printer port Eli had wired in as a joke months ago — he'd never gotten it to print anything useful before tonight. It read out, in dot-matrix type, a string of numbers: a timestamp, a frequency, and the words HANDSHAKE RECEIVED.

Eli peeled it off and folded it into his pocket, next to the half-finished rocket kit on the shelf that suddenly looked like it had somewhere to go.

"Same time next week?" he asked the radio.

The static didn't answer in words. It just beeped once, like a dog, or a ball, or an old friend.

story.ending_line: Next weekend, there was a rocket of his own to finish, and a frequency all his own left to find.

story.title: Maya and the Turtle Who Found the Titanic
story.subtitle: A bedtime voyage through the ship that taught the world to be safer at sea

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Drawing That Swam
chapters.text:
Maya was drawing a boat on her bedroom floor, long past bedtime. Her pencil scratched out tall smokestacks and little round windows.

In the bathroom down the hall, her toy boat still bobbed in the tub, forgotten. Maya yawned and added one more wave to her picture.

Then the paper shimmered. A tiny drawn turtle lifted right off the page, shaking ink off his shell like water. "Hello," he said. "I'm Compass. I swim through drawings. Want to see a real ship? A big one?"

Maya's mouth dropped open. "Yes!"

The room swirled like bathwater going down a drain, and suddenly they stood in a loud, clanging shipyard in **Belfast, Ireland**. Hammers banged. Sparks flew.

"This is **1909**," said Compass. "Workers just laid the **keel** — that's the backbone at the very bottom of the ship. They're building something called **Titanic**."

Maya looked up, and up, and up. The ship's side rose like a steel cliff. "It's going to be the biggest ship in the whole world," Compass said. "Almost **882 feet** long — longer than two whole soccer fields."

"It has sisters too," he added. "Two other ships just like her, called Olympic and Britannic."

Maya grabbed her pencil from her pocket — turtles always let you keep your pencil — and sketched the giant hull. "I'm going to draw every bit of this," she whispered.

"CLANG! CLANG!" went the hammers, as if they agreed.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Splash Day
chapters.text:
Two years later, Compass brought Maya back to the same shipyard. Crowds cheered. Flags snapped in the wind.

"Today she launches," said Compass. "That means she slides off the land and into the water for the very first time."

Maya counted the tall smokestacks poking up from the ship. "One, two, three, four!"

"Good counting," said Compass. "But here's a funny secret. Only three of those actually let out smoke. The fourth one was just for looks, to make her seem even grander."

Maya giggled. "A pretend chimney?"

"A very fancy pretend chimney," said Compass.

Someone shouted, and the great ship began to move. It groaned, it creaked, and then — SPLOOSH! — Titanic hit the water in a wave that soaked the front row of cheering people.

Maya clapped so hard her hands stung. She quickly drew four smokestacks on her page, then circled the fourth one and wrote a tiny "PRETEND" beside it.

"You're keeping very good notes," Compass said, swimming a happy little loop in the air. "Next stop: the day she sails away."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Ship That Could Not Sink (They Thought)
chapters.text:
The next scene smelled like salt and steam. Crowds packed the docks at **Southampton, England**. It was **April 10, 1912**.

"She's leaving for **New York City**," said Compass. "Her very first trip ever."

A sailor nearby patted the ship's rail like it was a good dog. "Sixteen rooms down below," he told a little boy, "all sealed up tight so water can't sneak between them. Nearly unsinkable, this one."

Maya tilted her head. "What does unsinkable mean?"

"They believed the ship was built so cleverly it could never go under," Compass said gently. "People really did believe that. We'll see how that story turns out."

Maya noticed little round holes along the ship's side. "Like portholes for the whole ocean to see through!"

She pulled out her pencil and drew the watertight rooms as little boxes, each one sealed with a careful line. "If one box gets wet," she said slowly, "the others stay dry. Like puzzle pieces."

"Exactly like that," said Compass, proud as could be.

The ship's horn blew — a sound so big it rumbled in Maya's chest — and Titanic slid out to sea.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Meeting the Captain
chapters.text:
Up on deck, wind tugged at Maya's hair. A man in a crisp uniform stood by the rail, watching the water.

"That's **Captain Edward John Smith**,” whispered Compass. "One of the most experienced captains who ever sailed. He's steered ships for years and years."

The captain noticed Maya's drawing and leaned down. "That's a fine sketch of my ship," he said kindly. "Mind if I add something?" He drew a tiny flag at the very top mast.

Nearby, a lady scooped up a small fluffy dog. "This is Lady," she said. "She's a Pomeranian, and she goes everywhere I go."

Maya reached out slowly and let the little dog sniff her fingers, the way her mom taught her to meet new animals — gently, and only if they wanted to say hello.

"Everyone on this ship thinks they're perfectly safe," Compass said quietly, swimming close to Maya's shoulder. "But ships, even giant ones, still need to be careful out on the ocean."

Maya nodded, tucking that thought away like a smooth stone in her pocket.

The sun set pink and gold over the water, and the great ship sailed on, farther from land than Maya had ever been.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Bump in the Dark
chapters.text:
That night, the ocean turned cold and still. Stars glittered like spilled glitter glue.

It was **April 14, 1912**, almost midnight. Maya felt the ship shudder, just a little. A small bump, nothing more.

"What was that?" she asked, grabbing Compass's shell.

"The ship touched an iceberg," Compass said calmly. "A giant chunk of ice floating in the sea. Don't worry — nobody on deck is scared. The crew knows exactly what to do."

Down in a tiny room, two men sat at a strange machine with buttons and wires. "That's the wireless room," said Compass. "Like an old-fashioned walkie-talkie. **Jack Phillips** and **Harold Bride** are sending a message for help."

One operator tapped out letters: CQD... then SOS. "Those are special signals," Compass explained, "that mean 'please come help us, right now.'"

Maya watched the message fly out into the dark like an invisible bird. "Will someone hear it?" she asked.

"Someone will," said Compass, nodding. "Help is already turning this way."

Maya let out a breath she didn't know she was holding, and squeezed her pencil tight.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Into the Boats
chapters.text:
Sailors moved briskly across the deck, swinging small boats out over the water on ropes.

"Those are lifeboats," said Compass. "They carry people safely away from the big ship and float until help comes."

A strong, cheerful woman climbed in and grabbed an oar before anyone could stop her. "I'll row," she announced. "Sitting still never helped anybody."

"That's **Molly Brown**," Compass whispered. "People will call her 'unsinkable' one day, because nothing ever scared her for long."

Maya watched a lady tuck two small fluffy dogs under her coat before stepping into a boat. The little dogs' ears poked out, safe and dry.

Faraway, music drifted across the water — gentle, steady, almost like a lullaby. "Some folks say the ship's band kept right on playing to help everybody feel calm," said Compass. "Nobody's completely sure which songs. But it's a nice story, and it's probably at least a little bit true."

Maya hummed along without knowing the tune, patting the rail softly, the way you pat something you're saying goodbye to.

One by one, boats dropped gently onto the black water, and rowed off toward the stars.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Ship Called Carpathia
chapters.text:
Hours passed. Maya shivered, even though Compass said turtles and dream-visitors never truly get cold.

Then, far off, a light blinked on the horizon.

"That's the **Carpathia**," said Compass, voice brightening. "Another ship. She heard the call for help and raced through the night, as fast as her engines could go."

The little lifeboats rowed toward the light. One by one, people climbed a rope ladder up Carpathia's side, wrapped in warm blankets, holding tight to the hands that pulled them up.

Maya counted dogs, counted blankets, counted smiles. "They made it," she whispered.

"Carpathia picked up everyone who was in those lifeboats," said Compass. "Every single person in a boat was saved."

Maya thought about the empty seats some boats still had, the ones that could have carried more people. "They didn't have enough boats for everybody who was on the ship, did they?" she asked quietly.

"No," Compass said gently. "And that's exactly why things changed afterward. Grown-ups looked at what happened and said: next time, every single ship must carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. They even started a new ice patrol, with ships that watch for icebergs and warn everyone nearby."

Maya nodded slowly. "So the ocean got a little bit safer."

"Much safer," said Compass. "Because people learned."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Ship on the Seafloor
chapters.text:
The scene melted like crayon in the sun, and suddenly it was a different year entirely — cool, blue, and deep.

"This is **1985**," said Compass. "A long time later. A curious ocean explorer named **Robert Ballard** sent cameras far, far down into the dark water."

On a little glowing screen, Maya saw it: Titanic, resting quietly on the seafloor, nearly **12,500 feet** down — deeper than any swimming pool, deeper than almost anywhere Maya could picture. It sat about **370 miles** from a place called Newfoundland, broken gently into two big pieces.

"She waited down there a long time before anyone found her," said Compass. "Divers later brought up plates, shoes, even little bottles, and put them in museums so people could see them."

"Like a museum full of treasure," Maya said.

"Exactly like that. There's even a whole museum shaped like a ship's pointy front, built in Belfast in **2012**, right where Titanic was born."

The screen faded. The ocean faded. And Maya blinked, back on her own bedroom floor, pencil still in hand.

Her drawing had changed. A tiny turtle doodle now swam in the corner of her ship picture, waving one flipper.

"Will you come back?" Maya asked the real Compass, already fading into the page.

"Whenever you draw a boat," he said, "I'll be swimming close by."

Maya tucked herself into bed, pencil on her nightstand, picture propped against her lamp.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Maya. Smooth sailing, and sweet dreams.

facts.text: RMS Titanic was a British liner built for the White Star Line by the Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast, Ireland.

More than 1,500 of the roughly 2,224 people aboard died, while about 700 survived.
Titanic had lifeboats for only about 1,178 people, far fewer than the total number aboard.
Captain Edward John Smith, one of White Star's most experienced commanders, stayed aboard as the ship went down.

Passenger Margaret 'Molly' Brown helped row her lifeboat and later earned the nickname 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'
The wreck was found 1 September 1985 by Robert Ballard's expedition, about 12,500 feet (3,800 m) deep.
