story.title: Hana and the Wayfinder Compass: The Titanic
story.subtitle: A journey across a glowing chart, from a Belfast shipyard to the bottom of the sea

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Keel at Belfast (1909)
chapters.text:
Hana was supposed to be asleep an hour ago.

Instead she lay on her bedroom carpet, chin propped on her fists, staring up at the big paper chart pinned over her bed — a reproduction of the old White Star Line shipping routes her dad had found rolled up in a flea-market bin. Next to her elbow sat her favorite thing in the whole room: a dented brass compass, its glass scratched, its needle slightly wobbly, which her grandfather had given her and sworn was "older than both of us put together."

She traced the dotted line on the chart with one finger — the one that ran from a port called Southampton, England, all the way across the blue paper ocean to New York.

The compass needle twitched.

Hana froze. Compasses do not twitch. They especially do not twitch and then spin in slow circles, glowing blue like a nightlight left at the bottom of a pool.

"Okay," Hana whispered. "That is new."

"Evening, Navigator," said a calm voice from the brass casing. "Chart's unrolling. You coming, or lying there with your mouth open all night?"

The blue light swallowed the room, and when it faded, Hana stood in a freezing, noisy shipyard full of iron and steam, in a city the compass called Belfast, Ireland, in the year 1909.

"That's a **keel**," said the compass, floating at her shoulder, as workers lowered a long steel spine onto blocks the size of her own bed. "The backbone of a ship — the first piece laid down, before anything else gets built onto it. They laid this one on **31 March 1909**."

A soot-streaked riveter walked past carrying a bucket of glowing rivets like they were nothing.

"Who's building this?" Hana asked him.

"Harland and Wolff, miss. Biggest shipyard in the world. White Star Line's paying us to build their new queen of the ocean." He nodded at an identical steel skeleton rising in the next slip. "That's her sister, the **Olympic**. Ours is the second of three — there's a baby sister coming too, the **Britannic**."

"What's this one called?" Hana asked.

The riveter grinned. "Titanic. Fitting name, don't you think?"

By the time the hull was finished, Hana had walked its full length three times just to believe it. It would be **882 feet long** — longer than two and a half football fields laid end to end, the compass admitted when Hana wouldn't stop doing the math out loud. The largest ship anyone had ever built.

"Not bad," Hana said, "for a backbone and a dream."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Thirty-One Days to Launch (1911)
chapters.text:
Two years rolled by in one blink of blue light, the way time does when a compass is driving.

By **31 May 1911**, the ship had a name painted on her bow and twenty thousand people lining the Belfast docks to watch her slide into the water for the first time — a launch, not a voyage, just a test to see if she'd float at all.

"She will," said the compass. "Obviously."

Hana wasn't so sure. The hull looked big enough to flood a city. A shipwright beside her, grease on her sleeves, led Hana down through hatches into the ship's belly, where thick steel walls cut the hull into sixteen separate rooms, floor to ceiling, like a very long ice-cube tray.

"**Watertight compartments**," the shipwright said. "Walls that keep water in, or out. If the hull tears open in one spot, these doors seal shut, and only that one room floods. She could take damage in two, even four of these, and still float."

"So she's unsinkable," Hana said.

The shipwright paused, just a half-second too long.

"That's what the newspapers call her," she said carefully. "I'd call her very, very safe. Nothing with a hull and an engine is a promise."

Hana filed that away the way she filed unlabeled streets on old maps — interesting, worth remembering.

Up on deck, she counted four enormous funnels rising overhead. "Why so many?"

"Three for smoke," said the compass. "The fourth's mostly there to look impressive. Ships were starting to get judged on their funnels, same as some people judge a captain by his hat."

"That seems like a very silly way to judge a ship," Hana said.

"Welcome to 1911," said the compass.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Southampton, Noon (10 April 1912)
chapters.text:
The blue light rippled and spat Hana onto a crowded dock, where a brass band played and more people than she'd ever seen waved handkerchiefs at a ship so tall it blocked the sun.

"**10 April 1912**," said the compass. "Her **maiden voyage** — the very first trip anywhere for this ship. Southampton, England, to New York City, with stops in France and Ireland along the way."

Hana pulled the very chart from her own bedroom wall, somehow folded small enough to fit her coat pocket, and matched the dotted line to the gangway in front of her.

"I know this part," she said. "I've traced this a hundred times."

"Tracing it and standing on it," said the compass, "are different sports."

A porter rushed past with a trunk on his shoulder, and Hana bumped into a girl about her own age craning her neck toward the top deck.

"First time on a ship?" Hana asked.

"First time on any ship," the girl said, grinning wide. "My whole family's going to America. Starting over."

Hana looked up at thousands of tons of brand-new steel about to cross an entire ocean, and felt something between excitement and a small, cold shiver she couldn't explain.

"Good luck," she said, and meant it more than she expected to.

The horn sounded so loud the dock seemed to shake, and the ship that had started as a steel backbone two years ago eased away from England, pointing her bow at the open sea.

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Captain and the Wireless Room
chapters.text:
Four days out, the ship felt like its own floating town — restaurants, a gymnasium, even a squash court — until the compass tugged Hana toward a door marked PRIVATE.

Inside sat a cluttered room buzzing with static, two men hunched over a machine with headphones clamped to their ears.

"**Wireless** room," the compass explained. "No telephone wires — just radio waves, carrying messages through the air to other ships and to shore. That's Jack Phillips and Harold Bride. Right now they're mostly sending passenger telegrams. Soon, this same machine will matter a lot more."

On the bridge, a stern man in a crisp white-topped cap studied a chart almost exactly like the one in Hana's pocket.

"**Captain Edward John Smith**," murmured the compass. "One of White Star's most trusted commanders. This is meant to be his last voyage before retiring."

Hana liked him immediately — the careful way he rechecked his charts, exactly like she liked to check her own maps twice.

"How many lifeboats does a ship this big carry?" she asked, mostly out of curiosity.

The compass went quiet a second too long.

"Twenty," it said finally. "Enough space for about **1,178 people**."

Hana's chart-reading brain did the math automatically, and didn't love the answer. "That's not everyone aboard."

"No," said the compass. "It isn't. The rules back then counted lifeboats by the size of the ship, not by how many people were actually sailing on her. Nobody thought they'd need more. It's one of the parts of this story people still argue about."

Hana looked at the twenty small boats lashed along the deck, then up at thousands of warm, glowing portholes above her, and said nothing at all for a while.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: 11:40 P.M. (14 April 1912)
chapters.text:
The sea had gone glassy and still — the kind of still that makes grown-ups nervous for reasons they can't quite explain — and the air had turned so cold Hana's breath fogged even through the compass's magic.

"Why's everyone up top with binoculars?" she asked.

"Ice warnings," said the compass. "Other ships have been radioing all day — more ice than usual for April. The lookouts are watching."

A bell rang three times from high above, sharp and sudden, and a voice bellowed down through the dark: "Iceberg, right ahead!"

Hana's stomach dropped the way it does at the top of a rollercoaster. The ship turned — slowly, impossibly slowly for something so huge — and a wall of ice taller than the deck slid past so close Hana could almost have touched it, scraping along the hull with a long, low groan.

Then it was gone, swallowed back into the dark, and the ship sailed on.

"That's it?" Hana said, half a laugh of relief escaping her. "We missed it!"

"Mostly," said the compass gently. "At **11:40 p.m. on 14 April 1912**, the iceberg scraped her side underwater, where nobody could see. It popped the seams of several watertight compartments at once — more than she was built to lose."

Hana remembered the ice-cube-tray hull, the shipwright's careful pause. *Nothing with a hull and an engine is a promise.*

"How many compartments can she lose?" Hana asked quietly.

"Four, and still float," said the compass. "The iceberg opened at least five."

Below, water was rising, quiet and patient. On the bridge, Captain Smith studied the reports, his face gone very still, then gave an order Hana already knew was coming.

"Uncover the boats," he said.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: Twenty Boats, Two Thousand People
chapters.text:
Chaos, Hana discovered, could be strangely quiet.

Up on the tilting deck, stewards helped women and children into the lifeboats first, voices low and steady — nobody screaming, nobody running, just a long, cold line of people doing the next right thing, one at a time.

And over all of it, astonishingly, floated music.

"That's **Wallace Hartley**," said the compass, nodding at a man with a violin under his chin, leading seven other musicians through a steady, cheerful tune. "Legend says the band kept playing almost the whole time, to keep people calm. Survivors really did remember hearing music — though nobody's completely sure which songs. Some stories grow a little taller with each telling. This might be one. But the calm part is true."

A woman in a fur coat elbowed past three men toward an officer loading a lifeboat, planted her feet, and started handing out orders like she owned the ship.

"Row faster, ladies, unless you'd like to freeze solid admiring the view," she announced, grabbing an oar herself.

"**Margaret Brown**," the compass said. "Everyone will call her **Molly** after tonight. She'll help row that boat for hours. People will start calling her 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown,' and she will absolutely love it."

Hana laughed despite herself, then spotted something small wriggling under a woman's coat two boats down — a fluffy orange face poking out, ears flat with worry.

"Is that a—"

"**Pomeranian**," said the compass. "A couple of little dogs are getting smuggled into boats tonight, tucked under coats. Nobody has the heart to say no."

Hana crouched by the boat as it lowered. "What's her name?"

"Lady," the woman said, hugging the dog tighter, hands shaking. "I couldn't leave her."

"I don't think anyone would have asked you to," Hana said, and meant it.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: CQD… SOS…
chapters.text:
Back in the wireless room, Jack Phillips hammered his key so fast his fingers blurred, headphones jammed against his ears.

"**CQD**," the compass translated. "The old distress call — means 'all stations, urgent.' He's also trying something brand new, just in case: **SOS**. Three short, three long, three short. Nobody's sure yet which signal other ships will recognize faster, so he sends both, again and again, into the dark."

Far away, a smaller ship called the **Carpathia** picked up the call in the middle of the night. Her captain didn't hesitate — he turned her hard around and drove her straight through the same icy water everyone else was trying to avoid.

"How far away was she?" Hana asked.

"Fifty-eight miles," said the compass. "She covered it in about four hours. That's a dead sprint, for a ship."

Hana pictured it on her mental chart: a tiny dot racing through black water toward another tiny dot, guided by nothing but static and nerve.

By the time the sun came up, grey and freezing over a flat, quiet sea scattered with ice, **Carpathia** was there, pulling lifeboat after lifeboat out of the water, wrapping survivors in blankets, handing round hot soup to hands too cold to hold the cups steady.

More than 1,500 people had died that night. But **more than 700** climbed up Carpathia's rope ladders into the morning light — including the girl from the Southampton dock, and Molly Brown, and a small orange dog named Lady, still tucked inside a coat.

Hana stood at the rail, wrapped in a blanket someone had draped over her shoulders without asking, watching the empty horizon where the ship she'd seen born in Belfast had quietly gone under the sea.

"She's really gone," Hana said.

"She is," said the compass, quiet for once. "But she isn't finished yet. Not by a long way."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Found, 12,500 Feet Down (1985)
chapters.text:
The blue light rippled once more, and the cold Atlantic morning dissolved into a conference hall decades later, full of serious people in suits arguing over sheets of paper.

"After the disaster," said the compass, "the countries who sailed these waters got together and wrote new rules. They set up the **International Ice Patrol**, to watch for icebergs and warn ships year-round. And they wrote a treaty called **SOLAS** — Safety of Life at Sea — that said every ship must carry enough lifeboats for every single person aboard. No exceptions."

"That seems like something they should have figured out already," Hana said.

"A lot of the best safety rules," the compass agreed, "get written in pencil right after someone needed them and didn't have them."

The light rippled again, and Hana found herself inside a small, humming submersible — a tiny submarine built for diving deep underwater — squinting through a round window at absolute darkness.

"**1 September 1985**," said the compass. "An oceanographer — someone who explores the ocean for a living — named **Robert Ballard** is down here right now, looking for her. She's been missing for seventy-three years."

A shape rose out of the black: a wall of rust-streaked steel, enormous, unmistakable, lying broken in two pieces on the seafloor, **12,500 feet** down, nearly **370 miles** off the coast of Newfoundland, Canada.

Hana pressed her hand flat against the cold glass, the way you'd touch a photograph of someone you missed.

"There you are," she whispered.

"There she is," the compass agreed, softer than Hana had ever heard it. "Still keeping her secrets. Still teaching people things, all these years later."

The blue light rose up one last time, warm now instead of cold, and set Hana down gently on her own bedroom carpet, under her own chart, her own ceiling back where it belonged.

The compass sat still in her palm, needle pointing calmly north, glow fading to nothing.

On the carpet beside her knee lay one small, heavy, rust-spotted rivet — real, solid, and entirely hers to keep.

Hana closed her hand around it and looked up at the dotted line from Southampton to New York, then reached for a pencil to add one more mark: a small X, far out in the blue, where a ship still rested, found at last.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow, she'd draw the rest of the map — every ship, every voyage, all the way home.

true_facts.text: Titanic was built at the **Harland & Wolff** shipyard in **Belfast** for the **White Star Line**.
Her **keel** — the ship's steel backbone — was laid down on **31 March 1909**, and she was launched on **31 May 1911**.
Finished, she stretched **882 feet** long, the biggest ship anyone had ever built.
Sixteen **watertight compartments** inside her hull were supposed to make her almost impossible to sink.
She left **Southampton, England** on **10 April 1912**, bound for **New York City**.
**Captain Edward John Smith**, one of the line's most trusted commanders, stayed aboard until the end.
Her lifeboats only had room for about **1,178 people** — not everyone aboard.
She struck an iceberg at **11:40 p.m.** on **14 April 1912**.
People say the ship's band, led by **Wallace Hartley**, kept playing music to keep everyone calm — though nobody's completely sure which songs.
Passenger **Molly Brown** grabbed an oar and helped row her lifeboat, earning the nickname **'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'**
The wireless operators sent both the old **CQD** distress call and the brand-new **SOS** signal into the night.
The steamship **Carpathia** raced through the dark and pulled survivors from the lifeboats the next morning.
The wreck was finally found on **1 September 1985** by explorer **Robert Ballard**, sitting **12,500 feet** down.
After the disaster, countries created the **International Ice Patrol** and a new rule called **SOLAS**, requiring enough lifeboats for everyone aboard every ship.

request.care_notes: Focus on the engineering marvel of the ship, how it was built, the safety lessons learned (lifeboats, communication systems), and the rescue efforts. Avoid graphic descriptions of the sinking, drowning, or suffering. Emphasize human stories of bravery and the historical importance of the disaster in changing maritime safety forever.

fact_pack.summary: The RMS Titanic was a huge new ocean liner that sank on its first voyage after hitting an iceberg in April 1912. Its story of bravery, mistakes, and mystery still fascinates people, especially since the wreck was found on the seafloor in 1985.

facts.text: RMS Titanic was a British liner built for the White Star Line by the Harland & Wolff shipyard in Belfast, Ireland.
Titanic's keel was laid on 31 March 1909, and she was launched on 31 May 1911.
Titanic left Southampton, England, on 10 April 1912 on her first voyage, bound for New York City.
At about 11:40 p.m. on 14 April 1912, Titanic struck an iceberg in the icy North Atlantic Ocean.
Titanic sank at around 2:20 a.m. on 15 April 1912, less than three hours after hitting the iceberg.
At about 882 feet (269 meters) long, Titanic was the largest ship in the world at the time.
More than 1,500 of the roughly 2,224 people aboard died, while about 700 survived.
Titanic had lifeboats for only about 1,178 people, far fewer than the total number aboard.
Captain Edward John Smith, one of White Star's most experienced commanders, stayed aboard as the ship went down.
Titanic had four funnels, but only three carried real smoke; the fourth was mostly for looks.
Titanic's hull had 16 watertight compartments, leading people to call her nearly unsinkable before the iceberg proved otherwise.
The steamship Carpathia raced through the night and rescued Titanic's survivors from their lifeboats the next morning.
Wireless operators Jack Phillips and Harold Bride sent distress calls using both the old CQD signal and the newer SOS.
Legend says the ship's band, led by Wallace Hartley, kept playing music on deck as Titanic sank; survivors did report hearing music, though exact songs are debated.
Third-class passengers had far lower survival rates than first-class passengers, reflecting the ship's unfair class divisions.
A few small pet dogs, including two Pomeranians, survived because owners carried them into lifeboats.
Passenger Margaret 'Molly' Brown helped row her lifeboat and later earned the nickname 'the Unsinkable Molly Brown.'
The wreck was found 1 September 1985 by Robert Ballard's expedition, about 12,500 feet (3,800 m) deep.
The wreck sits about 370 miles (600 km) off Newfoundland, Canada, split into two main pieces.
After the disaster, the International Ice Patrol was formed and the SOLAS treaty required enough lifeboats for everyone aboard.
Titanic was the second of three sister ships built for White Star Line, alongside Olympic and Britannic.
Titanic Belfast, a museum shaped like a ship's prow, opened in 2012 on the old shipyard site for the disaster's 100th anniversary.
James Cameron's 1997 film 'Titanic' became one of the highest-grossing movies ever made.
Many objects recovered from the wreck, from dinner plates to shoes, are now displayed in museums worldwide.

story.title: Ben and the Pixel Who Pressed Start
story.subtitle: A bedtime trip through the history of video games.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Green Wobbly Line (1958)
chapters.text:
Ben sat on his bedroom floor, way past bedtime. He was drawing pixel art — a blocky green sword, square by square, on graph paper. His tablet lay beside him, paused mid-build in his Minecraft world.

CLICK. The tablet screen went black, then flickered green.

Ben blinked. "That's not supposed to happen."

A tiny square of light popped out of the screen. It grew arms. It grew a face made of eight fuzzy green pixels.

"Hiya," said the square. "Name's Byte. Wanna see where games came from?"

Ben's eyes went wide. "Games have a start?"

"Oh, buddy," said Byte, grinning. "Buckle up."

The room folded like paper. Suddenly Ben stood in a big room full of humming machines, at a place called **Brookhaven National Laboratory**, in the year **1958**.

A man in a lab coat fiddled with a round, glowing screen. "That's an **oscilloscope**," Byte explained. "Scientists used it to look at wiggly lines made of electricity."

"That's **William Higinbotham**," Byte said. "He's a **physicist** — a scientist who studies how things move. He got bored of wiggly lines. So he made something better."

Higinbotham flipped a switch. A glowing dot appeared, bouncing left, right, over a flat green line.

"It's... tennis?" Ben said slowly. "On a science screen?"

"**Tennis for Two**," Byte said proudly. "First video game anybody ever lined up to play."

A line of scientists was already forming behind them, shuffling their feet, eager for a turn.

"Go on," Byte whispered. "Be the first kid ever to play it."

Ben grabbed the little metal controller. He turned the knob. He pressed the button at just the right second.

BOING. The dot bounced clean over the line.

"IT BOUNCES!" Ben yelled.

The scientists burst out clapping. Higinbotham tipped his hat, like Ben had just won a trophy.

"Not bad," said Byte, "for the very first player in video game history."

Ben grinned so wide his cheeks hurt. "What's next?"

Byte's pixels sparkled. "Oh, buddy. We've only just pressed start."

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Spinning Spaceships (1962)
chapters.text:
A deep hum rattled Ben's teeth. The air smelled like hot metal and chalk dust.

"Where are we now?" Ben asked.

"**MIT**," said Byte. "A university full of giant computers. The year is **1962**."

A computer the size of a refrigerator blinked lights at them. A college student named **Steve Russell** sat typing fast, friends crowded around him.

"He's building a game," Byte said. "Two spaceships. Shooting at each other. On a computer called the **PDP-1**."

Ben peered at the screen. Two tiny dots, shaped like rockets, spun in slow circles.

"It's called **Spacewar!**," said Byte. "First game anybody built just for computers. Just for fun."

Steve Russell groaned. "My ship keeps drifting into the sun!"

Ben looked closer. A bright blob sat in the middle of the screen, tugging both ships toward it.

"That's the sun," Ben said. "It's pulling them in. Like a magnet."

Steve blinked. "Huh. Kid's got a point."

Ben grabbed the spare control box. He nudged his little ship hard, away from the pulling star, right as it drifted too close.

WHOOSH. His rocket zipped clear, a torpedo trailing behind it.

"GOT HIM!" Ben shouted, as the other ship spun away, beaten.

The room of students cheered. Someone slapped Steve on the back. "First kid to dodge the sun on purpose!"

Byte floated proudly beside Ben. "Two games down. About a hundred more to go."

Ben laughed. "This is the best bedtime ever."

"Just wait," said Byte. "Next stop smells like a garage."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Box in the Garage (1972)
chapters.text:
The air smelled like sawdust and warm wires.

A tall man leaned over a wooden box, covered in switches and dials.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," said Byte. "People later called him the father of video games."

"He's got a box full of wires," Ben said. "That's it?"

"That box," said Byte, "plugs into a television. Lets you play games right there in your living room. Nobody's done that before."

Baer squinted at a tangle of wires and groaned. "Nearly there. Nearly—"

Ben crouched beside him. "What's it called?"

"Right now? The **Brown Box**," Baer said. "Not catchy, I know."

Ben grinned. "Needs a better name."

Baer connected the last wire. Two white squares glowed onto a nearby TV screen. One dot chased the other, bouncing off invisible walls.

"It works!" Baer said, and gave Ben a high five.

"Can it play more games?" Ben asked. "Like, different ones?"

Baer rubbed his chin. "Right now, just a few. Someday, maybe more."

Byte leaned toward Ben. "Good question. Keep that one in your pocket."

The scene shimmered. Years folded past like pages. The wooden box had turned shiny and white, sitting in a toy store window.

"**1972**," Byte said. "Baer's box became the **Magnavox Odyssey**. First home video game console ever sold. A **console** is just a machine you plug into your TV to play games."

Ben pressed his nose to the glass. "People get to have this. In their own house."

"Yep," said Byte. "Living rooms were never the same."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Jammed Quarter Machine (1972)
chapters.text:
Ding. Ding. Ding. Coins rattled nonstop somewhere nearby.

Ben and Byte stood in a noisy room, lit by one glowing screen in the corner.

"**Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called **Atari**," said Byte. "Also in **1972**. And they made this."

On the screen, two white paddles bounced a square ball back and forth. BEEP. BOOP.

"**Pong**," Byte said. "Simplest game ever made. Everybody loved it."

A man in an apron shook the machine gently, frowning. "Thing's jammed again."

Ben leaned down, listening. "It sounds... full."

"Story goes," said Byte, "one Pong machine got so popular, it jammed completely full of quarters. That might be a bit of a tall tale. But it shows you how fast folks fell for this beepy little game."

The man popped open a small door. Quarters poured out, clattering across the floor like a shiny waterfall.

Ben's jaw dropped. "That's like a hundred games of Pong!"

"At least," laughed Byte.

The owner scooped coins into a bucket, grinning ear to ear. "Best invention since the jukebox."

Ben grabbed the paddle knob for a quick round. BEEP. He scored. BOOP. The machine lit up, little proud blips of sound.

"Video games," Ben said, "started with two white lines and a beep."

"And," said Byte, "a whole lot of quarters."

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Aliens Marching Down (1977 to 1978)
chapters.text:
A whole wall of plastic rectangles stood stacked in front of Ben, like books in a library.

"**1977**," said Byte. "Atari made a new console called the **Atari 2600**. Instead of games built right in, you could plug in a **cartridge** — a little plastic case with a game saved inside. Pop one out, pop another in."

Ben picked one up, turned it over. "So it's like switching Minecraft worlds?"

"Exactly like that," Byte said. "Except way clunkier."

Ben slid a cartridge into the slot. CLACK. The screen flickered to life.

Rows of blocky aliens marched slowly across the top of the screen, inching down with every step.

"**Space Invaders**," Byte said. "Made in **1978** by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**, for a company called **Taito**. Whole arcades went alien-crazy for it."

Ben grabbed the controller, swiveling his little cannon left and right. PEW. PEW.

Two aliens dropped. The rest crept closer.

"They're getting faster!" Ben said, grinning nervously.

"Fewer aliens, faster they go," said Byte. "Keeps you on your toes."

Ben squinted, timed his shot, and — PEW — the last alien blinked out.

"CLEARED IT!" Ben cheered, pumping his fist.

Other kids nearby turned and clapped, dropping more coins into their own machines.

"Not bad," said Byte, "for someone who's never even held a joystick before tonight."

Ben wiped imaginary sweat off his forehead. "Bring on the next one."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Pizza With No Slice (1980 to 1983)
chapters.text:
The air smelled like buttery popcorn and electric buzzing.

A bright yellow circle zoomed across the screen, gobbling little dots, chased by four colorful ghosts.

"**Pac-Man**," said Byte. "Made in **1980** by a designer named **Toru Iwatani**, for a company called **Namco**."

"Why's he shaped like that?" Ben asked, pointing at the hungry yellow circle.

"Story goes," Byte said, "Iwatani looked at a pizza with one slice missing. That might just be a fun story people tell. Either way — look at that mouth."

Ben grabbed the joystick, guiding Pac-Man around a corner, just ahead of a ghost's nose.

"Close one!" Ben laughed.

The scene shifted. Shelves and shelves of games stood in a store, dust gathering on the boxes.

"**1983**," said Byte, quieter now. "So many games got made so fast, lots of them weren't very good. People stopped buying. Stores had too many games nobody wanted. Folks call it the **video game crash** — sales just dropped and dropped."

Ben frowned at the dusty shelves. "That's kind of sad."

"A little," said Byte. "But it meant only the best games would get made next. Including one you might like."

He pointed at an old news picture: diggers out in the desert, in **New Mexico**, pulling old game cartridges out of the dirt.

"People used to say a whole truckload of unsold **E.T.** games got buried in a landfill — a giant dump for trash," Byte said. "In **2014**, diggers actually found the cartridges. Turned out the story was true!"

Ben grinned. "So even a buried video game can come back."

"Just like the whole industry did," said Byte.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Plumber and the Falling Blocks (1984 to 1985)
chapters.text:
Snow was falling outside a tall building in **Moscow**, in the year **1984**.

Inside, a man typed quietly at a glowing green screen, lines of colorful blocks tumbling down it.

"That's **Alexey Pajitnov**," said Byte. "He loved puzzles. He just invented a little game called **Tetris**."

Blocks fell, one after another. Ben watched a gap form near the bottom.

"You need a straight one," Ben said, pointing. "The long skinny block."

Right on cue, a long block dropped. Ben reached out and nudged it sideways. CLUNK. It slid into the gap. The whole row vanished with a soft FWIP.

Pajitnov blinked at the screen, delighted. "Nice reflexes, kid."

"I stack blocks all the time," Ben said proudly. "In Minecraft."

"Good practice," laughed Byte.

The scene shifted again, bright and sunny now. **1985**. A mushroom kingdom glowed on a television screen.

"Nintendo needed something big," Byte said, "to get people excited about games again, after the crash. So they made a console called the **NES**, and bundled it with this."

A mustached plumber in overalls jumped over a gap, bonked a block with his head, and grabbed a coin. DING.

"**Super Mario Bros.**," said Byte. "Designed by **Shigeru Miyamoto** in **1985**. Mario's the most famous video game character there is."

Ben grabbed the controller and jumped Mario clean over a pit.

"HERE WE GO!" Ben shouted, as Mario landed on a flagpole, bells ringing.

"Two legends," said Byte. "One falling block, one jumping plumber. Both still played today."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Faster Than a Hedgehog (1991 to 1994)
chapters.text:
WHOOSH. A blue blur zipped across the screen so fast Ben almost missed it.

"**1991**," said Byte. "Sega needed a hero speedy enough to race against Mario. Meet **Sonic the Hedgehog**."

Ben grabbed the controller. Sonic curled into a spiky ball and rolled down a loop-the-loop, picking up golden rings along the way.

"He's SO fast!" Ben laughed, mashing the button as Sonic zoomed past waterfalls of pixels.

"Faster than Mario could ever jump," Byte agreed.

The scene spun again. A shiny silver disc floated in front of them, spinning gently in the air.

"**1994**," said Byte. "A company called **Sony** jumped into consoles too, with the **PlayStation**. Instead of cartridges, it used **CDs** — the same shiny discs that hold music. More room meant fuller sound and smoother pictures."

Ben held the disc up to the light, rainbow colors shimmering across it. "It's like a tiny rainbow."

"A tiny rainbow full of a whole game," said Byte.

Ben carefully slid the disc into a slot. The console whirred. A racing game roared to life, engines growling, crowds cheering.

"Vroom vroom!" Ben said, steering an imaginary wheel.

Byte chuckled. "Games were starting to look like little movies."

"What's next?" Ben asked, bouncing on his toes. "Please say something with blocks."

Byte's pixels sparkled extra bright. "Buddy. You have no idea."

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: A Cube of His Own (2006 to Today)
chapters.text:
A white remote floated in front of Ben, dangling from a wrist strap.

"**2006**," said Byte. "Nintendo made a console called the **Wii**. Instead of just pressing buttons, you swing the controller around, like a tennis racket or a bowling ball."

Ben grabbed it and swung hard. On screen, a tiny bowler hurled a ball straight down the lane. STRIKE! Pins scattered everywhere.

"People who'd never played games before," Byte said, "suddenly wanted to play."

"Even grandmas?" Ben asked.

"Especially grandmas," said Byte.

The scene melted into soft green hills, made of chunky square trees and square sheep.

Ben gasped. "Wait. I know this place."

"**2011**," said Byte. "A developer in Sweden named **Markus Persson** — folks called him **Notch** — built a game made entirely out of blocks. You might've heard of it."

"**Minecraft**," Ben whispered, grinning so wide his cheeks hurt again. "It became the best-selling video game ever made."

"All because one guy liked building with blocks," said Byte. "Kind of like someone else I know."

Ben puffed his chest out proudly.

One last shimmer, and they stood in a bright museum hallway, glass cases glowing all around them.

"**2015**," Byte said. "The **World Video Game Hall of Fame** opened, in **Rochester, New York**. Every game we visited tonight has a spot somewhere inside."

Ben peered into a case: a tiny paddle from Pong, a Mario mushroom, a Tetris block, a glowing green Minecraft cube.

"Someday," Byte said, "your name could be part of this story too."

The hallway folded away like paper. Ben blinked, and he was back on his bedroom floor, graph paper still in his lap.

His tablet glowed softly, one tiny pixel square blinking in the corner, right where Byte had first appeared.

Ben smiled and tucked the tablet under his pillow. "Night, Byte."

The little square blinked twice, like a wink, then faded to black.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Ben. Game on.

**Ralph Baer** built a wooden game machine called the **Brown Box** that plugged into a TV.
Baer's box became the **Magnavox Odyssey** in **1972**, the first home video game console ever sold.

People said unsold **E.T.** game cartridges were buried in a dump in **New Mexico** — and diggers really found them in **2014**.

In **1984**, **Alexey Pajitnov** invented the falling-block puzzle game **Tetris** in **Moscow**.
In **2011**, **Markus "Notch" Persson** released **Minecraft**, which later became the best-selling video game ever.

story.title: Theo and the Continue Controller
story.subtitle: One dusty joystick, eight levels, and the whole history of video games.

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Beeping Dot (1958)
chapters.text:
Theo was building a soccer stadium in Roblox Studio, one brick of bleachers at a time. It was past ten o'clock. His parents did not know that part.

He had just finished a goal-kick script when his screen flickered green. Not blue. Not black. Green, like an old movie computer.

A single white dot bounced on a glowing line, back and forth, like the simplest tennis match ever made.

"Okay," Theo said to his empty room. "That is not supposed to happen."

The dot blinked twice, like it was waking up. Then it folded itself into a small, blocky shape with a grin.

"Name's Byte," it said, in a voice like dial-up internet learning to talk. "You press Start, I show you where games came from. Deal?"

"Is this a virus?" Theo asked.

"It's history," said Byte. "Rude of you to assume the worst."

A dusty grey controller he didn't own sat on his desk, one glowing button in the middle, labeled CONTINUE. Theo pressed it.

WHOOOSH. The room folded like a loading screen. When it unfolded, it wasn't his room anymore.

He stood in a humming laboratory, machines the size of refrigerators all around him.

"Brookhaven National Laboratory," Byte announced. "Long Island, New York. The year is **1958**."

A man in glasses leaned over a box with a round glass screen — an **oscilloscope**, built to draw wiggly lines of electricity, not games.

"That's William Higinbotham," Byte said. "He's tired of visitors staring at dials all day. So he gave them something to play."

On the little screen, a glowing line arced over a flat line, like a net. The bouncing dot was back, except now it had a court.

"**Tennis for Two**," said Byte. "The first video game most people ever got to play with their own hands."

Higinbotham noticed Theo and held out a spare knob. "Want a game before closing time, kid?"

Theo grabbed it. He dialed the angle the way he'd aim a free kick, and the dot soared clean over the net.

"GOAL!" Theo shouted, before remembering tennis doesn't have goals. Higinbotham laughed anyway.

"Not bad for your first game ever," said Byte. "Next stop gets a lot nerdier."

"Bring it," Theo said, already grinning.

chapters.heading: Level 2: Spacewar! (1962)
chapters.text:
The lab dissolved into a room stuffed with reel-to-reel tapes and blinking lights.

"MIT," said Byte. "Massachusetts. The year is **1962**."

In front of them sat a machine the size of a wardrobe, called a **PDP-1** — basically a whole room's worth of computer, back when computers didn't fit on a desk.

A student named Steve Russell was hunched over it, typing with two fingers like he was racing someone.

On the round screen, two tiny spaceships circled a bright dot, taking turns zapping each other with little dashes of light.

"**Spacewar!**," Byte said. "Steve and his friends wrote it for fun, after hours, when nobody official was watching the machine."

Theo leaned closer. The ships drifted too slowly — like someone had forgotten gravity was a thing.

"Your star should pull them in," Theo said. "Like in Roblox, when I script a black hole zone. Things need to curve, not just float."

Steve looked up, startled. "Huh. Kid's got a point."

He typed for a minute, grumbling happily to himself, and added a pull toward the center star.

The ships swung in tighter arcs now, slingshotting around the middle like they meant it.

"That's better," Steve said. "Much better."

Byte nudged Theo with an elbow make of pixels. "Not every kid gets to debug the second video game ever made."

"I didn't debug it," Theo said. "I just said the word 'gravity.'"

"Same thing, around here."

Theo took the controls for one round, spun his ship past the star, and clipped the other ship's engine with a lucky shot.

"That's one for the home team," he said.

Byte was already reaching for the glowing CONTINUE button. "Come on. Somebody's about to turn this into a television habit."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box and the Jammed Machine (1967–1972)
chapters.text:
The room changed to a cluttered workshop full of wires, cardboard, and a small television set balanced on a crate.

"Ralph Baer," Byte said. "An engineer who had one stubborn idea: games should play on your television, at home, not just in a lab."

A man with sleeves rolled up was wiring two paddle-shaped controllers to a plain brown box.

"This is a **prototype**," Byte explained, "which just means a rough first try, built to test if an idea even works."

On the television, two white rectangles batted a square dot back and forth.

"By **1972**," said Byte, "this box became a real product you could buy: the **Magnavox Odyssey**. First home video game console, ever."

Theo picked up a paddle. He nudged the dot, and it bounced off his rectangle with a soft little blip.

"Feels like practicing goal kicks in my backyard," he said. "Except the ball never rolls into the hedge."

The scene shifted sideways, arcade machine cabinets rising up around them like a forest.

"Same year," Byte said. "Different team. **Nolan Bushnell** and **Ted Dabney** started a company called Atari, and they built an arcade version of this same idea."

A glowing cabinet buzzed to life in front of them: **Pong**. Two paddles, one ball, one score counter climbing upward.

"There's a story," Byte said, "that one early Pong machine actually jammed — because so many coins got stuffed inside that the coin tray overflowed. Nobody's totally sure it's true, but it tells you how fast people fell in love with it."

Theo fed in a coin anyway, just to see. The machine beeped, happily, and did not jam.

"Close one," Byte said.

Theo played three rounds and won two of them, mostly by aiming his paddle the way he'd time a slide tackle.

"Two home consoles, one arcade hit, same year," he said. "Busy twelve months."

"You have no idea," said Byte. "Press on."

chapters.heading: Level 4: Cartridges and a Hungry Circle (1977–1980)
chapters.text:
The arcade forest thinned into a bright, noisy room full of kids feeding coins into glowing machines.

"**1977**," Byte said. "Atari just released the **Atari 2600**. Before this, a console only played one built-in game, forever. This one takes **cartridges** — plastic game cases you swap in and out, like changing what's in a backpack."

Theo turned one over in his hands. It looked like a chunky plastic brick, nothing like downloading a Roblox game in three seconds.

"One cartridge, one game," he said. "That's it. No updates. No patch notes."

"Welcome to the slow internet," said Byte.

The lights dimmed, and rows of blocky aliens marched across a screen, lowering step by step.

"**1978**," Byte said. "**Space Invaders**, by a designer named **Tomohiro Nishikado**. It took over arcades everywhere, practically overnight."

Theo grabbed the controls, fired, and dropped three aliens before the row got dangerously low.

"They're not even scary," he said. "Just determined."

"Oddly the right description," said Byte.

The cabinet beside it lit up yellow. A round, pie-shaped character chomped a glowing dot and let out a happy little gulp.

"**1980**," Byte said. "**Pac-Man**, made by **Toru Iwatani**. One story says he got the idea looking at a pizza with a slice missing. Nobody's completely sure that part is true, but it's a fun one to believe."

Theo took the joystick and steered Pac-Man around a corner, gobbling dots in a tidy row.

"CHOMP," he said, under his breath, timing turns the way he'd dribble a soccer ball past a defender.

A ghost drifted toward him. Theo grabbed a flashing power dot, and suddenly he was chasing the ghost instead.

"Turned the tables," Byte said. "Story of this whole era. Everybody's trying something nobody's tried yet."

"Can we keep one of these cartridges?" Theo asked.

"Press CONTINUE," said Byte, "and find out what happens to a few of them."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Crash and the Desert Dig (1983)
chapters.text:
The noisy arcade faded into a quiet store, shelves stuffed with game boxes nobody was buying.

"**1983**," Byte said. "This is the part people call the video game **crash** — which just means the market shrank fast, almost overnight."

Theo looked around at the shelves. "What happened? Did everyone just... stop liking games?"

"Not exactly," said Byte. "Stores got flooded with games that were rushed out too fast, before they were any good. Players got burned, and stopped trusting the shelf."

Theo picked up a box with a cartoonish alien on the front. "Even this one?"

"Especially that one," said Byte. "There's a famous story that a huge pile of unsold cartridges — including that very game — got buried in a landfill in New Mexico. A **landfill** is just a giant, official dump for trash."

"They buried video games? In the desert?"

"People actually dug some of them back up in **2014**," Byte said, "just to check if the story was true. It mostly was."

Theo pictured archaeologists in sun hats, carefully brushing dirt off a plastic cartridge like it was a dinosaur bone. He decided he liked that image a lot.

"So the whole industry just... got buried for a while?" he asked.

"Slowed down, badly," said Byte. "But slowed down is not the same as finished. Somebody was about to show up with a plumber and fix the whole mess."

"A plumber," Theo repeated. "Fixing a video game crash. Sure. Why not."

"Press CONTINUE," Byte said, grinning with its whole blocky face, "and meet him."

chapters.heading: Level 6: Falling Blocks and a Jumping Plumber (1984–1985)
chapters.text:
The store vanished, replaced by a small, cold computer room with frost on the windows.

"Moscow," Byte said. "**1984**. Meet **Alexey Pajitnov**."

A man at a boxy computer was arranging colored blocks that fell from the top of the screen, snapping them into tidy rows.

"**Tetris**," Byte said. "Puzzle pieces falling, forever, and you just keep fitting them together."

Theo took the controls and rotated a block, the way he'd line up a pass before it even reached his foot.

A full row lit up and vanished with a satisfying little flash.

"Oh, that's addictive," Theo said. "That is unfairly addictive."

"Wait till you see next door," said Byte.

The cold room melted into a sunny office with half-built game posters taped to the walls. A mustached man in overalls jumped across the screen, bonking a floating brick with his head.

"**1985**," Byte said. "**Shigeru Miyamoto** designed this one. **Super Mario Bros.**, starring a plumber named Mario — still the most famous character games have ever made."

Theo grabbed the controller and ran Mario forward, timing a jump over a gap the way he'd time a header.

He landed clean on a turtle shell, which was oddly satisfying, and kept running.

"This came packed in with a whole new console," Byte added. "The **NES**. It's the thing that got people buying games again after that whole desert-landfill situation."

"One plumber," Theo said, "fixing an entire industry."

"Nintendo's words, roughly," said Byte. "Also kind of mine."

Theo cleared one more jump, grinning the whole time, and didn't even notice he'd been playing for twenty straight minutes.

"Okay," he admitted. "I get it now."

chapters.heading: Level 7: A Fast Blue Hedgehog and a New Box (1991–1994)
chapters.text:
The office dissolved into a wall of glowing screens, each one faster and brighter than the last.

"**1991**," Byte said. "Sega needed somebody to compete with that plumber. So they built somebody completely different."

A blue hedgehog zipped across the nearest screen in a blur, grabbing rings as he went.

"**Sonic the Hedgehog**," said Byte. "Fast on purpose. Mario strolls. Sonic sprints."

Theo grabbed the controller and held the run button down, watching the hedgehog loop through a corkscrew track.

"This is basically what happens when I turn on sprint-boost in my own Roblox level," he said. "Except somebody actually drew the loops by hand."

The screens shifted again, and a disc-shaped console appeared, spinning gently in the air.

"**1994**," Byte said. "**Sony** jumped into consoles with the **PlayStation**. It used **CDs** instead of cartridges — which meant way more room for video, music, and voices."

Theo turned the disc over, catching the rainbow shimmer on its underside. "No more chunky plastic bricks."

"Progress," Byte agreed.

One more screen lit up, showing a maze of dark corridors and two players racing each other through it, laughing through tinny speakers.

"**Doom**, from **1993**," Byte said. "It's famous for letting friends plug their computers together and play against each other in the same room — people called those **LAN parties**, and they were basically indoor camping trips with extension cords."

Theo laughed. "That's just a Roblox game night, but with way more cables."

"History repeats," Byte said, "just with better Wi-Fi."

Theo took one last lap as Sonic, grabbed a ring with a satisfying chime, and finally let go of the button.

"Okay," he said. "What's left?"

"The part where it all turns into you," said Byte.

chapters.heading: Level 8: Shaking Controllers and Infinite Blocks (2006–2015)
chapters.text:
The screens scattered like confetti, and Theo found himself in a bright living room, a strange white remote in his hand.

"**2006**," Byte said. "Nintendo's **Wii**. First controller that cared where your whole arm was, not just your thumbs."

Theo swung the remote like a tennis racket, and on the screen, a tiny character swung back exactly the same way.

"People who'd never touched a game before loved this one," Byte said. "Grandparents. Whole living rooms full of people, swinging at nothing."

Theo swung again, grinning, nearly knocking over a lamp that wasn't really there.

The living room melted into soft green hills made of blocks, stretching out farther than he could see.

"You'll like this part," Byte said. "**2011**. A developer named **Markus Persson** — people called him 'Notch' — released a game called **Minecraft**. Blocky world, build anything you want."

"I know Minecraft," Theo said. "Everyone knows Minecraft."

"Everyone," Byte agreed. "It went on to become the best-selling video game ever made. One guy, one idea, blocks everywhere."

Theo punched a block out of a nearby hill, the way he had a thousand times before on a screen, except this time dirt actually crumbled in his hand.

"Kind of like what I do in Roblox Studio," he said. "Just... earlier."

"Everything you build stands on something older," said Byte. "**2015**, a museum called The Strong, in Rochester, New York, opened a whole hall of fame just for games like these. Tennis dots. Plumbers. Hedgehogs. Blocky worlds."

"All in one building?"

"All in one building."

Byte held up the glowing CONTINUE button one last time. "Ready to go build your own level of history?"

Theo pressed it.

WHOOOSH — and his bedroom folded back into shape around him, soccer trophies and all.

The old grey controller sat on his desk, screen dark, CONTINUE button dim but not gone.

On his monitor, his half-finished Roblox stadium waited, cursor blinking in the goal he'd never quite scripted right.

Theo cracked his knuckles and opened a brand new script file.

"Okay," he said to the empty room. "My turn to make one.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow after school, he had a whole game to build.

story.title: Zara and the Ember Geode
story.subtitle: A rockhound's journey into the fire inside the Earth.

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Rock That Glowed
chapters.text:
Zara lay on her bedroom floor, sorting her rocks into piles. Pink ones here. Gray ones there. One black, shiny rock sat all alone.

It was new. Grandma had found it on a hike and said, "This one feels warm."

Zara picked it up. It WAS warm. Then it got warmer. Then it glowed like a tiny coal, orange cracks running through the black.

"Whoa," Zara whispered.

The glow spread into a shimmering doorway, right there on her bedroom carpet. Through it, Zara could see red rivers and smoking mountains.

"Those are **volcanoes**," said a warm, crackly voice from inside the rock. "Openings in the ground where hot melted rock escapes. Want to see how they work?"

Zara grinned so wide her cheeks hurt. A rock that talked AND opened doors? This was the best rock in her whole collection.

"I'm Ember," said the voice. "Grab your rock bag. We're going down."

Zara stepped through the glowing door. The carpet turned to warm stone under her feet.

"That melted rock is called **magma** while it's still underground," Ember said. "Once it comes out on top, we call it **lava**. Same stuff. New name."

"Like how I'm Zara at home and Zara-saurus when I'm being silly?" Zara asked.

"Exactly like that," said Ember, and the orange cracks flickered like a laugh.

Far below them, a real river of lava glowed and crept across black rock, slow as syrup.

"Can it hurt us?" Zara asked.

"Not from way up here," said Ember. "We're just watching. Watching is always safe."

Zara nodded and tucked that rule into her pocket, right next to her new favorite rock.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Ring of Fire
chapters.text:
Ember carried Zara up high, above the glowing river, until the whole round Earth curved below them like a giant marble.

"Look," said Ember. Tiny red dots circled the edge of the ocean like a necklace.

"Those are volcanoes," Ember explained. "Most of them sit where Earth's **plates** meet. Plates are giant puzzle pieces of rock that the whole ground sits on. They push, pull, and slide, super slowly."

"Slower than my baby cousin crawling?" Zara asked.

"Much slower," laughed Ember. "This circle of volcanoes is called the **Ring of Fire**. It curves all around the edge of the Pacific Ocean, and it holds about **75 out of every 100 volcanoes** on Earth that are still active."

Zara counted the red dots with her finger, bouncing in the air. "That's SO many!"

"One country has more than anybody," Ember said. "**Indonesia**. It has more active volcanoes than any other place on Earth."

"More than anybody anybody?" Zara gasped.

"Anybody anybody," Ember agreed.

Zara spotted a cluster of red dots close together, practically glowing shoulder to shoulder.

"Can we visit one?" she asked. "A real one? Please?"

Ember's cracks brightened like a smile. "I was hoping you'd ask. Hold on to your rock bag."

The curved Earth tilted, and they zoomed down toward a chain of green islands sitting alone in a wide blue ocean, far from any plate edge at all.

"Wait," Zara said. "Didn't you say volcanoes are at the edges?"

"Most of them," said Ember. "But not these. These are something different. Come see."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: Hawaii's Hot Spot
chapters.text:
They landed on black, bumpy rock, warm under Zara's sneakers. Steam curled up from cracks in the ground.

"Welcome to **Hawaii**," said Ember. "These islands didn't form at a plate edge. They formed over a **hotspot** — a spot deep inside the Earth where hot rock keeps rising up, like a candle flame that never blows out."

Zara pressed her hand near a warm crack, not touching, just feeling the heat on her palm.

A deep rumble rolled through the ground, and Zara jumped.

"That's just **Kilauea** saying hello," said Ember. "It's one of the most active volcanoes on the whole planet. It has been erupting, off and on, for **decades** — that means for many, many years."

"Is it mad?" Zara asked.

"Nope," said Ember. "Just busy. Over there is its big brother."

Zara looked up, and up, and UP at a mountain so wide it seemed to go on forever.

"That's **Mauna Loa**," said Ember. "The biggest active volcano on Earth. It rises over **4,000 meters** above the sea — that's taller than thirteen Empire State Buildings stacked up."

"It's not even pointy," Zara noticed. "It's all wide and gentle, like a shield."

"Good eye, rockhound," said Ember. "Wide, gentle ones like this are called **shield volcanoes**. Pointy, steep ones, like Japan's Mount Fuji, are called **stratovolcanoes**. Same fire inside. Different shapes outside."

Zara scooped a tiny piece of cooled black rock into her bag. "Hawaii rock," she whispered happily. "Added to the collection."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Letters From Across the Bay
chapters.text:
The air shimmered, and suddenly Zara stood on a hillside above a sparkling blue bay. A great gray mountain loomed on the far shore.

"That's **Vesuvius**," said Ember, quieter now. "Back in the year **79**, it erupted so hard it covered two whole Roman towns, **Pompeii** and **Herculaneum**, in thick ash."

Zara's eyes went wide. "Were people there?"

"They were," said Ember gently. "But a young man named **Pliny the Younger** watched from far across the bay, safe on this very hill, and wrote down everything he saw. Big dark clouds. Ash falling like snow."

"He just watched and wrote?" Zara asked.

"That's exactly right," said Ember. "And it mattered. Scientists still use his letters today. They even named his kind of huge, explosive eruption after him."

Zara looked at the quiet mountain, imagining the ash clouds Pliny saw.

"I'd watch from far away too," Zara decided. "And I'd write it ALL down, just like him."

"That's the rockhound way," said Ember. "Watch close enough to learn. Far enough to be safe."

Zara nodded firmly, tucking the rule next to the one from before.

The mountain sat still and gray under the sun, sleeping for now, its story already written by a curious boy who never looked away.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Loudest Bang Ever Heard
chapters.text:
"Cover your ears," said Ember, "just in case."

"In case of WHAT?" Zara asked, covering them anyway.

They stood on a ship's deck, far out at sea, the sky turning strange and orange.

"This is **1883**," said Ember. "An island volcano called **Krakatoa** is about to make the loudest sound in recorded history."

A distant island cracked and roared, far, far away across the water.

"It was so loud," said Ember, "that people heard it almost **3,000 miles** away, on a tiny island called Rodrigues. That's like someone in Hawaii hearing a bang from New York."

"That's not even possible!" Zara gasped, giggling.

"And yet it happened," said Ember.

The sky shifted again, and they stood somewhere colder, with frost on the grass.

"Different volcano, different trick," said Ember. "In **1815**, a volcano called **Tambora**, also in Indonesia, had the biggest eruption ever recorded. It threw so much ash into the sky that it blocked some sunlight, even far away in Europe and America."

"It got cold there?" Zara asked, pulling her sleeves down.

"So cold that **1816** got called the **Year Without a Summer**," said Ember. "Snow in summer. Crops struggled to grow."

Zara shivered, then laughed. "One mountain did THAT? From all the way over there?"

"One mountain," Ember confirmed. "Volcanoes don't just shake the ground. Sometimes they shake the whole sky."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Scientist Who Watched Closely
chapters.text:
Green hills rolled by below them now, with one gray, snow-capped mountain standing taller than the rest.

"**Mount St. Helens**," said Ember. "The year is **1980**. Scientists have been camping nearby, watching it closely, because the mountain has been rumbling for weeks."

"Like it's about to sneeze?" Zara asked.

"A little like that," said Ember, smiling. "On **May 18th**, the whole side of the mountain let go in the biggest landslide — a giant slide of rock and dirt — ever recorded. Then the volcano erupted right behind it."

Zara watched, safe and far above, as the mountain's shape changed before her eyes.

"It blew about **1,300 feet** right off the top," said Ember. "That's like knocking the top floors clean off a skyscraper."

"Whoa," Zara breathed. "Were the scientists okay?"

"Many scientists study volcanoes just like this one, very carefully, to understand them better and to help keep people safe," said Ember. "That's exactly why people study volcanoes at all. So we can learn their warning signs."

"What ARE the warning signs?" Zara asked, pulling out a little notebook from her rock bag.

"Tiny earthquakes, for one," said Ember. "Scientists use machines that feel the ground wobble, even the tiniest wobbles humans can't feel. They also use machines flying way up in space, called satellites, to see if the ground is swelling up like a balloon."

Zara wrote it all down in careful, wobbly letters: EARTHQUAKES. SWELLING GROUND. WATCH CLOSE.

"You're turning into a real volcano scientist," said Ember.

Zara beamed so bright she almost glowed like the rock herself.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Island That Grew From Nothing
chapters.text:
The ocean stretched out gray and choppy below them, cold wind whipping Zara's hair.

"**1963**," said Ember. "Watch the water."

Steam burst up from the waves. Then rock. Then more rock, piling higher every minute.

"A whole new island is being born," said Ember. "Right now. Near **Iceland**. They'll name it **Surtsey**."

"A volcano made an ISLAND?" Zara shouted. "From nothing?"

"From underwater lava, piling up and up until it poked above the waves," said Ember. "Iceland has tons of volcanoes, because it sits right where two giant plates are slowly pulling apart, like two puzzle pieces sliding away from each other."

Zara watched the new island hiss and steam, rock stacking on rock.

"Can I keep a piece?" she asked.

"This piece is much too new and much too hot," said Ember. "Give it a few hundred years to cool."

Zara laughed. "I don't think I can wait THAT long."

"Good thing you've already got plenty of rocks at home," said Ember.

The island kept growing behind them as they lifted away, a brand-new piece of the world, built from fire and water and time.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: The Tallest Mountain Anywhere
chapters.text:
The sky turned dusty orange-red, and the ground beneath Zara's feet crunched like dry powder.

"Where ARE we?" Zara asked.

"We're not on Earth anymore," said Ember. "Welcome to **Mars**."

Zara gasped. Ahead of them rose a mountain so enormous it didn't even look real, its top lost in the pink sky.

"That's **Olympus Mons**," said Ember. "The biggest volcano anyone has ever found, anywhere. It stands about **13.6 miles** high. That's almost three Mount Everests stacked on top of each other."

"THREE Mount Everests?" Zara yelled, spinning around to try and see the whole thing at once. She couldn't.

"Even bigger than Mauna Loa," said Ember. "Space has its own giants too."

Zara took one last look, then noticed something odd under a nearby cliff on Earth, back where they'd started their trip. Dark soil, almost black, with little green shoots poking through.

"Is that from a volcano too?" she asked.

"It is," said Ember. "Old volcanic ash breaks down into soil that's wonderful for growing plants. That's why farmers live near some volcanoes, even the ones that might erupt again someday. The ground is just that good for growing food."

"So volcanoes help too," Zara said slowly. "Not just big bangs."

"Big bangs, new islands, good dirt, warm rocks," said Ember. "Earth's fire does a lot of jobs."

The glowing doorway shimmered back into view, carpet and bedroom showing through it.

"Time for bed, rockhound," said Ember softly.

Zara stepped through, back onto her own soft carpet, her rock bag heavy and full. The black, shiny rock sat cool and quiet in her hand now, its cracks dimmed to a sleepy orange glow.

She set it gently on her shelf, right beside all her other favorites, and climbed into bed with volcano dreams already bubbling up inside her.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Zara. Goodnight, rockhound. Sleep tight, and dream of fire deep under the ground.

story.title: Juno, Milo, and Theo and the Glowing Volcano Brick
story.subtitle: A rumbly, bouncy, bedtime trip inside the Earth

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Glowing Brick
chapters.text:
It was way past bedtime.

Milo was still building a LEGO mountain. Juno lined up her tiny dinosaurs on the rug. Theo had been building a volcano level on his tablet, lava pixels and all.

Then one brick on Milo's mountain started to glow. It glowed orange, like a tiny sun. "Whoa," said Theo, setting the tablet down.

Milo tapped the brick. POP! A little round rock jumped out. It had a big smile and tiny legs.

"Hi!" said the rock. "I'm Pip. I'm light as a feather, so I bounce instead of walking." He bounced on the carpet like a basketball.

Juno giggled. "You look like a dino egg!"

"Close," said Pip. "I come from a volcano. Want to see one? A real volcano makes the ground glow, just like my brick did."

Milo's eyes went wide. "Can we go inside it?"

"Hold my hand," said Pip. "Well — hold my bounce."

The three kids grabbed on. The glowing brick went WHOOOOSH. The bedroom melted into orange light.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: The Mountain That Breathes
chapters.text:
They landed on warm, crunchy ground. Steam puffed up nearby, like a kettle.

"A volcano," said Pip, "is a hole in Earth's hard, rocky skin. Hot melted rock and gas sneak out through it."

"Melted rock?" asked Juno. "Like melted cheese?"

"Kind of!" said Pip. "Underground, we call it magma. That's runny, glowing-hot rock. Once it spills outside, we call it lava."

Theo nodded. "So magma is the rock's secret name, before it comes out to play."

"Exactly," said Pip, bouncing happily. "And when a volcano erupts, that means it spits out hot rock, smoke, and steam."

Milo knelt down. He patted the warm ground, careful not to touch anything hot. "Could I build this with LEGO?"

"You could build anything," said Pip. "But first — look up."

Far off, a mountain glowed red at the top. Juno gasped. "It's like a sleepy dragon, breathing!"

Pip laughed, a sound like gravel in a tin can. "Not a dragon. Just Earth, breathing out heat."

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Ring of Fire
chapters.text:
Pip bounced them onto a cloud shaped like a map.

"Look," he said. "Most volcanoes sit along the edges of giant puzzle pieces. We call them plates. Earth's outside is made of them."

Theo squinted at glowing dots circling the ocean. "It looks like a controller outline. One big loop."

"Good eye!" said Pip. "That loop is called the Ring of Fire. It circles the Pacific Ocean. About seventy-five out of every hundred of the world's awake volcanoes live right there."

Juno counted dots with her finger. "One, two, three... so many!"

"One country has more than any other," said Pip. "Indonesia. It has more volcanoes than anywhere else on Earth."

Milo pointed at a cluster of dots. "That's so many! Like LEGO studs on a baseplate."

Pip grinned. "Plates push, and pull, and slide. Wherever they rub together, a volcano might pop up."

Theo whistled. "BUMPER CARS!"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: Hawaii's Gentle Giant
chapters.text:
Next, Pip bounced them onto black, bumpy rock, warm under their feet.

"Welcome to Hawaii," said Pip. "These volcanoes didn't grow at the edge of a plate. They grew over a hotspot — a spot deep down that stays extra hot, like a fire that never goes out."

"Like a nightlight that never turns off?" asked Milo.

"Just like that," said Pip. "One here, called Kilauea, has been erupting almost all the time, for years and years."

Juno peeked over a ridge. Orange lava glowed and oozed, slow as syrup. "It's not scary," she said. "It's kind of pretty."

"It erupts gently, mostly," said Pip. "Not every volcano explodes big."

Theo looked at a huge, wide mountain nearby. "What's that one?"

"Mauna Loa," said Pip. "The biggest awake volcano on Earth. It rises over four thousand meters above the sea."

Milo spread his arms wide. "Round and wide, like a shield!"

"Exactly that shape," said Pip, bouncing proudly.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: A Brand New Island
chapters.text:
Pip bounced them over open water, blue and sparkling.

"Watch the sea," said Pip. "Something new is about to be born."

Bubbles fizzed. Then: FIZZ, SPLOOSH! Steam shot up from the waves.

"In 1963, near Iceland, a volcano under the sea kept erupting," said Pip. "It pushed up so much rock, a whole new island grew. They named it Surtsey."

Juno clapped. "A baby island!"

"Iceland has lots of volcanoes," said Pip, "because two giant plates there are slowly pulling apart. Where they pull, melted rock can rise up."

Theo watched steam curl into the sky. "That's wild. A country just grows new land?"

"Sometimes," said Pip. "Slowly, and safely, far from any boats."

Milo grinned. "I want to build Surtsey with LEGO when we get home. Bubble by bubble."

"Good plan," said Pip, bouncing in a circle. "Bubble by bubble is exactly how it happened."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Biggest Volcano Ever
chapters.text:
Pip bounced them up, up, up — past clouds, past stars.

"Where are we going?" asked Theo.

"Mars," said Pip. "This planet has the biggest volcano anyone knows about."

Below them loomed a mountain so tall, it poked through clouds.

"That's Olympus Mons," said Pip. "About thirteen miles high. Stack Mount Everest on Mount Everest on Mount Everest. Still not as tall."

Theo's jaw dropped. "That's basically a cheat code of a mountain."

Juno tipped her head back, all the way. "It doesn't even fit in my eyes!"

Milo tried to imagine it in LEGO bricks. "I'd need every brick in the world."

Pip bounced proudly. "Mars has no plates sliding around, like Earth's. So one volcano just kept growing. And growing."

"FOREVER VOLCANO!" said Juno.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The Sleepy Giant Underground
chapters.text:
Back on Earth, Pip led them to a wide, grassy valley with steamy pools.

"This is Yellowstone," said Pip. "It sits on top of a supervolcano — a giant volcano hiding deep under the ground."

Juno's eyes went round. "Is it going to erupt? Right now?"

"No," said Pip quickly. "Its last big eruption was about six hundred forty thousand years ago. Scientists watch it closely. They see no sign it will erupt again soon."

Juno let out a breath. "Phew. Sleepy giant, stay sleepy."

Theo tapped his chin. "How do scientists even watch something underground?"

"Good question," said Pip. "They use listening machines that feel tiny shakes in the ground. They also use sky machines. Those machines watch the ground puff up, like rising bread."

Milo nodded slowly. "So the volcano can't sneak up on anybody."

"Exactly," said Pip. "Earth always gives little warnings first."

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: Home, With a Souvenir
chapters.text:
Pip bounced them toward a patch of dark, crumbly dirt.

"One more thing," he said. "When volcano ash breaks down, it makes wonderful dirt for growing plants. That's why some farmers live near volcanoes, even sleepy, rumbly ones."

Milo looked at a field of green plants growing right by the warm ground. "Dangerous dirt makes yummy food?"

"Sometimes the risky places grow the best gardens," said Pip.

Then the ground beneath them began to glow and hum again, the same orange glow from Milo's brick.

WHOOOOSH! The world spun. They landed, soft and safe, right back on the bedroom carpet.

Pip bounced once more, smaller now, and settled onto the rug as a tiny, smiling LEGO brick.

"Thanks, Pip," whispered Juno, patting him gently.

Milo tucked the glowing brick onto his nightstand. "Same time tomorrow?"

"Always," said Pip, with a sleepy sparkle.

Theo yawned, a huge yawn, and put his tablet down for the night.

story.ending_line: Goodnight, Juno. Goodnight, Milo. Goodnight, Theo. Sleep soft, and dream in orange light.
